paragraphs.text: Maximus, On Various Difficulties in Dionysius and Gregory, to Thomas the Sanctified. To Thomas, a Holy Man. To the sanctified servant of God, spiritual father and teacher, the lord Thomas: Maximus, humble and a sinner, an unworthy servant [?]

By diligent zeal for divine things you have acquired an unchangeable habit of unerring contemplation, and so, most beloved of God, you have become a most temperate lover not simply of wisdom but of its beauty. The beauty of wisdom is knowledge put into practice, or practice made wise. The mark of both, as being completed by the two together, is the principle of divine providence and judgment. In accordance with it you have woven mind together with sense through the Spirit, and have truly shown how God is able by nature to make man in the image of God. You have made the wealth of goodness known, richly showing in yourself, by the beautiful blending of opposites, God embodied in the virtues. Having measured yourself to his height by imitating his self-emptying, you did not disdain to come down even to me, asking about things of which you already have knowledge through experience. These are passages from Dionysius and Gregory, those holy, supremely celebrated and

blessed men, truly of the elect, of those who from the beginning, according to the purpose of the ages, were joined to God. They truly received the whole outpouring of wisdom attainable by the saints, and by laying aside the soul's natural life they made this their very being. For that reason they had Christ alone living in them, and, what is greater still, he became the soul of their soul and was made manifest to all through all their deeds, words and thoughts. From this one is persuaded that the things set forth are not theirs but Christ's, who by grace exchanged himself for them. But how shall I say "Lord Jesus" when I have not yet received the Spirit of holiness? How shall I speak of the mighty acts of the Lord, I who am slow of speech and have nailed my mind to attachment to perishable things? How shall I make any of his praises heard, I who am deaf, and through my love of the passions have the hearing of my soul wholly turned away from the blessed voice of the Word? How will the Word become manifest to me, who am defeated by the world? His nature is to conquer the world, not to be manifest to the world, since to a disposition that loves matter he is by nature unknowable. How is it not presumptuous for the defiled to lay hands on what belongs to the holy, and the unclean on what belongs to the pure? I would therefore have declined to undertake what was commanded, fearing the reproach of rashness, had I not feared still more the danger of disobedience. Caught between these two, I choose the reproach of rashness as more tolerable, and flee the danger of disobedience as unpardonable. By the intercession of the saints and the help of your prayers, and with Christ our great God and Savior granting me to understand piously and to speak fittingly, I will make my answer on each passage as concise as possible, for my discourse is addressed to a teacher able to draw great things from small. I begin with Gregory of godly mind, since he is nearer to us in time. Of the holy Gregory the Theologian, from the first oration On the Son, on the passage: "Therefore the monad, moved from the beginning to a dyad, came to rest at a triad." And again of the same, from the second

oration On Peace, on the passage: "The monad being moved because of its richness, the dyad being surpassed, for it is beyond matter and form, from which bodies come, and the triad being defined because of its perfection." Servant of God, if you have considered the apparent disagreement and were perplexed about the true agreement, in meaning no expressions could be found more at one than these. For the dyad being surpassed is the same as not stopping at the dyad, and again the triad being defined is the same as the movement of the monad coming to rest at the triad. For the monarchy we honor is neither ungenerous, circumscribed in one person, nor disorderly, as if pouring out to infinity. It is the monarchy constituted by the Trinity equal in honor by nature, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, whose wealth is their oneness of nature and the single outleaping of their splendor. The Godhead neither pours out beyond these, lest we bring in a mob of gods, nor is it confined within less than these, lest we be condemned for impoverishing the Godhead. This, then, is not an account of the cause of the superessential cause of beings, but a demonstration of pious belief about it. For the Godhead is a monad but not a dyad, and a Trinity but not a multitude, as being without beginning, incorporeal and free of strife. The monad is truly monad, for it is not the source of the things after it by contraction following expansion, so as to be naturally poured out and proceed into multitude; it is the enhypostatic identity of the consubstantial Trinity. And the Trinity is truly Trinity, not completed by a number that can be resolved, for it is not a composition of monads that could undergo division; it is the consubstantial existence of the tri-hypostatic monad. For the Trinity is truly monad, because that is how it is, and the monad is truly Trinity, because that is how it subsists, since there is one Godhead, existing monadically and subsisting triadically. If you heard the word "movement" and wondered how the Godhead, which is infinitely beyond the infinite, is moved, understand that the motion is in us, not in it. We are first illumined with the principle of its being, and then enlightened about the mode of how it subsists, since being is always conceived before the how of being. The movement of the Godhead, then, is the knowledge that comes by manifestation to those able to receive it, concerning both that it is and how it subsists. Of the same, from the same first oration, on the passage: "In sum: apply the loftier expressions to the Godhead and to the nature superior to

passions and body, and the lowlier to the composite one, who for your sake was emptied and became flesh, and it is no worse to say, became man." The Word of God, being wholly full essence, for he is God, and wholly undiminished hypostasis, for he is Son, emptied himself and became the seed of his own flesh. Being compounded with it by an ineffable conception, he became the hypostasis of the flesh he assumed. By this new mystery he truly became wholly man without change, and the same one was the hypostasis of two natures, uncreated and created, impassible and passible, receiving without deficiency all the natural principles of the natures whose hypostasis he was. If he essentially received all the natural principles of the natures whose hypostasis he was, then the teacher very wisely attributed the passions of his own flesh to him who had become composite by the assumption of flesh according to hypostasis, lest they be thought to belong to the flesh alone. For the flesh was his, and according to it he was truly God passible, [?] sin. Showing, then, the difference between nature, according to which the Word remained simple even when incarnate, and hypostasis, according to which he became composite by the assumption of flesh and was called passible by the economy, the teacher says these things: "lest, predicating what belongs to the hypostasis out of ignorance of the nature, we unwittingly, like the Arians, worship a God passible by nature." He added, "It is no worse to say, became man," not only because of the Arians, who teach the Godhead in place of a soul, and the Apollinarians, who teach that the soul is without mind, and so curtail the perfection of the Word's nature that is like ours and make him passible in the nature of the Godhead. He added it also to show us that the only-begotten God has become perfect man in truth, accomplishing our salvation himself through flesh that is active by nature and ensouled with mind and reason. For he truly became man in all things except sin alone, whose principle was never sown in the nature at all; but not without natural energy, whose principle is the definition of the essence, marking out by nature all those in whom it is essentially inherent. For what is predicated of things commonly and generically is the definition of their essence, and its removal certainly brings about the corruption of the nature, since nothing that exists, if deprived of what belongs to it by nature, remains preserved as what it was. Of the same, from the same oration, on the passage: "For he who is now despised by you was once even

above you. He who is now man was also uncompounded. What he was, he remained; what he was not, he assumed. In the beginning he was without cause, for what is the cause of God? But later he also came to be for a cause. And the cause was that you, the insolent, might be saved, you who despise the Godhead for this very reason, that it accepted your grossness. Having consorted with flesh through the medium of mind, the God below became man, since it was blended with God and became one, the stronger prevailing, so that I might become God as much as he became man." "For he who is now despised by you," he says, "was once even above you": that is, existing beyond every age and of himself beyond nature, even if now for your sake he has willingly come under both. "He who is now man was also uncompounded": simple both in nature and in hypostasis, as being God alone, bare of body and of everything belonging to body. Now, by assuming flesh with an intellectual soul, he became what he was not, composite in hypostasis, while remaining what he was, simple in nature, in order to save you, man. For the sole cause he had of his birth in the flesh was the salvation of the nature, whose passibility he took upon himself like a kind of grossness. Through the medium of mind he consorted with flesh, the God below becoming man, and becoming for the sake of all everything that we are except sin: body, soul, mind, all of which death had passed through; and the common product of these, man, God made visible because of what is grasped by mind. The Word himself, then, properly emptied without change into our naturally passible condition, and truly brought under natural sense-perception through the incarnation, was called visible God and God below, having made his infinitely transcendent power manifest through flesh passible by nature. For the flesh was manifestly blended with God and became one, the stronger prevailing, since the Word who assumed it properly deified it by hypostatic identity. The teacher said "one" in the masculine, not "one thing" in the neuter, to show that even in the identity of the one hypostasis the natural otherness of the things united remained unconfused, since the one indicates the hypostasis and the other the nature. As for "so that I might become God as much as he became man," it is not for me to say this, defiled as I am by sin and utterly without appetite for the life that truly is. It is for you, who are recognized by the perfect recovery of the nature through grace alone, and who are to be raised [?] by the power that accords with it as far as the God who is God by nature, made flesh, shared in our weakness. The deification of those saved by grace is measured in return, as he himself knows, against his self-emptying, and they will become wholly godlike and able to contain the whole God, and him alone. For this is the perfection toward which those hasten who believe that this promise will truly be fulfilled.

Of the same, from the second oration On the Son, on the passage: "For as Word he was neither obedient nor disobedient, for these belong to those under authority and to secondary beings: obedience to the better disposed, disobedience to those who deserve punishment. But as the form of a servant he comes down to his fellow servants and servants, and takes on a form not his own, bearing the whole of me in himself with all that is mine, so that he might consume in himself what is worse, as fire consumes wax or the sun the vapor of the earth, and I might share in what is his through the blending. For this reason he honors obedience by deed and experiences it through suffering. For the disposition is not enough, as it is not for us either, unless we also carry it through in actions, since action is the proof of disposition. Perhaps it is not worse to suppose this too: that he tests our obedience and measures everything of ours by his own sufferings, by the art of his love for mankind, so that he may know by his own experience what is ours, and how much is demanded of us and how much is forgiven us, when weakness is reckoned along with suffering." "For as Word," God by nature, he says, he is entirely free of obedience and disobedience, since by nature he is, as Lord, the giver of every commandment, of which obedience is the keeping and disobedience the transgression. For the law that extends to a commandment, with its fulfillment and transgression, belongs to beings moved by nature, not to him whose being is by nature rest. "But as the form of a servant," that is, having become man by nature, he comes down to his fellow servants and servants, taking on a form not his own, and putting on together with the nature also the passibility of our nature. For the penalty of the one who sinned is alien to him who is by nature sinless, and that penalty is the passibility of the whole nature, condemned because of the transgression. But if he was emptied into the form of a servant, that is, a man, and came down to take on a form not his own, that is, became by nature a passible man, then the self-emptying and the condescension are [?] in him as one who is at once good and loving toward mankind: the first shows that he truly became man, the second that he truly became a man passible by nature. Therefore the teacher says:

"bearing the whole of me in himself with all that is mine," that is, the entire human nature, by the union according to hypostasis, together with its blameless passions. By these he consumed what is worse in us, the thing on account of which passibility was brought into the nature. I mean the law of sin that came from the disobedience, whose power is the disposition of our will contrary to nature, which brings passion into the passibility of the nature by slackening and straining it. Having dissolved our penalty in himself, he not only saved those held fast by sin but also imparted divine power, which works immutability of soul and incorruption of body, in the identity of the will with what is good by nature, for those who strive to honor grace by deed. I think the saint is teaching this when he says: "so that he might consume in himself what is worse, as fire consumes wax or the sun the vapor of the earth, and I might share in what is his through the blending," that is, having become by grace free of passion, like him. I also know another explanation of "he takes on a form not his own," which I learned from a holy man, wise both in word and in life. When he was asked, he said that obedience was alien to the Word by nature, as was subjection. Yet he fulfilled it on behalf of us who had transgressed the commandment, and so accomplished the entire salvation of the race, making what is ours his own. "For this reason he honors obedience by deed," having become by nature a new Adam on behalf of the old, "and experiences it through suffering," having willingly submitted to the same sufferings as we. For according to this truly great teacher, "he grew weary, and hungered, and thirsted, and was in agony, and wept" by the law of the body. This is clear proof of an active disposition and evidence of his condescension to his fellow servants and servants. For he remained Master by nature and became a servant for the sake of the one who is a servant by nature, in order to make him master of the one who by deceit had tyrannically mastered him. Therefore, doing servile things in a masterly way, that is, fleshly things divinely, he displayed in the things of the flesh the impassible power that rules by nature, abolishing corruption through suffering and creating indestructible life through death. And doing masterly things in a servile way, that is, divine things in a fleshly way, he displayed his unspeakable self-emptying, deifying through passible flesh the race that through corruption had become earthly. By this interchange he clearly confirmed both the natures of which he himself was the hypostasis and their essential energies, that is, movements, of which he himself was the unconfused union, admitting no division of the two natures of which he was the hypostasis. For he acted in a manner proper to himself, monadically, that is, uniformly, and through each of the things he did, by the power of his own divinity, he inseparably manifested together with it the energy of his own flesh. For since he is one, nothing is more unified than he,

nor again is anything at all more unified or more saving than he with what is his own. For this reason, even when suffering he was truly God, and when working miracles the same one was truly man, because he was the true hypostasis of true natures in ineffable union. Acting through them correspondingly and fittingly, he was shown truly to keep them unconfused [?], since the same one remained impassible and passible by nature, immortal and mortal, visible and intelligible, as God by nature and man by nature. Thus, then, to give my own view, the Master by nature honors obedience and experiences it through suffering. He does so not only to save the whole nature, having cleansed it of what is worse by what is his own, but also to test our obedience. He, who by nature encompasses all knowledge, learns by experience of what is ours what pertains to us: how much is demanded of us and how much is forgiven us with a view to the perfect subjection, through which he brings to the Father those who are saved, who have appeared like him by the power of grace. How great and truly awesome is the mystery of our salvation! For as much is demanded of us as he did by nature in what is ours, and as much is forgiven us as he, beyond us, did in what is ours by union. Unless, perhaps, the habit of a will that loves sin makes the weakness of the nature into matter for evil. And this great teacher is clearly of this mind, confirming it by what follows. For he says: "For if the light was persecuted because of its veil, shining in the darkness, that is, in this life, by the other darkness, I mean the evil one and the tempter, how much more will the darkness be, since it is weaker? And what wonder is it if, when he escaped altogether, we are in some measure overtaken? For it is a greater thing for him to have been persecuted than for us to be overtaken, in the judgment of those who reason rightly." On the letter of Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of Athens, to Gaius the Therapeutes: "How, you ask, is Jesus, who is beyond all, ranked essentially with all men? For he is not called man here as the cause of men, but as being himself truly man in his whole essence." Since according to the simple understanding of Holy Scripture God, as cause of all, is signified by all the names of the things

brought forth from him, Gaius the Therapeutes perhaps supposed that even after the incarnation God is again called man only in this way. The great Dionysius corrects him with these words, teaching that the God of all, made flesh, is not simply called man, but is called so as being himself truly man in his whole essence. The only true demonstration of this essence is the power that naturally constitutes it, which one would not miss the truth in calling natural energy. This is properly and primarily what characterizes the essence, as being the movement that gives it its form, the most generic of all the inclusive properties naturally belonging to it. Without it there is only non-being, since, according to this great teacher, only what in no way exists has neither movement nor existence. He teaches most clearly, then, that God made flesh rejected nothing at all of what is ours except sin, since that did not belong to the nature either, declaring expressly that he was not simply man but himself truly man in his whole essence. Through what follows he insists that the name too properly belongs to him who took essence in human fashion, and says: "But we do not define Jesus in human terms." For we do not teach that he is a mere man, cutting apart the union that is beyond understanding. We use the name "man" of him essentially, not as of the cause of men, since he who is God by nature truly took essence like ours. "For he is not man only," since the same one is also God, "nor superessential only," since the same one is also man, for he is neither a mere man nor bare God, "but truly man, he who is preeminently the lover of mankind." For out of infinite longing for men he became that which by nature is the very object of longing. He suffered nothing in his own essence from the inexpressible self-emptying, and through the unspeakable assumption he neither changed nor diminished anything of the whole of human nature, whose principles properly constitute it. "Beyond men," since he was conceived divinely without a man; "and in accordance with men," humanly, since he was born by the law of gestation. "The superessential, having taken essence from the essence of men": for he did not merely make a phantom shape in the form of flesh appear to us in himself, as the drivel of the Manichaeans has it, nor bring down with him from heaven flesh co-essential with himself, as the myths of Apollinaris have it. He himself became truly man in his whole essence, by assuming flesh endowed with an intellectual soul and united to him according to hypostasis. "And he who is ever superessential was no less overflowing with superessentiality." For in becoming man he was not made subject to the nature; on the contrary, he rather [?]

…took the nature up to himself and made it another mystery. He himself remained wholly incomprehensible. He showed that his own incarnation, which had received a birth beyond being, was more incomprehensible than any mystery. Through it he became comprehensible only to the extent that through it he was known to be still more incomprehensible. “For he is hidden even after his manifestation,” says the teacher, “or, to speak more divinely, even in his manifestation. For this too of Jesus is hidden, and the mystery concerning him has been drawn out by no word and no mind; even when spoken it remains unspeakable, and even when understood it remains unknown.” What could prove the divine transcendence of being more conclusively than this? It reveals hiddenness through manifestation, the unsayable through speech, the transcendent unknowing through the mind, and, greater still, what is beyond being through taking on being. Indeed, through the superabundance of that transcendence, “even having truly come into being, he took on being beyond being.” That is, he made new the laws of natural generation and truly became man without the seed of a man. The Virgin shows this. She conceived the Word who is beyond being in a manner beyond nature, without a man, and he was formed in a human way from her own virginal blood, by an ordinance foreign to nature. “And he did the things of man beyond man.” Without being affected himself, he made the nature of the elements new under his steps. Unstable water clearly shows this. It bore the weight of material, earthly feet and did not give way, but was made firm by a power beyond nature so that it did not flow apart. For with dry feet, having bodily bulk and the weight of matter, he truly passed across the liquid and unstable substance, walking on the sea as on solid ground. By the power of his own divinity, and inseparably from it, he showed through that walking the natural activity of his own flesh as well. Movement from place to place belongs by nature to the flesh, not to the divinity beyond infinity and beyond being that is united to it according to hypostasis. For once the Word who is beyond being had taken on being in a human way, he had, together with the human essence and undiminished, as his own, the motion of that essence which characterizes him generically as a man. This motion took natural form in all that he did as a man. He truly became man: he breathed, spoke, walked, moved his hands, used his senses naturally to perceive sensible things, hungered, thirsted, ate, slept, toiled, wept, and was in agony, although he was self-subsistent power. The same holds for everything else by which he acted in his own person. Just as a soul naturally moves the body that is joined to it by nature, he moved the assumed nature, which truly became and was called his own. Or, to speak properly, he himself became, without change, what the nature really is, and so fulfilled the economy on our behalf without any illusion. So he did not abolish the constitutive

activity of the assumed essence, just as the teacher did not abolish the essence itself when he said, “He took on being beyond being, and did the things of man beyond man.” Instead he showed in both cases the newness of the modes, preserved within the permanence of the natural principles, without which nothing that exists is what it is. Suppose we say that the negation by way of transcendence posits the assumed essence but removes its constitutive activity. Then by what reasoning shall we show that the same negation, applied equally to both, signifies the existence of the one and the complete abolition of the other? Or again, suppose we remove the constitutive motion of the assumed nature because it is not self-moved, being truly moved by the divinity united to it according to hypostasis. Then we shall not confess even the essence itself, since it has appeared as not self-subsistent, that is, not existing by itself, but receiving its being in God the Word himself, who truly took on being from it. We would have an equal reason to reject both. Otherwise we shall confess motion together with the nature, for without motion there is not even a nature. We know that the principle of being is one thing and the mode of how it is is another: the first confirms the nature, the second the economy. The coming together of these two produced the great mystery of the supernatural nature of Jesus. It showed that both the difference of the activities and their union are preserved at the same time. The difference is seen without division in the natural principle of the things united. The union is recognized without confusion in the unique mode of what was done. For what, and which, and where, and how will a nature be once it has been stripped of its constitutive power? “For that which has no power at all neither exists, nor is anything, nor can anything at all be posited of it,” says this great teacher. If none of this makes sense, we must piously confess both the natures of Christ, of which he himself was the hypostasis, and his natural activities, of which he himself was the true union, in accordance with both natures. For he acts in a way fitting to himself, uniquely, that is, in a single form, and in everything he inseparably shows the activity of his own flesh together with the divine power. How will the same one be God by nature and again man by nature if he does not lack nothing of what belongs by nature to each? What and who will he be known to be, if what he does naturally does not confirm that he is unchangeably what he is? And how will he be confirmed in each of the things from which, in which, and which he is, if he remains motionless and inactive? So he took on being beyond being. He created for nature another beginning of generation and another kind of birth. He was conceived by the seed of his own flesh, and when he was born he became a seal of virginity for her who bore him, showing in her that contradictory things which cannot be mixed are true together. For the same woman is both virgin and mother, making nature new by the coming together of opposites,

since virginity and childbirth are opposites, and no one would imagine that nature could join them. Therefore the Virgin is truly the Mother of God (Theotokos). In a manner beyond nature she conceived and bore the Word who is beyond being, who took the place of seed, since the mother who gives birth is properly the mother of what was sown and conceived. “And he did the things of man beyond man.” By the highest union, without change, he showed that the human activity is naturally joined to the divine power. For the nature, united without confusion to the other nature, has wholly interpenetrated it, having nothing at all detached or separated from the divinity united to it according to hypostasis. For the Word who is beyond being, having truly taken on our being in a way beyond us, joined to the affirmation of the nature and of its natural properties the negation by way of transcendence. He became man, having a mode of how he is that is beyond nature, joined to the principle of being of the nature. He did this so that he might confirm the nature by the newness of the modes, while it undergoes no alteration in its principle, and might show that his power beyond infinity is likewise known in the coming-to-be of opposites. Indeed, he made the passions of nature works of his will, not, as with us, results of natural necessity. Contrary to how it is with us, he passed through what in us is passible by nature. In himself he showed as moved by his sovereign will that which in us naturally sets the will in motion. The teacher makes this clear in what follows, where he says: “Why should one go through the rest, which are very many? Through them whoever sees divinely will know, beyond mind, that even what is affirmed of Jesus’ love for humankind has the force of a transcendent negation.” For the Word who is beyond being, having taken on, through an ineffable conception, all that belongs to nature together with the nature, had nothing human, affirmed according to the principle of nature, that was not also divine, denied as beyond nature. The knowledge of these things was beyond mind, since it cannot be demonstrated. Its only grasp is the faith of those who genuinely revere the mystery of Christ. Giving as it were a summary account of this mystery, he says: “For, to put it briefly, he was not even man,” since by nature he was [?] of natural necessity, and was not subjected to the law of generation that governs us; “not as though not man,” since he was truly man in his whole essence, bearing by nature the natural things that belong to us; “but, as being from men,” since he was of one essence with us, being by nature man as we are, “beyond men,”

by the newness of the modes, which we are not, he set bounds to nature. “And having truly become man beyond man”: he held the modes beyond nature and the principles according to nature joined to each other without harm, though their coming together was impossible. He himself, for whom nothing is impossible, became their true union. He did not act through either of the things of which he was the hypostasis in separation from the other, but rather confirmed each through the other. Being truly both, as God he moved his own humanity, and as man he revealed his own divinity. He suffered, so to speak, divinely, for it was voluntary, since he was not a mere man. He worked wonders humanly, for it was through flesh, since he was not God unclothed. So the sufferings are wondrous, made new by the natural divine power of the one who suffered, and the wonders are passible, accomplished by the natural passible power of the flesh of the one who worked them. Knowing this, the teacher says: “And thereafter he did divine things not as God,” that is, not only divinely, separated from flesh, for he was not only beyond being; “nor human things as man,” that is, not only fleshly, separated from divinity, for he was not only man; “but as God become man, he has lived out for us a certain new theandric activity.” For he who supremely loves humankind truly became man by assuming flesh endowed with an intellectual soul. Through the ineffable union, his divine activity became human in its natural union with the activity of the flesh. So he fulfilled the economy for our sake theandrically, that is, he did both divine and human things divinely and humanly at once, or to put it more clearly, he lived out a divine and at the same time a human activity. So the wise man, by denying that divine and human things are divided from each other, affirmed the union. Yet he did not overlook the natural difference of the things united, for the union, though it drove out division, did no harm to the difference. And if the mode of the union keeps the principle of the difference preserved, then the saint’s expression is a circumlocution. Using a fitting term, it points to the twofold activity of Christ, who is twofold in nature, since the essential principle of the things united has in no way been diminished by the union, either in number or in quality. But it does not, as some think, affirm some middle term by negating the extremes. For in Christ there is no middle term affirmed by negating the extremes. “New,” as characteristic of a new mystery, whose principle is the ineffable mode

of the natural union. For who has known how God becomes flesh and remains God, how, remaining true God, he is truly man? He shows himself truly to be both in natural existence, and each through the other, while changed in neither. Faith alone grasps these things, honoring in silence the Word, of whom there is no principle innate in the nature of beings. “Theandric,” however, does not mean simple, nor some composite thing, nor something belonging either to bare divinity alone by nature, or to mere humanity alone, or to some composite nature standing between them. It belongs to God become man, that is, perfectly incarnate, [?] fitting. Nor again does it mean one, as though the word “new” could not be understood otherwise, as some have supposed, than as signifying one. For newness concerns quality, not quantity. Otherwise it would necessarily bring in with it such a nature too, since the defining mark of every nature is the principle of its essential activity, and that is something no one would ever call double unless he were fond of tales of goat-stags. Even granting this, how will the one who is by nature such, having one activity, and that a natural one, accomplish by the same activity the miracles and the sufferings, which differ from each other in the principle of their nature, without a privation occurring through the loss of the natural state? For nothing that exists, held together by the definition and principle of a nature, naturally does opposite things by one and the same activity. Therefore it is not right to speak of simply one activity, or one natural activity, of divinity and flesh in Christ, since divinity and flesh are not the same in natural quality. Otherwise the nature too would be one, and the Trinity would become a quaternity. “For he has not become the same as the flesh,” he says, “either in nature, or in power, or in activity.” For in nothing in which the Son is by nature the same as the Father and the Spirit through the one essence has he become the same as the flesh through the union, even though by its union with him he made it life-giving, though it is mortal by nature. Otherwise he would be shown to be of a changeable nature: he would have altered the essence of the flesh into what it was not, and made the union identical with the nature. So let us understand the theandric activity as it has been explained. He lived it for us, not for himself, and by it he made nature new through things beyond nature. For “living” (politeia) is a life conducted according to the law of nature. Since the Lord is twofold in nature, he fittingly appeared to have a corresponding life, framed at once and without confusion by both divine and human law. This life too was new, not only as strange and astonishing to those on earth and never yet known in the nature of beings, but also as the mark of the new activity of the one who lived in a new way. Perhaps he who devised a fitting name for this mystery called it theandric to show the mode of the exchange that takes place in the ineffable union. This mode makes what belongs by nature to each part of Christ belong in turn to the other, without either part changing into the other or being mixed with it in its natural principle.

Consider a sword heated red-hot in the fire. Its cutting has become burning, and its burning cutting. For just as the fire was united to the iron, so too the burning of the fire was united to the cutting of the iron. The iron became burning by its union with the fire, and the fire became cutting by its union with the iron. Yet neither suffered any change toward the other through the exchange that comes from the union. Each, even within the property of the compound formed by union, has remained without falling away from what is naturally its own. So too in the mystery of the divine incarnation, divinity and humanity were united according to hypostasis. Neither departed from its natural activity because of the union, nor did either possess that activity after the union as unrelated to and divided from the one compounded and subsisting together with it. For the incarnate Word, with the whole active power of his own divinity, had the whole passive power of his own humanity naturally joined to it in an indissoluble union. Being God, he worked the miracles humanly, for they were accomplished through flesh that was passible by nature. Being man, he underwent the passions of nature divinely, for they were fulfilled by divine authority. Or rather, he did both theandrically, since he was God and man at once. By the one he gave us back to ourselves, revealed as what we had become. By the other he gave us to himself, as we became what he showed. Through both he confirmed the truth of the things from which, in which, and which he was, since he alone is true and faithful and wishes to be confessed by us as what he is. Having him, you who are sanctified in word and life, imitate his long-suffering as he is formed in you. Receive the present writing and show yourselves merciful judges of what it contains. Overcome with compassion the slips of your child, who looks for this alone as the reward of his obedience. And be my mediators for reconciliation with him, bringing about the peace that surpasses all understanding. Of that peace the Savior himself is Prince. By practical [?] virtue he frees those who fear him from the turmoil of the passions. He is Father of the age to come, begetting by the Spirit, through love and knowledge, those who have filled the world above. To him be glory, majesty, and might, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to the ages. Amen.

From the same. To John, Archbishop of Cyzicus, Maximus sends greetings in the Lord. Those who are more eager lovers of noble things and more zealous students of the knowledge that concerns them are praised by everyone, perhaps justly, for their love of learning. They approach better people and teachers of better things with greater earnestness, because by asking questions they receive, without shame, knowledge and understanding of what they did not know. In this way they free themselves from ignorance and

inexperience and the reproach that goes with them. But what words could praise you worthily? Or what man will be found able even to grasp in thought the greatness of your virtue? You are tested shepherds of rational sheep. You know how to lead them up and bring them into the fold above with the notes of a spiritual pipe, since you have already acquired the habit of the mystical knowledge of divine things, which others cannot attain. In keeping with this, you have been worthily entrusted with Christ’s Church, and you skillfully steer its helm like a ship’s. You bring it, with its cargo of faith and the beauty of a godly life, to the harbor of the divine will, unharmed by any of the temptations on the sea of life. Yet about the things you know, and which God has appointed you to interpret, you do not consider it beneath you to ask questions. You ask not only the wiser, if anyone at all is higher than you in knowledge, but also those who are worth nothing and who have no learning of any kind. As is your custom, you trust that you will find something notable even among the undistinguished. So I too received your honored letter. It bade me write down and send you the account given at that time of each of the chapters you found difficult in the discourses of St. Gregory the Theologian, which we labored over when we were together. I marveled, as was fitting, at your virtue, and praised the all-radiant and lofty quality of your Christlike poverty in it. Or rather, I praised the Lord who is fittingly glorified through you and in you. He made you, and through the very works and the truth he clearly displays the power of becoming that was granted to you, adorned with his own properties. This reaches even to me, small, worthless, and unlearned, and utterly bare of all virtue and knowledge. Seeing you humble yourselves in this way, I forced myself to accept your command as far as I am able. For your sake I took no account of being thought rash by the many. But you too, as is your custom, grant me the dear and welcome reward of my obedience, for I look for your earnest prayers. Pray that Christ God, the ready help of those who fear him, may come as my ally in this discourse, or rather that he, as the Word, may supply the word with which to speak piously. I ask you, as you read, not to look for elegant diction from me. I do not have words that ring in the ear, and I do not know how to make them resound with elaborate rhythmic divisions. Since I am unpracticed in such learning and inexperienced in its study, I consider it welcome even

…it would be something to pray for if I could grasp even in some small measure the meaning of this holy and great teacher, even in common language, much less venture on lengthy expositions. For this man, the Theologian, as you know, is concise in speech and rich in meaning, and so he compels anyone who wants to unfold his purpose to go through a great many words, however skilled in rhetoric and philosophy that person may be, and above all me, a layman. But if your God-loving zeal moves you, as it usually does, to recast what I have written in a form both concise and eloquent, or even to correct the whole sense toward something loftier, you will receive a full reward: the prayers of the God-bearer to the Master of all, since you did not allow his divine and supernatural thoughts to be swept away by failed and grovelling attempts. In keeping with your letter, I have carried out an inquiry into each chapter and set it down in writing, and I ask you to be kind and generous judges of what I say.

From the oration On Love of the Poor, on the words: "I spare it as a fellow worker, and I do not know how to escape its rebellion, or how not to fall away from God, weighed down by the fetters that drag me down or hold me fast to the ground."

Do not suppose, most excellent friend, that this blessed man meant the same thing by "being held fast" as by "being dragged down", if you have made any effort to understand something worthy of his great mind. Otherwise he would appear wordy, with a mind that did not attend to his words, unless he were taken to have resolved to guide his followers in every way to what is best and most useful by placing a fitting meaning in almost every syllable. But that is not the case, far from it. Rather, he joins speech to a wise mind and sets a loftier mind over lofty speech, so that the lofty may be announced by the lofty, and so that through both the greatness of the truth, until now inaccessible to many or even to all, may be shown to some degree. So that the whole riddle of these words may become clear to us, let us examine the blessed man's words as they stand: "I spare it," he says, "as a fellow worker, and I do not know how to escape its rebellion, or how not to fall away from God, weighed down by the fetters that drag me down or hold me fast to the ground." In saying this he is certainly not speaking only of himself. Through himself he is addressing humanity in common, knowing that everyone who longs for salvation devotes himself wholly either to practice or to contemplation. For no one has ever been able to attain salvation without virtue and knowledge. "If, then," he says, "I am one of those who wait upon God through contemplation and delight in the blessed beauty, having peace and holiness in every way, as having

simplified myself toward God in an undivided identity of will, by fittingly bringing the irrational powers of the soul under reason, leading them through reason to the mind and making them its own (I mean anger and desire), turning the first into love and the second into joy, if indeed it is proper to joy to leap and exult in a godly way, like John, the great forerunner and herald of the truth, who leapt in the womb, or like David, king of Israel, when the ark came to rest. For both we and God the Word, the Maker and Master of the universe, are in a womb in the present condition of life (even if this statement is harsh because it is unfamiliar to most people, it is true nonetheless). He is there dimly, as in a womb, scarcely showing himself through this sensible world, and only to those who are like John in spirit. Human beings are there as in the womb of their material circumstances, glimpsing only to some degree the Word hidden in beings, and even this only if they can boast of John's graces. For compared with the ineffable glory and splendour of the age to come and with the character of the life proper to it, the present life is no different from a womb wrapped in darkness. In it God the Word, though perfect and more than perfect, became an infant out of his love for humankind, for the sake of us who have become infants in mind. If then, as has been said, I am such a person and have climbed to the divine summit attainable by human beings in the present life, but I neglect my godlike state and willingly incline myself toward affection for the body, I have been dragged down, weighed down by the fetters, that is, by cares, and I have fallen from God. For I have assigned the care and search that belong to the kingdom of heaven alone to that to which it was not right to assign them, I mean to earthly life, and I have allowed my mind to be carried along with the senses rather than to be borne toward God. But if I am one of those who are still armed through the practical life, waging war on the passions, and I have not yet cleanly escaped the snares of the enemies who want to capture me through them, and I love the body indiscriminately, then clearly I am held fast by it, because I have preferred attachment to it over the separation that comes through virtue." So the contemplative, who has already become unattached to the body in his settled state, is dragged down when he neglects the divine visions. The practical person who is fighting the body is held fast when he gives way in his struggle against it and chooses to be a slave of the passions rather than to toil for virtue, which is the freedom of the soul.

From the same oration, on the words: "What is this wisdom concerning me, and what is this great mystery? Or does God wish that we, who are a portion of God and have flowed down from above, should always look to him in our struggle and battle with the body, so that we may not be puffed up and exalted because of our dignity and despise the One who created us,

and that the weakness yoked to us should be a training for our dignity?"

Some people who read these words, apparently expecting no reward for the toil of searching for the truth, take refuge in the easy route, which already finds many starting points in the doctrines of the Greeks. They claim that there was once, as they suppose, a henad, a unity of rational beings, in which we were connatural with God and had our abode and foundation in him alone. They further claim that a movement took place, and that the rational beings, scattered from it in various ways, led God to create this bodily world so as to bind them to bodies as punishment for their earlier sins. And they think that the teacher is hinting at this through these words. But they have failed to realize that they are positing impossibilities and conjecturing about things that cannot be, as the true argument will show as it proceeds with reasonable proof. For the divine is unmoved, since it fills all things, while everything that has received its being from non-being is also subject to motion, since it is certainly borne toward some cause. If this is so, then nothing that is in motion has yet come to rest, since it has not yet brought the power of its motion of desire to rest in the ultimate object of desire (for by nature nothing else brings to a stop what is being carried along except that object, once it appears). So nothing in motion has come to rest, since it has not yet attained the ultimate object of desire, because that object has not yet appeared and stopped the motion of the things borne toward it. But if they insist that this did once happen by command, and that the rational beings were moved away from their foundation and abiding in the ultimate and only object of desire and so were scattered (I ask, so as not to be speaking idly, what is the proof?), then they will necessarily, and with good reason, have to suppose that the rational beings will undergo the same falls under the same conditions endlessly. For what they have once been able to despise through experience, no argument will prevent them from being able to despise forever. And what could be more pitiable than for rational beings to be carried about in this way and to have, or hope for, no unchangeable ground of stability in the good? But if they say that the rational beings can fall but do not wish to, because of the experience they have had of the opposite, then the good will necessarily be loved by them not for its own sake, as good, but because of its opposite, as something that is not lovable by nature or in the proper sense. For whatever is not good and lovable for its own sake, and does not draw every motion to itself, is not good in the proper sense. For this reason it cannot reasonably hold fast the desire of those who delight in it. Indeed, those who maintain this opinion would have to confess gratitude to evil

as the thing through which they were taught what they needed and learned how to stay fixed in the good. If they resolved to be consistent with themselves, they would of necessity have to call it a kind of generation [?], and more useful than nature itself, since by their account it teaches what is beneficial and gives birth to the most precious possession of all, I mean love, through which all things that come from God are by nature gathered toward God, abidingly and unchangeably. Again, in the case of the intelligible and sensible things that have come from God, generation is conceived as prior to motion. For motion cannot exist before generation. Motion belongs to things that have come into being: the motion of intelligible things is intelligible, and that of sensible things is sensible. For nothing that has come into being is entirely motionless by its own principle, not even inanimate and sensible things, as it seemed to those who studied beings more carefully. For they said that all things move, either in a straight line, or in a circle, or in a spiral, since every motion is contained in the simple and the composite mode. If, then, the generation of things is conceived as prior to their motion, then their motion is considered after their generation, as being conceptually posterior to it. This motion they call natural power, pressing on toward its proper end; or passion, that is, motion occurring from one thing to another, which has impassibility as its end; or activity, which has the self-perfect as its end. But nothing that has come into being is its own end, since it is not self-caused either. If it were, it would also be unbegotten, without beginning and unmoved, having nothing toward which it could in any way be moved. For such a thing transcends the nature of beings, since it exists for the sake of nothing, if the definition of it is true, even though the one who states it is an outsider: "The end is that for the sake of which all things exist, while it exists for the sake of nothing." Nor is anything created self-perfect, since then it would also be without activity, as being full, and as having its being from nowhere; for the self-perfect is in some sense also uncaused. Nor is it impassible, since then it would also be unique, infinite and uncircumscribed. For the impassible by nature undergoes nothing at all, in that it neither loves another nor is moved toward another by desire. Therefore nothing that has come into being, once in motion, has come to rest, since it has not yet attained the first and only cause from which beings derive their being, nor has it come to be within the ultimate object of desire. So it cannot be supposed that the scattering of rational beings from a pre-existing henad brought the generation of bodies along with it as a consequence. The saints Moses, David and Paul bear witness to this, as does their Master, Christ. Moses recounts that our forefather did not taste of the tree of life, and says elsewhere: "For you have not yet come to the rest and to the inheritance that the Lord our God is giving you." David

cries out: "I shall be satisfied when your glory appears to me," and: "My soul has thirsted for God, the mighty, the living; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?" Paul writes to the Philippians: "If somehow I may attain to the resurrection of the dead. Not that I have already obtained it or have already been perfected, but I press on to lay hold of that for which I was also laid hold of by Jesus Christ." To the Hebrews he writes: "For whoever has entered his rest has also himself rested from his works, as God did from his own," and again, in the same Epistle, he firmly declares that no one has received the promises. And Christ says: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." So nothing that has come into being has ever yet stopped its natural power in its motion toward its proper end, nor ceased from its activity by resting it upon its proper end, nor gathered the fruit of the passion that belongs to motion, I mean impassibility and immobility. For it belongs to God alone to be the end, the perfect and the impassible, since he is unmoved, full and impassible. To things that have come into being it belongs to be moved toward the end that has no beginning, to cease their activity in the perfect end, and to undergo, but not to be or become without quality in their essence; for clearly everything that has come into being and been created is not free of relation. The word "passion" must be understood sensibly. What is meant here is not the passion that involves alteration or corruption of a power, but the passion that naturally exists together with beings. For all things that have come into being undergo motion, since they are not self-motion or self-power. If, then, rational beings have come into being, they are certainly in motion: from their beginning they move by nature, because they exist, and toward their end they move by choice, for the sake of well-being. For the end of the motion of moving things is eternal well-being itself, just as their beginning is being itself, that is, God, who both gives being and graciously bestows well-being, as beginning and end. For from him come both our moving at all, since he is our beginning, and our moving in a certain way toward him, since he is our end. If the intellectual being moves intellectually, in a way proportionate to itself, then it certainly understands. If it understands, it certainly loves what it has understood. If it loves, it certainly undergoes ecstasy toward it as the object of its love. If it undergoes this, it clearly presses onward. If it presses onward, it certainly intensifies the force of its motion. If it intensifies its motion forcefully, it does not stop until it is wholly in the whole beloved and is wholly embraced by the whole of it. It willingly accepts, by its own choice, the whole of this saving circumscription, so that it may be wholly qualified by the One who circumscribes it, so that it no longer wishes at all to be known from itself,

that is, the thing circumscribed wishes to be known wholly from what circumscribes it rather than from itself, like air thoroughly lit up by light, or iron wholly fired through by fire, or anything else of this kind. From these examples we form a conjecture, by way of likeness only, about the participation in goodness that awaits those who are worthy: the participation that will be, not one that once existed and was corrupted. For what is hoped for is beyond all these things, since, as it is written, it lies beyond sight and hearing and thought. And this is perhaps the subjection of which the divine Apostle speaks, by which the Son subjects to the Father those who willingly accept being subjected, after which and through which "the last enemy, death, is abolished." For what is in our power, that is, our free will, through which death made its entry among us and confirmed the dominion of corruption over us, will have yielded entirely and willingly to God, and by ceasing to will anything other than what God wills, it will have the privilege of being ruled well. As the Saviour himself, prefiguring in himself what is ours, says to the Father: "Yet not as I will, but as you will." And after him the divine Paul, as though he had denied himself and no longer knew of having a life of his own, says: "I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me." Do not let what I am saying trouble you. I do not say that free will is abolished, but rather that it is established firmly and unchangeably in accordance with nature, that is, that it yields by deliberate choice, so that we may long to receive our motion from the same source from which we have our being. Then the image will have ascended to the archetype, like the impression of a seal perfectly fitted to its original, no longer having anywhere else to be carried and no longer able to be. Or, to put it more clearly and more truly, it will no longer even be able to wish it, because it has laid hold of the divine energy, or rather has become God by deification. It will delight more in going out of itself, beyond what naturally belongs to it and is conceived of it, because of the grace of the Spirit that has prevailed over it and has shown that it has God alone at work within it. So there will be one single energy throughout all things, that of God and of those worthy of God, or rather of God alone, since he will wholly interpenetrate all the worthy in a manner befitting his goodness. For it is entirely necessary that the self-determining motion of all things by desire toward anything else should cease, once the ultimate object of desire has appeared and is participated in, and is contained, if I may put it this way, uncontainably, in proportion to the capacity of those who participate in it. "Toward this all the conduct and thought of the lofty-minded hastens, and in it all desire comes to rest, and beyond it nothing is carried in any way, for there is nowhere further to go; toward it every movement of the earnest tends, and for those who have reached it there is rest from all contemplation," says this blessed teacher.

For then nothing will be seen outside God, nor anything that seems to counterbalance God and so might lure anyone's desire to incline toward it, since all things, intelligible and sensible alike, will be embraced by him in his ineffable manifestation and presence. In the same way, in the daytime, when the sun has appeared, the light of the stars and the stars themselves are hidden by its great and incomparable light, from which they too derive their being as lights, and the senses cannot even tell that they are there. With God this is even more the case, inasmuch as the gap and difference between the uncreated and the created is infinite. For then, I believe, we will learn the essential existence of beings, what they are, how they are and for what purpose they are, and we will no longer be moved by desire toward anything for the sake of knowledge. For the knowledge of each of the things that come after God, and in each of them, will have been brought to completion for us, and only the infinite, divine and incomprehensible will lie before us, to be enjoyed and participated in proportionately. This is what this God-bearing teacher profoundly explains when he says that "we shall one day know as we are known, when we unite this godlike and divine thing, our mind and reason, to what is akin to it, and the image ascends to the archetype, for which it now has desire."

Let this suffice, then, on the fact that the much-talked-of henad does not exist, and on how the state of things to come will be, as indicated by the thoughts and reasonings of Scripture that are now within our reach. Now, with God guiding me, I shall speak about how, being a portion of God, we have flowed down from God. For anyone who knows that beings were brought from non-being into being by God through reason and wisdom, and who wisely applies the contemplative faculty of the soul to the infinite natural difference and variety of beings, and with the investigating reason conceptually discerns the Logos according to whom they were created, will surely come to know that the one Logos is many logoi. He is discerned in the indivisible difference of created things, because of their unconfused particularity in relation to one another and to themselves. And again he will know that the many are one, through the reference of all things to him, who exists unconfused in himself, the essential and hypostatic God the Word of God the Father, the beginning and cause of all things, in whom all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities

or authorities: all things were created from him and through him and for him. For he holds the logoi of created things, which subsisted before the ages, and in accordance with them, by his good will, he brought into existence from non-being the visible and invisible creation. By reason and wisdom he made, and still makes, all things at the proper time, both universals and particulars. For we believe that a logos of the angels preceded their creation, as did a logos of each of the essences and powers that fill the world above, a logos of human beings, and a logos of everything that has received its being from God, not to mention each individual thing. And he himself, by his infinite transcendence, is ineffable and incomprehensible in himself, beyond all creation and beyond all the difference and distinction that exist and are conceived within it. Yet he himself is also shown forth and multiplied in all the things that come from him, in a manner befitting his goodness and in proportion to each, and he recapitulates all things in himself. Through him they have their being and their continuance; from him created things came to be as they did and for the purpose for which they did; and whether at rest or in motion they participate in God. For all things, because they have come into being from God, participate in God proportionately, whether by intellect, or reason, or sense, or vital motion, or an essential and habitual aptitude, as the great Dionysius the Areopagite, the revealer of God, holds. Each of the intellectual and rational beings, then, angels and humans, by the very logos according to which it was created, which is in God and is with God, both is called and is a portion of God, because its logos pre-exists in God, as has been said. Certainly, if it moves in accordance with that logos, it will come to be in God, in whom the logos of its being pre-exists as its beginning and cause. And if it longs to lay hold of nothing other than its own beginning [?], it does not flow away from God. Rather, by its ascent toward him it becomes God and is called a portion of God, because it participates fittingly in God. For it has laid hold of its own beginning and cause naturally and rationally, through fitting motion, and after reaching its own beginning, and after its ascent and restoration to the logos according to which it was created, it is no longer able to move anywhere else, or to be moved in any way, since its motion toward the divine goal has received as its limit that divine goal itself. The divine Basil also shows this in his interpretation of the holy prophet Isaiah, where he says: "The true Sabbaths are the rest stored up for the people of God… [?] reaches those Sabbaths of rest, the one to whom the world has been crucified, who has clearly withdrawn from worldly things and has arrived at his own place of spiritual rest; and whoever comes to be in it will no longer be moved from his own place, of stillness and tranquillity

[?] BOOK OF AMBIGUA [?]. … existing in that state. So God is the place of all who are counted worthy of such blessedness, as it is written: "Be to me a protecting God and a strong place to save me." In him the logoi of all things are firmly fixed. It is by these that he is said to know all things before they come into being, since they exist in him and with him, who is the very truth of all things. Yet all these things, both those that are and those that will be, were not brought into being at the same moment as their logoi, or as their being known by God. Rather, each is created at its proper time, fittingly and according to its own logoi, as the Creator's wisdom determines, and so receives actual being in itself. For the Creator is always in act, while created things exist in potential but not yet in act. The infinite and the finite cannot exist together, and no argument will ever be able to show that being and what is beyond being can exist together. Nor can anyone bring into one the measureless and what is within measure, the unrelated and what is in relation, or that of which no form of category is predicated and what is constituted through all of these. For all created things are entirely defined by their essence and their coming into being, and are contained by their own logoi and by the logoi of the external things around them. Set aside, then, the highest, apophatic theology of the Word, according to which he is neither spoken nor thought, and is not at all any of the things known in connection with something else [?], since he is beyond being, and is in no way participated in by anything whatever. With that set aside, the many logoi are the one Logos, and the one is many. According to the creative and sustaining procession of the One into beings, which befits his goodness, the One is many. According to the providence by which the many are turned back and led by the hand toward the One, they are one. He is like an all-ruling source, or a center that already holds the starting points of the straight lines that go out from it, and he gathers all things together. We are, then, and are called, a portion of God, because the logoi of our being pre-existed in God. But we are said to have flowed down from above because we have not moved in accordance with the logos, pre-existing in God, by which we came into being. There is another way, too, in which someone taught to approach the logoi of beings piously can easily work through the argument on this point. No one doubts that the one Logos of God is the essence of the virtue in each person. For our Lord Jesus Christ himself is the essence of all the virtues, as it is written: "who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." These things are clearly said of him absolutely, since he is wisdom itself, righteousness itself and holiness itself. They are not said of him in a qualified way, as they are of us when we speak of "a wise man" or "a righteous man." If so, then plainly everyone who shares in virtue by a firm habit unquestionably shares in God, the essence of the virtues, as one who has

genuinely cultivated by choice the natural seed of the good. Such a person has shown that the end is the same as the beginning and the beginning the same as the end, or rather that beginning and end are one and the same, as an unadulterated advocate [?] of God. For the purpose behind each thing is believed to be both its beginning and its end. It is his beginning because from there he received, besides being, the good by participation, by nature. It is his end because by intention and choice he has eagerly finished the praiseworthy course that leads unerringly toward it. By this course he becomes God, receiving from God the being God. To the natural goodness of being in the image he has added, by choice, the likeness that comes through the virtues, through the innate ascent toward his own beginning and his kinship with it. And so in him too the apostolic saying is fulfilled: "For in him we live [?] and move and have our being." He comes to be in God through attentiveness, because he has not corrupted the logos of being that pre-exists in God. He moves in God according to the logos of well-being that pre-exists in God, as he is made active through the virtues. And he lives in God according to the logos of eternal being that pre-exists in God. Here and now, in his most dispassionate state, he is already identical with himself and unmoved. In the age to come, in the deification that will be given, he will lovingly cherish and embrace these logoi that pre-exist in God, or rather God himself, in whom the logoi of good things are fixed. He is a portion of God: as existing, through the logos of his being in God; as good, through the logos of his well-being in God; and as God, through the logos of his eternal being in God. For he has honored these logoi and acted according to them. Through them he has placed himself wholly in God alone, and has wholly imprinted and formed God alone in himself. So he himself is and is called God by grace, and God by condescension is and is called man for his sake. In this the power of the mutually given disposition is shown. Through love of God it deifies man for God, and through love of humankind it humanizes God for man. By a beautiful exchange it makes God man because of man's deification, and man God because of God's becoming man. For the Word of God, who is God, wills always and in all things to bring about the mystery of his embodiment. But someone may abandon his own beginning, even though he is a portion of God through the logos of virtue in him, according to the reason given, and be carried irrationally toward non-being. Such a person is rightly said to have flowed down from above, because he has not moved toward his own beginning and cause, according to which, for which and through which he came into being. He is in unstable drifting and terrible disorder of soul and body. By his voluntary inclination toward the worse,

he has brought about his own failure to attain the cause that is unerring and always the same. Of him the phrase "flowed down" can properly be used. It lay in his power to plant the steps of his soul firmly on God without struggle, yet he willingly exchanged the better, which exists, for the worse, which does not. The holy Dionysius the Areopagite teaches us that these logoi I have spoken of are called by Scripture "predeterminations" and "divine wills." Likewise the circle of Pantaenus, who became the teacher of the great Clement, author of the Stromateis, say that Scripture is accustomed to call them "divine wills." So when some who were proud of outside learning asked them how Christians think God knows beings, the questioners assumed that he knows intelligible things intellectually and sensible things through the senses. The Christians answered that he knows neither sensible things through the senses nor intelligible things intellectually. For he who is beyond beings cannot grasp beings in the way beings do. "Rather, we say that he knows beings as his own wills," they said, and they added the reasoning behind this. If he made all things by will, and no argument will contradict this; and if it is always pious and right to say that God knows his own will; and if he willingly made each thing that has come into being; then God knows beings as his own wills, since he made beings willingly. Starting from this, I think it is with these logoi in view that Scripture says to Moses, "I have known you above all," and of some people, "The Lord knew those who are his," and again to others, "I do not know you." Clearly it was the deliberate movement of each person, either in keeping with God's will and logos or against them, that prepared him to hear the divine voice. I think this God-bearing man had understood these and similar things when he said: "when we unite this godlike and divine thing, our mind and reason, with what is akin to it, and the image ascends to the archetype for which it now longs." At the same time, through these few words, he is teaching and leading away those who suppose that some being has ever reached its full measure. He is also hinting at the account of how we are a portion of God and alluding to the character of the future blessed state. And he is urging toward its unshakable, unmoving and never-failing enjoyment those who are being purified by hope for it and are hastening toward it. For he knew that if, toward that of which we bear reflections in essence and logos, there goes straight, according to logos and nature,

every rational creation of angels and human beings — all those who through inattention [?] have not corrupted any of the divine logoi naturally fitted to them by the Creator for their movement toward the end, but have prudently kept themselves whole and unswerving, knowing that they are and will be instruments of the divine nature — then God wholly pervades them wholly, in the manner of a soul. He uses them as he sees fit, as members of a body that will be sound and useful to the Master. He fills them with his own glory and blessedness, and gives and graciously grants them eternal and ineffable life. That life is entirely free from every characteristic [?] of the present life, which holds together through corruption. It is not sustained by the air we breathe or by streams of blood flowing from the liver. It is sustained by God, who is wholly participated in by them wholly. He becomes to the soul what the soul is to the body, and through the soul as intermediary he comes to the body, in a way that he knows. So the soul receives immutability and the body immortality, and the whole human being is deified, made divine by the grace of God who became man. He remains wholly man in soul and body by nature, and becomes wholly God in soul and body by grace, and by the divine radiance of blessed glory that fittingly fills him throughout. Nothing brighter or loftier than this can be conceived. For what is more desirable to the worthy than deification? In it God, united to those who have become gods, makes the whole his own through his goodness. That is why such a state, which comes through divine contemplation and the enjoyment of gladness that follows it, has rightly been called pleasure and passion [?] and joy. It is pleasure, because it is the end of natural activities (for that is how pleasure is defined). It is passion [?], as an ecstatic power that draws what undergoes toward what acts. This follows the illustrative example already given of air in relation to light and of fire in relation to iron. [?] It persuades, naturally and truly, that there is nothing other [Variant readings: "εὐθυπορῆσαι μέν", Gale's edition; the same edition omits the words "according to nature". "διαφθορᾶς" ("corruption"), Gudian codex. "the fire of the iron", Gale's edition.]

than this summit of beings, and impassibility duly follows [?]. It is joy, because nothing is opposed to it, whether past or future. For they say that joy neither knows a past grief nor admits a surfeit [?] arising from fear of what is expected, as [?] does. The divinely inspired words, and the Fathers who learned the divine mysteries from them, have everywhere affirmed joy as a name that points to the truth to come. Let us take it, then, as shown briefly, as far as my small ability allows, from nature, Scripture and the Fathers alike, that nothing that has come into being has ever come to a halt in its movement, or attained the rest proper to it according to the divine purpose. Let us also take it as shown that the stability of those counted worthy to abide in God cannot be made to swerve. To give what has been said some small support from reasoning: how could those who have once come to exist in God experience satiety [?] in their desire? Satiety, by its own principle and definition, extinguishes appetite, and it comes about in two ways. Either appetite is extinguished because it disdains its objects as small, or it loathes them, despising them as shameful and repulsive. These are the things that naturally produce satiety. But God, being by nature infinite and precious, rather naturally stretches the appetite of those who enjoy him through participation toward the infinite. If this is true, as indeed it is, then there never was the so-called henad of rational beings which, having grown sated with abiding in God, was divided and through its scattering brought about the origin of this world. Otherwise we would make the good circumscribed and dishonorable, as though it were bounded by some satiety and became a cause of instability for those whose state it could not hold unmoved. So it seems to me that some decree this doctrine in vain, inventing things that do not exist. Worse still, they falsely claim that this blessed father held these views. Relying on that, they think they can not only hold without fear that souls are sent into bodies from a former kind of life as punishment for evils done before, but also try to deceive others plausibly into thinking so, through the credibility of his person. In this they act [?] neither well nor piously. But let us leave them as they are, and let us piously consider the teacher's meaning in another way, in addition to what has been said. I do not think that he wishes here to explain the cause of human coming-into-being,

but the cause of the wretchedness that came upon it afterward. He lamented the pitiable state of our body, saying, "O this union and this estrangement! What I fear I cherish, and what I love I dread," and so on. He puzzled, as if with himself, over the cause of the evils in which we are entangled and the most wise providence at work in it, saying, "What is this wisdom concerning me, and what is this great mystery?" Then he gives the solution clearly, in these words: "Or does he wish that we, being a portion of God and having flowed down from above, should always look to him in our wrestling and battle with the body, so that we are not lifted up and puffed up by our dignity and come to despise the one who created us, and that the weakness yoked to us should be a discipline for our dignity?"
