It is as if he said this. Man was made by God, through his goodness, out of soul and body. The rational and intellectual soul given to him is in the image of its maker. By desire, and by a total love drawn from all its strength, it was to cling tightly to God in knowledge, receive the likeness as well, and be deified. By wise providence toward what is lower, and in keeping with the commandment to love one's neighbor as oneself, it was to take prudent care of the body. Through the virtues it was to make the body rational [?] and bring it into kinship with God as a fellow servant. The soul itself would mediate the Creator's indwelling, and would make him who bound them together the indissoluble bond of the immortality given to it. So what God is to the soul, the soul would become to the body. And the one Creator of all would be shown to preside, by analogy and through humanity, over all beings. The many things that stand apart from one another by nature would come into one, converging on one another around the one nature of man. And God himself would become all in all, embracing all things and giving them subsistence in himself, since no being would any longer have a movement that is unrestrained and without share in his presence. Because of this presence we are, and are called, gods, children, body, members, portion of God and the like, by reference to the end of the divine
Since, then, man came into being as this and for this, but in our forefather used his readiness of power for the worse, transferring from the … [Matthew 13:39. 1 Corinthians [?] 2:1.]

and God, who arranges our salvation in a way that befits his goodness, fittingly attached the punishment that duly follows to the irrational movement of our intellectual power. Perhaps, as is reasonable, he punished with death the very thing on which we squandered the power of love that the intellect owes to God alone. In this way, having loved what is nothing, we might at last learn through suffering and be taught to lead this power back again toward what truly is. He makes this clearer as he goes on, saying: "But it seems to me that this is another reason why none of the goods here is reliable or lasting for human beings. This too, if anything is, has been well devised by the artificer Word and by the wisdom that surpasses all mind: that we are made sport of by visible things. They change and are changed now one way, now another. They are carried up and down and overturned, and they slip away and flee before they can be grasped. So, seeing their instability and irregularity, we may move our anchorage to the future. For what would we have done if our prosperity were stable? Even though it does not last, we are so bound to it, and the pleasure and deception it brings hold us so enslaved, that we cannot think of anything better or higher than present things. And this though we were made in the image of God, and hear and believe that this image is above and draws us to itself." And again, in the oration to the civic officials, he says: "That we may know that we are nothing in relation to the true and first wisdom, but may always incline toward him alone and seek to be lit up by the rays from there, [?] the irregularity of visible and changing things, transferring us to what stands firm and abides." So, as I think, in these passages the teacher is not explaining the cause of humanity's coming into being, as has been said. He is explaining the wretchedness that was brought into our life at our coming into being because of the transgression. This is clear to those who study his divine writings more diligently and carefully. Of this wretchedness he sets before us, in these words, the cause: whence it comes, through what, for what, and for whose sake. Through it he shows the salvation wisely arranged for us by the [?] of God. But of our coming into being, hinting in a mystery at the power for which it happened, he uses another mode of discourse, making his whole pious aim on this point clear. This is shown in the oration on the Nativity [?], where he says: "Mind and sense, then, already distinguished from each other in this way, stood within their own boundaries and bore within themselves the magnificence of the Creator Word, silent praisers of his mighty work and resounding heralds. But there was not yet a blend of the two, nor any mingling of opposites, the mark of a greater wisdom and of lavishness in the natures, nor was the whole wealth of goodness yet made known. Wishing to display this, the artificer Word, wishing also to make one living being out of both,

I mean of invisible and visible nature, creates man. Taking the body from matter that already existed, and placing life in it from himself (which the Word knows as an intellectual soul and the image of God), he sets him on the earth as a kind of second cosmos, great in smallness, another angel, a worshipper of mixed nature," and so on. And in the oration On the Lights: "Since these things were so [?]; but worship had to be confined not only to those above, and there had to be some worshippers below as well, so that all things might be filled with the glory of God, since they also belong to God [?]; for this reason man is created, honored by the hand of God and by the image." I suppose that these passages, though few, are enough to show the teacher's whole thought on these matters to anyone who is not altogether contentious and does not count fighting alone as glorious. But if someone still disputes how the teacher called us a portion of God, an account of this has already been given in many ways above. To make it more convincing, however, by resting it on the words of the Spirit, the holy and blessed apostle Paul will be enough. He brought the wisdom hidden in God before the ages, lit up the whole lightless life of human beings, and drove the gloom of ignorance from their souls. He sets out the following on this subject to the Ephesians: "That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart being enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, what is the wealth of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his strength. This he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above every rule and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. And he put all things under his feet, and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all." And again, after other things: "And he himself gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, some pastors and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ, until we all reach the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, a mature man, the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be infants, tossed by the waves and carried about by every wind of teaching, by human trickery,"

…in cunning, in the wiles of deceit; but speaking the truth in love, let us grow up in every way into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting ligament, according to the working in due measure of each individual member, makes the body's growth for the building up of itself in love." I do not think that anyone who has learned to be devout needs any further testimony [?] to make plain the truth truly believed among Christians, since they have learned clearly from these words that we are members and body and fullness of Christ God, who fills all things in all, according to the purpose [?] hidden before the ages in God the Father, being summed up into him through his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ our God. For the mystery hidden from the ages and from the generations has now been made manifest through the true and perfect incarnation of the Son and God. He united our nature to himself hypostatically, without division and without confusion, and through his own holy flesh, taken from us and ours and endowed with an intellectual and rational soul, he joined us to himself as through a firstfruits, and deemed us worthy to be one and the same with himself according to his humanity, just as we were predestined before the ages to be in him as members of his body. He fits us together and knits us to himself in the Spirit, as a soul is joined to a body, and leads us to the measure of the spiritual stature of his fullness. This mystery has shown that we too came into being for this end. It has also shown that God's all-good purpose for us before the ages underwent no innovation whatever in its own principle, but came to fulfilment through another, newer mode, one that was introduced later. For God had made us like himself, in that we bear by participation the exact marks of his goodness. He had purposed before the ages that we should be in him, and had given us the mode leading to this most blessed end through the good use of our natural powers. But man voluntarily rejected this mode by misusing his natural powers. So, in order that man might not become estranged and far from God, another mode had to be introduced in place of the first, more wondrous and more befitting God, by as much as what is above nature is higher than what is according to nature. And this, as we all believe, is the mystery of God's most mystical sojourn among men. For if, says the divine Apostle, the first covenant had remained blameless, no place would have been sought for a second. Indeed, it is evident to all that the mystery accomplished in Christ at the end of the age is undoubtedly [?] the proof and fulfilment of what was let fall at the beginning of the age in our forefather. Therefore the teacher's [?] use of the word "portion" has been usefully made, according to the modes that have been explained, and anyone noble in soul and in manner would accept as piously spoken [?]

the expression, without stirring up in himself any gambling with reasonings, knowing that in such contexts "portion" is the same as "member". For if a member is a part of the body, and a member is the same as a portion, then the member will be the same as the portion. And if a portion is the same as a member, and the assembling and composition of members makes an organic body, and an organic body united to an intellectual soul presents a complete human being, then whoever says that the soul or the body is a part [?] or member of the human being will not miss the truth. And if the body is the instrument of the intellectual soul, as of a human being, and the soul, pervading the whole body entirely, gives it life and movement because it is simple in nature and incorporeal, then it is neither divided along with the body nor shut up within it. Rather, it is present whole to the whole and to each of its members, as each is naturally fitted to receive it according to the capacity for receiving its activity that naturally underlies it, and so it binds together, proportionately, the members that receive it in different ways, for the preservation of the body as one. Let whoever still has an unsettled and easily shaken mind about these things be led by this toward the great and ineffable mystery of the blessed hope of Christians, taking from small things on our own level images, by no means ignoble, of great things that are beyond us. Abandoning the unreasonable opinion that souls exist before bodies, he will believe with us the Lord, who says of those raised at the resurrection that they cannot die, evidently because of the purer manifestation of himself, the ultimate object of desire, and their participation in him. And again: "Everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die." If this had ever existed beforehand, it would have been impossible, as was shown earlier, for it to undergo any kind of death through some change. And let him not step outside natural reasonings, idly decreeing an opinion about the soul that has no foundation. For, as was stated earlier, body and soul are parts of a human being. Parts necessarily admit of relation, since the whole is certainly predicated of them. Things that are relative in this way are among those that are altogether and entirely simultaneous in their coming into being, as parts that by coming together complete a whole form, and they are distinguished from one another by thought alone, in order to discern what each is in essence. It follows that soul and body, as parts of a human being, cannot possibly exist in time before or after one another, since the principle of the relation [?]

…as I think, of the passion or of the natural [?] power of the parts, through the coming together of the one with the other, for the completion as a whole form [?] of their simultaneous generation as a whole form. So it is not possible for any form whatever to change from one form into another without corruption. And if they say that after death and the dissolution of the body the soul exists and subsists, and that it can exist and subsist apart from the body, their argument, it seems to me, does not proceed accurately. For the principle of generation and the principle of essence are not the same. The one indicates when and where a thing is, and to what it is related; the other indicates that it is, what it is, and how it is. If this is so, the soul always exists after it has come into being, because of its essence; but because of its generation it is not unattached. Rather it exists with the relation of "when", "where" and "to what". After the death of the body the soul is not called simply "soul", but the soul of a human being, and the soul of a particular human being. For even after the body it has, as its form, the whole, namely the human, predicated of it by relation, as of a part. Likewise the body, though mortal by nature, is not unattached, because of its generation. For after the separation of the soul the body is not called simply "body", but the body of a human being, and the body of a particular human being, even if it decays and by nature dissolves into the elements from which it was made. For even so it has, as its form, the whole, namely the human, predicated of it by relation, as of a part. In both cases, then, the relation, I mean of soul and of body, understood inseparably [?] as of parts of the whole human form, presents their simultaneous generation and also demonstrates their difference from one another in essence, without in any way whatever injuring the principles naturally inherent in them according to essence. It is therefore altogether impossible to find or speak of a body or a soul without relation. For with the one, the fact of belonging to someone is brought in together with the other, so that if one existed before the other, something [?] would have to be understood in addition [?]. For the relation [?] is unmovable [?]. So much for these matters. If the argument has not fallen away from the truth, thanks be to God, who through your prayers has guided us to understand rightly. But if it has fallen short of the truth anywhere, you would know what the argument lacks [?], since you are inspired by God with the knowledge of such things.

From the same oration, on: "As long as matter by itself also carries its disorder, as in a stream." I think that the aim of the present passage also keeps to the sense of the previous chapter. For after going through as many arguments as possible against the lovers of matter and lovers of the body, he adds these words, so that from them one who devoutly

investigates the aim of the saint can [?] interpret it as follows. Man was made adorned by God with the beauty of incorruptibility and immortality. But he preferred the ugliness of the material nature around him to intellectual beauty, and became utterly forgetful of the splendid dignity of the soul, or rather of God, who had beautified the soul in his own likeness. So, by the divine decree that orders our salvation, he reaped a fruit worthy of his choice. It was not only the corruption and death of the body, and its liability [?] and susceptibility to every passion, but also the instability and changeability [?] of the material substance outside and around him, and its readiness and ease in undergoing alteration. For God then, because of our transgression [?], placed in it too, as in the body, the capacity for alteration, for suffering, for corruption and for complete dissolution [?], as the clothing [?] of dead bodies shows, according to what is written: "For the creation itself was subjected to corruption, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope." Or else he created it so from the beginning, according to foreknowledge, because of the transgression he foresaw. The purpose was that man, by suffering and being afflicted through it, might come to an awareness of himself and of his own dignity, and might gladly accept detachment even from the body. For the all-wise provider of our life often allows things to follow their own impulses naturally for our correction. At times, through the confusion and turmoil surrounding them and arising from them, he brings back those who handle them madly, leading our hitherto irrational love for present things back to what is naturally lovable. There are, they say, three general modes by which our passions are healed by way of discipline. Through each mode the disorder of matter, wisely [?] and orderly steered according to the principle that is above us and superior, toward the outcome known to God and befitting his goodness, becomes a remedy for the evil burden of the passions. For either we are paying the penalty for past sins, of which, through ignorance, we perhaps keep not even a trace in our memory; or perhaps, even when we remember them, we do not bear to apply the due correction for our offences, whether unwilling or unable because of the habit of vice that has grown in us, and so we are purified through weakness. Or we cast off a vice that is present and spreading, and are taught beforehand to guard against [?] one that is to come. Or by grace a man is set before other men as a marvellous example of the best and most devout courage, if he is lofty in mind and in virtue [?]

renowned, and able by himself, through his unshaken grappling with terrible things, to reveal the truth that until then was hidden. He therefore urges those who can conceive of nothing beyond the present life not to be confident in the health of the body and in the course of affairs carried along by the current, nor to exalt themselves over those deprived of these things, as long as the present life lasts and they are clothed in this corruption, which is subject to change and alteration, since it is uncertain what will befall them too from the irregularity and turmoil of the body and of external affairs. For this, I think, is what he means by "As long as matter by itself also carries its disorder", in place of saying: "As long as this universe is subject to corruption and alteration, and we are clothed in the body of humiliation, and perhaps are subject to the manifold evils that come from it because of its innate weakness, let us not exalt ourselves against one another because of the inequality among us. Rather, with prudent reasoning let us smooth out the unevenness of a nature equal in honour, filling up the deficiencies of others with our own abundance." Perhaps [?] the present unevenness was also permitted to prevail so that the power of the reason within us might be shown, preferring virtue to all things. For all human beings share the same change and alteration of the body and of external things, carrying and being carried, and possessing only this as stable and firm: instability and

Of the same, from the oration on Saint Athanasius, on: "For it has nothing higher, nor will it ever have." It seems to me that by these words this divinely minded teacher frees the one he is teaching from every relation, whether of comparison or of distinction, or however else it may be expressed. For those skilled in these matters say that this form of expression is non-relative, and that it is equivalent to saying that something is incomparably above all things, since it has the force of a negation by way of pre-eminence. From the same oration, on: "To whomever, then, it has been granted, having broken through matter and this fleshly thing, whether one should call it a cloud or a veil, through reason and contemplation, to be with God and to be mingled with the purest light, as far as is attainable for human nature, blessed is he for his ascent from here and his deification there, which genuine philosophy [?] bestows, and for coming to be above the material dyad through the unity understood in the Trinity." For my part I do not think that the account

given by the teacher concerning the virtue of the saints is deficient, even if some, as you have written, think so. They think so because he said that the philosophy according to God of those who pursued it was by reason and contemplation alone, without the practical, and so, on the contrary, separated [?] from action their true judgment and activity concerning beings, which I for my part dare to define as alone the truly most complete philosophy. I take him to be introducing it quite clearly when he declares that it is achieved by reason and contemplation, since action is wholly joined to reason, and the judgment concerning action is contained in contemplation. It belongs to reason to order the movement of the body, as right reasoning skilfully reins in, as with a bridle, its drift toward what is improper. It belongs to contemplation to choose and decide prudently on what has been well understood and judged, since it shows the truth itself through true knowledge, like an all-shining light. By both of these above all, every philosophical virtue is created and preserved, and by them it is also manifested [?] through the body. It is not manifested whole, for it cannot be contained by a body, being the stamp of divine power, but only certain shadows of it. And this is not for its own sake [?], but so that those bare of its grace may come to imitate the godlike conduct of God-loving men, and thereby, through participation in the good, they too may put off the ugliness of vice and come to share the portion of those worthy of God. Or else it is so that those in need of some help may obtain it from those who are able to give it, and, having received [?] the disposition of the virtuous, hidden in the depth of the soul but made manifest through the body in action, may themselves also sing the praises of God's providence, which becomes all things to all and is present to all through all things. So, if there were no one in need of being done good to, and no one who needed to be shaped toward virtue by an example, it would not be absurd to say that each person would be entirely sufficient for himself, ripened by the graces of the virtues in the soul, even without their being displayed visibly through the body. He, then, who has devoutly understood through contemplation how beings are, and through rational deliberation has defined the account concerning them accurately and rightly, and keeps that judgment for himself, or rather keeps himself unswerving in that judgment, has grasped and holds all virtue at once. After the truth has been known, he is no longer drawn [?] toward anything else, and he has passed beyond all things with zeal, taking no account whatever of anything that is, or is called, of the flesh and of the world. He now has inwardly the [?], contained without conflict by reason, since the intellect [?] brings to itself all the best impassible principles concerning what is in our power [?], according to which all virtue and knowledge exists and subsists. These are powers of the rational soul, needing the body not at all in order to exist, but in order to appear

not refusing to make use of it at the proper time, for the reasons already given. For they say that to the discursive intellect belong, specifically, the intellections of intelligible things, the virtues, the sciences, the principles of the arts, the faculty of choice and the faculty of deliberation; and generally, judgments, assents, avoidances and impulses. Some of these, they say, belong only to the contemplation of the intellect, and others to the scientific power of reason. If the saints preserved their own life guarded by these, then this blessed man, by "reason" and "contemplation", comprehensively introduced all the principles of virtue and knowledge embraced by the saints. Through these, attending knowingly to the understanding of God by contemplation, and prudently by reason through the virtues, they imprinted the divine form on themselves. He certainly did not think it necessary to name bodily action, knowing that it does not produce virtue but displays it, and is only the servant of divine thoughts and reasonings. To make what is said clear in another way as well: those who have examined accurately the principles of our affairs say that of the rational faculty one part is contemplative and the other practical. The contemplative part is that according to intellect, concerned with how beings are; the practical part is the deliberative, which defines right reason for practical matters. They call the contemplative part "intellect" and the practical part "reason", and the one "wisdom", the other "prudence". If this is true, then the teacher named action [?] "reason" from its cause, not from its matter, calling it the habit that has nothing opposed to it [?]. For the contemplative abides in the truths rationally and knowingly, not by warfare and struggle, and because of his delight in them he does not bear to look at anything else besides them. If this must be made still clearer in another way, again those who have trained themselves in the principles of perfection in virtue say this. Those who have not yet become pure of their communion with matter through relation are occupied with practical matters, since their judgment about beings is still mixed; and they are changeable, not yet having put off their relation to changeable things. But those who by reaching the summit draw near to God through relation, and reap blessedness from understanding him, are turned only toward themselves and God. Having genuinely broken the bonds of material relation, they have become entirely estranged from practical matters and from matter, and have been made at home with contemplation and with God. That is why, they say, they also remain unchangeable, since they no longer have the relation to matter by which whoever is held by matter through relation is necessarily changed, contrary to nature, together with matter, which changes by nature. And knowing that very great power is needed

for putting off attachment to matter by one who wishes to be freed from it, the teacher says, "To whomever it has been granted, having broken through [?] by reason and contemplation, to be with God," and that the flesh is a cloud and a veil. Why does the teacher say that the flesh is a cloud and a veil? Because he knows that every human mind that goes astray and turns aside from its natural motion makes its motion about passion, sense and sensible things, having missed the motion that carries it toward God [?]. And he divided the flesh into passion and sense, indicating both of these, which belong to ensouled flesh, by "cloud" and "veil". For the passion of the flesh, which darkens the ruling part of the soul, is a cloud; and the deception of the senses is a veil, fixing the soul on the surfaces of sensible things and walling it off from the passage to intelligible things. Through these the soul falls into forgetfulness of natural goods and turns its whole activity toward sensible things, devising through them unseemly angers, desires and pleasures. How pleasure arises. For every forbidden pleasure naturally arises from passion, through the medium of sense, toward some sensible object. Pleasure is nothing other than a form of sensation shaped in the sensory faculty by some sensible object, or a mode of sensory activity constituted according to irrational desire. For desire added to sensation turns into pleasure, bringing it on [?]; and sensation moved by desire produces pleasure by taking hold of the sensible object. The saints, therefore, knowing that the soul, moved contrary to nature through the medium of the flesh toward matter, puts on [?] an earthly form, resolved instead, through the medium of the soul moved according to nature toward God, to make the flesh too God's own in a fitting way, adorning it as far as possible with divine [?] … through the practice of the virtues. How many motions of the soul there are, and of what kind. For, enlightened by grace, they knew that the soul has three general motions, gathered into one: that according to intellect, that according to reason, and that according to sense. The first is simple and inexplicable, and by it the soul, moving unknowably around God, in no way [?] …

…it recognizes him from none of the things that exist, because of his transcendence. The second, the motion that defines the unknown by its cause, is the one by which the soul, moving [?], applies to itself, by its activity and through knowledge, the principles concerned with him who is known only as cause, which give it form. The third is composite: by it the soul touches the things outside it and, as if from certain symbols, [gathers?] to itself the principles of visible things. Through these, in the true and unerring mode of its motion, they passed through the present age of contests [?]. They raised up sense, which spiritually holds the principles of sensible things, simply, through the medium of reason, to the intellect. They united reason, which holds the principles of beings, to the intellect in uniform fashion, by a single, simple and undivided wisdom. And they brought to God the intellect, purely released from all motion concerned with beings and resting even from its own natural activity. Through this they were wholly drawn together toward him. [?]

[?] …drawn by the divine reflection, if it is permitted to say so, they themselves were joined to God. For they say that God and man are models of each other: God becomes human for man's sake, through his love for mankind, to the same degree that man, through love, has been able to deify himself for God; and man is caught up by God in his intellect toward the unknown to the same degree that man, through the virtues, has made manifest God, who is invisible by nature. By this philosophy, then, which consists in reason and contemplation, and by which the nature of the body is necessarily ennobled as well, the saints were unerringly wounded with longing for God. Through the natural reflections of divine things that were in them, they came to God in a worthy manner, having passed through the flesh and the world like athletes. Seeing these things contained by one another, the one by nature, the other by sense [?], and each falling under the other, by the [?] of the one toward the other, [?] being free of circumscription by its own principle, they considered it shameful to let the immortal and ever-moving part of the soul be [?] circumscribed along with mortal and circumscribed things. So they bound themselves indissolubly to God alone, who is immortal and above all infinity, and never yielded to the counter-pulls of the world and the flesh. This is the fulfilment of all virtue and knowledge, and, I think, its end as well. And even if the saints were at times moved toward the spectacles of beings, they were not moved, as we are, in a material way, to see and know those very things for their own sake, but [?] [Apparatus: 53 epitithetai, Galland's ed.; tosouton, Galland's ed.] [?]

…of all things and in all things, the God who is and appears [?] fittingly, not to themselves but to God who had given them, through whom [?] general modes, as far as is attainable for human beings. They had been taught from an accurate contemplation of beings the modes by which God made all things (for he brought us into existence and gave us essence for being, for well-being, and for eternal being). Two of these are extremes and depend on God alone as their cause. The other is in the middle; it depends on our will and motion, through itself gives the extremes their proper designation, and if it is absent the name becomes useless to them, since they do not have the 'well' joined to them. So they understood that the truth in the extremes, which well-being naturally produces when, as the middle term, it is blended with the extremes, cannot otherwise come to be in them and be preserved than by ever-moving toward God. From then on they stretched the eye of the soul together with natural reason. They heard the Word himself crying out plainly that in some way one must not use the natural activities in reverse, because of the corruption that necessarily shows itself in the natural powers from the mode of misuse. And so they were taught to be carried evenly, according to the fitting principle of nature, toward its cause, so that from the source from which they simply have being they might also receive true being, added at some future time. 'For what gain,' they perhaps reasoned and said to themselves, 'will there be for one who is not the cause of his own being, if he moves toward himself or toward anything other than God, since he can procure nothing toward the principle of his being, either from himself or from anything other than God?' Therefore they taught the intellect to think about God alone and his virtues and to apply itself unknowingly to the ineffable glory of his blessedness. They taught reason to become the interpreter and hymn-singer of what had been understood, and to set out rightly the modes that lead [?] to these things. They taught sense, ennobled by reason, to form images of the various powers and activities in the universe and to report to the soul, as far as is attainable, the principles in beings. Wisely steering the soul like a ship by intellect and reason, they crossed with dry feet the watery and unstable path of life, which is carried now this way, now that, and floods over the senses.

Contemplation of the Crossing of the Sea through Moses. So perhaps that great Moses too, by the stroke of the almighty Word, of which the rod was perhaps a symbol, divided the deceit of sensible things like a sea, or, to put it more fittingly, removed it. To the people hastening toward the divine promises he gave firm and unshaken land beneath their footsteps. I mean that he showed that nature, which is subject to sense, is visible to right reason, easily circumscribed, and passable and easily crossed by a life adorned with virtues. He also showed that the surge of the divided waters on either side, which had until then covered it, brings no danger to those who cross it in this way. In the anagogical sense, the division of the waters of the intelligible sea is the separation, from their continuity with one another, of the vices that oppose the virtues by deficiency and by excess. Reason naturally effects this separation, striking them at a vital point [?], and for those hastening headlong toward God it does not allow them to be joined to one another in any way…

Contemplation of Moses' Ascent of the Mountain. So again, following God who called him and rising above everything here, he entered the darkness where God was, that is, the formless, invisible and incorporeal state, with an intellect free from every relation to anything other than God. Having come to be in it, as far as human nature could be granted, he received as a worthy prize for that blessed ascent the knowledge that circumscribes the coming-to-be of time and nature. He made God himself the type and model of the virtues and conformed himself to him like a painting that skilfully preserves its likeness to the archetype. Then he came down from the mountain, displaying on his face the grace of the glory he had shared. To other people too he gave and set forth himself ungrudgingly, having become, as it were, a type of the God-formed type. He shows this by doing it: he explained to the people what he had seen and heard, and in writing he handed down to those after him, as a God-given inheritance, the myst[eries] of God. [?] [Contemplation] of the Leadership of Joshua, of the Crossing of the Jordan, and of the Second Circumcision through Him with Knives of Stone. So Joshua, the successor of Moses (to pass over most of what is recorded about him, since there is so much), took over the people, who had earlier been trained in piety in the desert in many ways. After the death of Moses on the mountain, he purified them with a strange form of circumcision by knives of stone. And when the Jordan had been dried up by the [?] of the divine ark, all the people

…of all things and in all things, the God who is and appears, they might hymn in many ways, and gather for themselves great power of wonder and occasion for glorifying him. For they had received from God a soul that has intellect, reason and sense. Besides the intelligible sense it has this sensible one, just as it has uttered reason besides the inner reason, and the passive intellect besides the intellectual one. They also call this passive intellect the imagination of the living being; by it the other animals recognize one another, and us, and the places they have passed through. The wise in such matters say that sense is constituted in this faculty, which is its organ for apprehending the things imagined by it. They thought it right to offer the activities of these faculties, fittingly, not to themselves but to God who had given them, through whom [they have?] all things [?]. As far as is attainable for human beings, they had been taught from an accurate contemplation of beings that there are three general modes by which God made all things (for he brought us into existence and gave us essence for being, for well-being, and for eternal being). Two of these are extremes and depend on God alone as their cause. Therefore the intellect, to think about God alone and…

After the death of Moses on the mountain, he purified them with a strange form of circumcision by knives of stone. And when the Jordan had been dried up by the [?] of the divine ark, all the people

he brought across, and so he pointed to the Savior Word who was being signified typologically through him. After the end of the letter of the legal ordinances, the Word took up the leadership of the true Israel, the Israel that loves God, a leadership that comes about by the [?] of thoughts. He circumcises them of every defilement of soul and body by the very sharp word of faith in him. He frees them from every reproach of the things that provoke to sin. And he brings across the flowing nature of time and of moving things to the state of incorporeal beings those who carry, raised up on the shoulders of the virtues, the knowledge that is receptive of the divine mysteries. Contemplation of Jericho and of the Seven Circuits, of the Ark and the Trumpets, and of the Accursed Thing. So again, with seven circuits and as many trumpets, along with a mystical shout, he shook the city of Jericho, which seemed hard to capture or even impregnable. In this he mystically showed the same Word of God as conqueror of the world and consummator of the age by intellect and reason, that is, by knowledge and virtue. The ark and the trumpets were a type of these. The Word shows those who follow him that the sensible age is easily captured and easily destroyed, and that nothing in it is fit for enjoyment by those who love divine goods, since it is joined to death and corruption and is a cause of divine wrath. Achar the son of Carmi shows this. He is the turbulent and matter-loving thought, which, for wanting to bring some sensible thing into its house, received by divine sentence that most pitiable death. Reason brings about this death, drowning the one who deserves to be so punished in the depth of an evil conscience. Contemplation of Hazor, of Its King, and of Its Capture. So again, as it is written, 'At that time he took Hazor and killed its king with the sword, and destroyed everything in it that breathed.' Hazor had formerly ruled over all the lands. In this he was taught the principles of the mysteries of which it was set forth as a type: that our true Savior Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the destroyer of the evil powers and the one who gives an inheritance to those worthy of grace, at the time of his incarnation, taking through the cross the sin [?]

[?] Contemplation on 'The heavens declare the glory of God.' So David, who came after them in time but was like them in spirit (to pass over the Judges, whose lives contain many mysteries), heard the heavens declaring the glory of God and the firmament proclaiming the work of his hands. (This is the wonder, since the Creator did not put a soul in them.) With the ears of the intellect he received from soulless things the principles of theology. And, as far as is attainable for a human being, he was taught from their effects the modes of providence and judgment, without reaching the principles by which, clearly, the administration of the universe is varied in its particulars. Contemplation on 'My father and my mother have forsaken me.' So again, when he says, 'My father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up,' he means the law of the flesh's nature concerning generation and corruption, by which all of us, because of the transgression, are both born and kept in being, and sense, which nurses us like a mother. I think he declared covertly that those who desire incorruptible things must necessarily abandon and flee these. Through this the visible world is left behind and itself lets go, while the Lord takes them up. He adopts as sons the worthy by the spiritual law and is made their father through virtue and knowledge, and, being good, he gives himself wholly to them wholly, according to likeness. Or perhaps by the father and mother he hints at the written law and the bodily worship that goes with it. When these withdraw, the light of the spiritual law naturally dawns in the hearts of the worthy and grants freedom from slavery according to the flesh. Contemplation on the Vision of Elijah in the Cave at Horeb. So the renowned Elijah came after that fire, after the earthquake, after the great and mighty wind that broke up mountains. I take these to be zeal, discernment, and eager faith in full assurance. (For discernment, like an earthquake shaking things that are joined together, shakes through virtue the habit that wickedness has made dense and dislodges it from vice. Zeal, like fire, kindles those who have it with the fervor of the Spirit and persuades them to chastise the impious. And faith, like a violent wind, drives on the disobedient [?] for the sake of God's glory, toward the destruction of strongholds through the display of miracles. It makes the truly faithful person a supplier of the water of knowledge and of deifying fire, healing by the one the famine caused by ignorance,

and by the other making God favorable to those who sacrifice through their intimacy with him. It also slays the teachers of vice, the thoughts and demons of sophistry, and frees those held in slavery to the passions.) After all these things, perceiving the voice of a gentle breeze in which God was, he was mystically taught the divine state, untroubled and peaceful, wholly immaterial and simple, free from every form and shape, in uttered word, in ways of life and in character, a state that cannot be spoken or shown. Struck by its glory and wounded by its beauty, he longed to be with it rather than to be a zealot, that is, to be wholly with the truth rather than to fight for the truth. He judged it far more precious to see or know nothing opposed, by knowing God alone as wholly present through all things in all things. So, while still in the flesh, he is kept for it, having passed through matter in a divine chariot of virtues. He passed through matter as the veil that hinders the intellect's pure passage to intelligible things, and through the cloud of the flesh, which darkens the ruling part of the soul by its passions. So he too might become a partaker of the ineffable goods he longed for, as far as is possible for one still with flesh subject to corruption, and perhaps for us he might become a firm assurance of the things promised. For through the things enacted in this mystical way, God was suggesting this to him, crying out with unspeakable [cries]: that to be with God alone through peace is more profitable than every other good. Contemplation on Elisha, His Disciple. So Elisha, his disciple and the heir of his spirit, had sense that was no longer held by material imaginings but whose activities [?] had already been transformed [?] by the graces of the Spirit according to the intellect. Through another activity of the eyes he himself saw the divine powers around him, which stood opposed to the evil ones, and he granted his attendant the power to see them. So he was both taught and taught others that power is stronger than weakness, I mean the weakness of the flesh, around which the [hosts?] of wickedness lie in ambush for the discerning intellect, and that the soul, around which the ranks of angels encamp, standing about it like a royal image, has the advantage. Contemplation on Hannah and Samuel. So also blessed Hannah, mother of the great Samuel, was barren and childless. She asked God for the fruit of the womb and fervently promised to give back and return what would be given to God, who gives and bestows it, through service in the temple. In this she mystically taught that every soul barren of fleshly pleasures must, through the [?] of God, [receive?] the seeds of the virtues, so that, having conceived in the mind a word able to see by knowledge the things that lie ahead and obedient to God, and having given birth to it, [it may] off[er?]…

[?] …may be able, through its pious attendance on contemplation, treating it as a great and precious debt, to judge that it has nothing of its own, and so to show that God alone both gives and receives. As the law says somewhere: "My gifts, my offerings, my fruit-offerings, you shall take care to offer to me," since every good both begins from him and ends in him. For the Word of God, in those in whom he comes to dwell, naturally sets aside the movements of the flesh, holds the soul back from its inclination toward them, and fills it with every true discernment.

Contemplation on the priest who sets apart the unclean house.

When I hear that the priest, according to the ordinance of the law, enters a house that is unclean in any way, sets it apart, and prescribes to its owners what is needed for its cleansing, I understand that the Word, the high priest, is signified through him. Like a most pure light he enters the soul, uncovers its accursed counsels and thoughts together with its blameworthy deeds, and wisely suggests the ways of conversion and cleansing. I think the woman who received the great prophet Elijah indicated this more clearly when she said: "Man of God, you have come to me to remind me of my iniquities."

Contemplation on Saint Elijah and the widow of Zarephath.

For every soul that is widowed of good things and bereft of virtue and of the knowledge of God, once it receives the divine and discerning Word, is brought to remember its own sins. It is then taught, in some way, to feed with the loaves of the virtues the Word who nourishes it [?], to give drink to the fountain of life with the doctrines of truth, and to put care for him before its very nature. Through this care the jar, the flesh, will supply practical vigour in the virtues; the flask, the mind, will pour forth without ceasing the contemplation that keeps the light of knowledge alive; and the innate reasoning, like the widow's son in that story, will lay aside its former passionate life and be counted worthy to share in the divine and true life given by the Word.

Contemplation on the Transfiguration of the Lord.

In the same way, besides those already mentioned, some of Christ's disciples were granted, because of their diligence in virtue, to go up with him and be taken up to the mountain of his manifestation. They saw him transfigured, unapproachable in the light of his face. They were astounded by the brightness of his garments, and they recognized that he had been made more venerable by the honour of Moses and Elijah standing with him on either side. So they passed over from the

flesh to the spirit before they had laid aside life in the flesh. This happened through the change in their sense-activities [?] that the Spirit worked in them. He removed the veils of the passions from the intellectual power within them, and once the senses of their soul and body had been purified in this way, they were instructed in the spiritual principles of the mysteries shown to them. The all-blessed radiance that shone forth in rays from his face, overpowering every activity of the eyes, they were mystically taught to be a symbol of his divinity, which is beyond mind and sense and being and knowledge. From his having neither form nor beauty, and from knowing that the Word had become flesh, they were led by the hand to the one who is fair in beauty beyond the sons of men, and to the understanding that he was in the beginning, was with God, and was God. They were lifted up in knowledge, through the theological negation that hymns him as wholly uncontainable by all, to the glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.

The garments made white, they learned, bear a symbol of the words of holy Scripture. At that point these words became bright, clear and lucid to them. They were understood without any riddling enigma or symbolic shadow, and they revealed the Word who is in them and hidden. This happened when the disciples reached smooth and straight knowledge about God and were set free from passionate attachment to the world and the flesh. Or the garments are a symbol of creation itself, once the sordid opinion is removed that until then seemed to appear in it to those who are deceived and bound to sense alone. Through the wise variety of the different forms that make it up, creation reveals the power of the creating Word, much as a garment shows the dignity of the one who wears it. Both of these sayings will fit the Word, since in both he is fittingly hidden by obscurity for our sake, so that we may not dare to approach the uncontainable unworthily: in the letter of holy Scripture he is hidden as Word, and in creation as Creator, Maker and Craftsman.

For this reason I say that anyone who wishes to journey straight to God without blame necessarily needs both: knowledge of Scripture in the Spirit, and natural contemplation of beings according to the Spirit. In this way, as is fitting, one who desires to become a perfect lover of perfect wisdom will be able to show that the two laws, the natural and the written, are equal in honour and teach the same things to one another, with neither having more or less than the other.

Contemplation of the natural and the written law, and of how they converge with each other by exchange.

For I understand that the one, the natural law, being directed as evenly as possible according to reason through the spectacles inherent in it, like a book [contains] the harmonious fabric of the universe,

and has as its letters and syllables the bodies that come first for us, near at hand and particular, made dense by the many qualities that combine in them. As its words it has the bodies more general than these, which are distant and finer. From these the Word, who wisely engraved them and is ineffably engraved in them, takes shape as he is read. He gives only the notion that he is, not what he is. Through the pious gathering of the various impressions he leads us to one image of the truth, and as their Maker he gives himself to be seen, by analogy, through visible things. The other law, which is achieved through learning, is like another world made of heaven and earth and the things between them, that is, of ethical, natural and theological philosophy. Through the things wisely dictated in it, it [?] reveals the ineffable power of the one who dictated it. It shows that the two laws are the same as each other by exchange: the written law is the same as the natural in potency, and the natural in turn the same as the written in habit. Both reveal and conceal the same Word, the one through its wording and what appears, the other through its meaning and what is hidden.

We call the words of holy Scripture garments and understand its meanings as the flesh of the Word, so that by the first we conceal and by the second we reveal. In the same way we call the forms and shapes of created things presented to sight garments, and understand the principles according to which they were created as flesh, so that again by the first we conceal and by the second we reveal. For the Word, the Creator and Lawgiver of the universe, is hidden in appearing, being by nature invisible, and is manifested in being hidden, since the wise do not believe him to be subtle [?] by nature.

May it be granted to us to show this through [?]… to pass beyond all the power of figures and enigmas that portray the truth, and instead [to rise] to the Word himself, believing him to be [higher] than visible things and more majestic than sensible ones. May we not, looking only as far as the letter, make much of the body alone in the Jewish manner, making the belly our god and counting shame as glory, and so carry off the same lot as the God-killers. They did not recognize the Word who for our sake became like us through a body, and was made dense in syllables and letters for the sake of sense perception, which has drawn the whole power of our intellect toward itself. For the divine apostle says: "The letter kills, but the spirit gives life." The letter, when it is cherished only for its own sake, naturally kills the [meaning] within it for those who cherish it [?], just as the beauty of creatures, when it is not [seen] for the glory of its Maker [?] … [?]

St. Maximus the Confessor

…when it is looked upon [in that way], naturally deprives those who behold it of a piety that accords with reason. And again the Gospel says: "If those days had not been shortened," that is, the days of evil, "no flesh would have been saved," that is, no pious thought about God. The days of evil are shortened when the mistaken judgment based on sense, which produces them, is held within bounds by reason and falls behind the pious standard of righteousness that reason sets. For the law of the flesh is no different from Antichrist. It is always wrestling against the spirit and opposing the divine law in it [?], as long as the present life is desirable and lovely to those whom it has defeated, and the Word has not yet appeared and slain it by the word of his power. When he comes, he separates the mortal from the immortal and drives out the slavery that oppresses freedom. He shows truth itself, by itself, pure of falsehood, and divides material and temporary things from divine and eternal ones. The mind, deceived by its familiarity with material things through sense, naturally inclines toward them and is put to death by irrational affection. It is above all and chiefly for the mind's sake that the God-befitting descent of the Word takes place. He raises the mind from the death of ignorance, [frees it] [?] from its passionate disposition toward material things, and leads its desire back to what it naturally loves.

Therefore I think it necessary that we, as rational beings, should care for the body that is far better than the garments, that is, the divine and lofty meanings both of holy Scripture and of the spectacles of creation. We should hasten through reason to the Word, for, as he himself says, "Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing?" Otherwise we may be found out at the appointed time to have laid hold of none of these, and not to have grasped the Word who subsists and gives subsistence to all things. We would be like that Egyptian woman who laid hold only of Joseph's garments and wholly missed union with the one she loved.

If we do this, we too will go up the mountain of the divine transfiguration and behold the garments of the Word, by which I mean the words of Scripture and the visible creatures. They will be bright and glorious through the unfolding of the doctrines about him, and through lofty contemplation they will be fitting for the divine Word. We will in no way be kept back [?] from the blessed touch of the Word, as Mary Magdalene was when she thought the Lord Jesus was the gardener and supposed him to be the maker only of things subject to generation and corruption, and nothing beyond sense. Rather, we will see and worship the one who came to us from the dead while the doors were shut, once all sense-activity in us has been completely extinguished. And we will know the Word himself, God, who is all in all, and who in his goodness has made all intelligible things his body and all sensible things his garment. Perhaps it would not seem unfitting to say that these words refer to this:

[Note: "to deprive" — Gudian codex.]

"They will all grow old like a garment," because of the corruption that now prevails over visible things; "and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed," because of the grace of incorruption that we await.

A brief exposition of the five modes of natural contemplation.

Besides these things we will also know the principles, namely the last ones, those within our reach, of which creation is set before us as teacher. We will also know the five modes of contemplation joined to them, by which the saints divided creation and piously gathered the mystical principles within it. They divided it into being, motion, difference, mixture and position. Three of these, they said, were given primarily to lead us by the hand to the knowledge of God: the mode according to being, the mode according to motion, and the mode according to difference. Through these God becomes known to human beings who gather from beings the impressions of him [?] as Creator, Provider and Judge. Two of them, they said, train us in virtue and in familiarity with God: the mode according to mixture and the mode according to position. Through these a human being is formed and becomes god, [receiving] being god from beings. Seeing in his mind, as it were, the whole impression of God's goodness, he forms it in himself in its purest form according to reason. For whatever the pure mind naturally sees through pious knowledge, they say, it can also undergo, becoming that very thing by habit through virtue.

Thus being, they said, is a teacher of theology. Through it, as we seek the cause of beings, we are taught through those beings that the cause is. We do not attempt to know what it is in its being, since there is in beings no presentation of its impression through which we might in any way look up from effect to cause [in that respect]. Motion reveals the providence that governs beings. Through it we contemplate the unchanging identity of each created thing in its being, according to its kind, and likewise the inviolable way it is ordered. So we understand the one who holds together and guards, in an ineffable union, all things that are clearly distinguished from one another according to the principles by which each came to subsist. Difference indicates judgment. Through it we are taught that God is the wise distributor of the principles of individual things, according to the natural power in each being, which is proportioned to its underlying essence.

By providence I do not mean the providence that converts, the one that, as it were by a plan of salvation, brings back those in its care from what they should not do to what they should. I mean the providence that holds the universe together and preserves the principles according to which the universe first came to subsist. By judgment I do not mean the judgment that educates and, as it were, punishes sinners. I mean the saving and defining distribution of beings, according to which each created thing, joined to the principles according to which it came to be, has an inviolable

and unchangeable lawfulness in its natural identity, just as from the beginning the Creator judged and established, concerning each thing, that it is, what it is, how it is, and of what kind. Providence and judgment in the other sense are attached to our choices [?]. In many ways they restrain us from evil and wisely turn us toward good. By directing the things that are not in our power against those that are, they cut away evil, present, future and past. Yet by this I do not mean one providence and another, or one judgment and another. For I know it to be one and the same in power, though its activity toward us is different and manifold.

The mixture, or composition, of beings, they said, is a symbol of our will. For when the will is mixed with the virtues and mixes them with itself, it too constructs the most God-befitting world in the mind. Position, they said, teaches the moral character of the will, so that it holds firmly to the good [?] … [?], receiving no alteration whatever from chance events that might move it from its rational foundation.

Again, joining position to motion and mixture to difference, they divided the substance of the universe, without dividing it, into being, difference and motion. Understanding by skilful conceptual reasoning that the cause is contemplated in its effects in different ways, they piously grasped that it is, that it is wise, and that it is living. From this they were taught the divine and saving word concerning Father, Son and Holy Spirit. By it they were mystically enlightened not only about the principle of the cause's being, but were also piously initiated into the mode of its existence.

Again, surveying all creation according to position alone, they reduced the five aforementioned modes of contemplation to three. They recognized that creation, made of heaven and earth and the things between them, is by its own principle a teacher of ethical, natural and theological philosophy. Again, contemplating creation according to difference alone, that is, as containing and contained, by which I mean heaven and the things within it, they brought the three modes together into two, namely wisdom and philosophy. Wisdom encompasses [?] and receives in a God-befitting way all the pious modes that are spoken concerning it, and encloses within itself the mystical and natural principles concerning other things. Philosophy holds together character and will, action and contemplation, virtue and knowledge, and is referred by a relational affinity to wisdom as its cause. And again, according to mixture alone, that is, the harmonious composition of the universe, … through all things ineffably bound together into the completion of one world … only the Word who binds together and holds the whole and the parts [?] … [?]

…having understood the Word, they enclosed the two in one mode of contemplation. Through it, by a simple approach through the principles in beings, they ferried the mind across to the cause and bound it to him alone, as the one who gathers and draws to himself all things that come from him. They were no longer scattered among the principles of the individual parts of the whole, because they had passed beyond them [?]. Through their precise gazing at beings they were clearly persuaded that God alone, from then on, properly is. He is the being of beings and [their] motion [?], the clear distinctness of things that differ, the indissoluble cohesion of things that are mixed, and the immovable foundation of things that are placed. He is, simply, the cause of all being however it is conceived, and of motion and difference, mixture and position.

So they wisely transferred, by a fitting likeness, the mystical contemplation of the sensible world to the world that is completed in the mind, in the Spirit, through the virtues. Gathering the said modes into one in this contemplation, they formed in themselves, as far as possible, the one who fills, through and through, the being of the world of the will in the mind with the various forms of the virtues. They passed through all the principles of beings and the principles of the virtues themselves, or rather, together with these, they ran up unknowingly to the superessential and supergood Word who is beyond them, to whom they [lead] and from whom they have their being. Being united whole to the whole, as far as the natural power within them allows, they were so shaped by him, as far as they could receive it, that they are recognized from him alone. Like the clearest mirrors, they show the form of the whole of God the Word who looks into them, appearing without omission through his divine marks. For none of the old characteristics by which the human is naturally made known remains in them; all have yielded to better ones, like dark air wholly mingled with light.

Contemplation on Melchizedek.

This, I think, is what the wonderful and great Melchizedek knew and experienced, about whom the divine word in Scripture recounts great and marvellous things. He was counted worthy to rise above time and nature and to be made like the Son of God. By grace, as far as possible, he became such as the giver of grace himself is believed to be by essence. For when it is said of him that he was "without father, without mother, without genealogy," I take this to mean nothing other than the complete laying aside of natural characteristics that came about in him through the highest grace in virtue. And "having neither beginning of days nor end of life" [signifies] the knowledge that encompasses the property of all time and age,

…and bears witness to a contemplation that transcends the existence of every material and immaterial substance. And the words "Made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever" perhaps indicate that, through an unchanging habit of most godlike virtue and of divine gazing toward God, he was able to keep the eye of his mind unclosed to the very end. For virtue by its nature contends against nature, and true contemplation against time and eternity, so that the one may remain unenslaved and unmastered by all the other things that are believed to exist after God, since it knows God alone as its begetter, and the other may be uncircumscribed, lingering in none of the things that have a beginning or an end, since through itself it images God, who defines every beginning and end and draws to himself, in an ineffable ecstasy, every act of understanding of those who understand. From these, I mean knowledge and virtue, the divine likeness is shown, and through them the unshakable love for God alone is preserved in the worthy. By this love the dignity of adoption, bestowed in a manner befitting God, grants them to intercede with God continually and to stand in his presence, offering as its plea the very divine likeness of the one who intercedes. Hence I reasonably suppose that what the divine word has judged great Melchizedek to be ought not to be designated by time and nature, to which he was naturally subject but which he had already surpassed in life and reason and left entirely behind, but should be named from the things from which and through which he refashioned himself by his own choice, I mean virtue and knowledge. For in those whose will has nobly overcome, through the virtues, the law of nature, so hard to fight against, and whose movement of mind soars purely, through knowledge, above the property of time and eternity, it is not right to fix as their distinguishing mark the property of what they have left behind, but rather the magnificence of what they have taken on, from which and in which alone they henceforth exist and are recognized. Indeed, we too, when we naturally turn our attention to visible things, both recognize and name bodies from their colors: for example, we call illuminated air "light," any material set alight by fire "fire," and a whitened body "white," and so with all other such things. If, then, the divine Melchizedek by his own choice preferred virtue to nature and to everything that belongs to it, because of the noble choice that is the dignity of our free will, and in knowledge shot beyond all time and eternity, having in contemplation knowingly put behind him all things that come after God, lingering in no existing thing in which any limit whatever is observed; and if he has been born in the Spirit by grace through the Word toward God's divine, beginningless and immortal [substances], and bears in himself the sound and true likeness of God who begot him (for every birth naturally makes what is born the same as the one who begets it: "What is born of the flesh," it says, "is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit"), then fittingly

he was named not from the natural and temporal properties, which include father and mother and genealogy, and beginning and end of days, from which he had already set himself completely free, but from the divine and blessed marks by which he refashioned his form, which neither time nor nature nor reason nor mind nor, to put it in a word, any other existing thing can reach. So great Melchizedek is recorded as "without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life," as the true teaching of the God-bearing men has explained concerning him. This is not because of his created nature, which came from nothing and according to which he began and ceased to be, but because of the divine and uncreated grace, which exists eternally above all nature and all time, from the eternally existing God, and through which alone he is recognized as having been wholly born by his own choice. He alone has been preserved thus in Scripture, perhaps as the first to have risen above matter and form through virtue, which can be indicated by "without father, without mother, without genealogy"; and as having passed beyond, through knowledge, all things under time and eternity, whose being began in time from a coming-into-being that [?] at some point, without halting at any of them in the divine course of his mind, which is perhaps what is meant by "having neither beginning of days nor end of life"; and as having entered, in a transcendent manner, hiddenly and silently [?], and in short unknowably, into God himself, after removing in mind all existing things, and having been wholly qualified and transformed by him who is whole, which is what "Made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever" can signify. For each of the saints, in respect of whatever good he especially offered as first-fruits, is proclaimed in that respect a type of God the giver. In this sense this great Melchizedek too, because of the divine virtue wrought in him, has been deemed worthy to be an image of Christ God and of his ineffable mysteries. All the saints are gathered together in Christ as in their archetype and the cause of the good that appears in each of them, but this man especially, since he bears in himself more outlines of Christ than all the others.

An interpretation applied to the Lord of what is said about Melchizedek.

For our Lord and God Jesus Christ alone is by nature and in truth without father, without mother and without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life. He is without mother because of the immaterial, incorporeal and wholly unknowable character of his birth on high from the Father before the ages; without father because of his birth below, in time and in the body, from his mother, in whose conception he did not establish the mode that comes through seed; and without genealogy, as

the manner of both his births is altogether inaccessible and incomprehensible to all. And "having neither beginning of days nor end of life" applies to him as without beginning, without end and wholly infinite, since he is God by nature. And "he remains a priest forever," as one who ceases to be through no death, whether of vice or of nature [?], because he is God and the provider of all life, both natural and virtuous. Do not think that anyone is denied a share in this grace just because Scripture has defined it as belonging to great Melchizedek alone. For God has perhaps placed by nature in all the power for salvation, so that each who wishes may lay claim to divine grace, and whoever wants to become Melchizedek, Abraham and Moses, and simply to transfer all the saints into himself, may not be prevented, not by exchanging names and places, but by imitating their ways and their manner of life.

Another contemplation on Melchizedek.

Anyone, then, who has put to death his members that are on earth, and has shaken off the whole mind of the flesh, and has entirely cast off his attachment to it, through which the love we owe to God alone is divided, and has renounced all the marks of the flesh and the world for the sake of divine grace, so as to be able to say with the blessed apostle Paul, "Who will separate us from the love of Christ?" and what follows, such a one has become without father, without mother and without genealogy, like great Melchizedek, having no means by which he could be held fast by flesh and nature, because of the union that has come about with the Spirit.

A contemplation on having neither beginning of days nor end of life.

And if, besides this, he has also denied himself, losing his own life "for my sake," he "will save it." That is, giving up the present life with its desires for the sake of the better one, he possesses the Word of God alone, living and active, piercing through virtue and knowledge as far as the division of soul and spirit. And if he has nothing at all that lacks a share in his presence, he has become both without beginning and without end, no longer carrying in himself the temporal life in its motion, which has a beginning and an end and is shaken by many passions, but only the divine life of the Word [?] who has come to dwell in him, eternal and bounded by no death.

A contemplation on "He remains a priest forever."

And if, with great attentiveness, he knows how to keep watch over his own gift, caring through practice and contemplation for the goods that are above nature and time, he has also become

a perpetual and eternal priest, ever enjoying [?] divine converse. And because, by the unchangeableness of his will regarding the good, he imitates the one who is unchangeable by nature, he is not prevented, as the Jews were, by the death of sin from continuing forever. He offers a sacrifice of praise and confession, gloriously proclaiming God as the creator of all things and gratefully giving thanks to him as the provident and just judge of the universe, on the divine altar of the mind, from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat. For those who keep step with the letter alone cannot partake of the mystical loaves of divine knowledge and the life-giving cup of wisdom. They are content for their salvation with sacrifices [?] of the passions. They proclaim the death of Jesus by being inactive as regards sin, but do not confess his resurrection, for the sake of which and through which his death took place, through the contemplation of the mind illumined by the righteousness of good works. They very eagerly choose to be put to death in the flesh, but in no way accept [?] being made alive in the spirit, since the tabernacle among them still has standing, because the way into the holy places through word and knowledge has not yet been revealed to them. That way is the Word of God, who said, "I am the way." And they have no desire to pass, through contemplation, from knowing the Lord through practice as the Word made flesh to his glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.

A contemplation on Abraham.

Again, one becomes a spiritual Abraham who goes out from his land and his kindred and his father's house and comes into the land shown him by God. This is one who has broken off his attachment to the flesh and come to be outside it by separation from the passions. He has left the senses behind and no longer admits through them any deception of sin, and has passed beyond all sensible things, from which, through the senses, the soul comes to be deceived and to stumble. With the mind alone, free from every material bond, he comes into the divine and blessed land of knowledge and travels mystically through its length and breadth. In it he will find our Lord and God Jesus Christ, the good inheritance of those who fear him. In length, Christ is spoken of in theology by the worthy, as far as is attainable for human beings, as incomparable in himself. In breadth, he is glorified on our account, through his most wise providence that holds the universe together and through his wondrous and more-than-ineffable economy on our behalf. And this Abraham becomes, divinely [?], in practice and contemplation, a partaker of the ways in which he has been trained to honor the Lord, through which friendship with God and assimilation to him are naturally and securely confirmed. To speak briefly about these things: whoever has wrestled down by practice flesh, sense and world, through which the mind's

relation to intelligible things comes to be dissolved, and has approached God with the mind alone, by knowledge, through love, such a one is another Abraham, shown through equal grace to bear the same character of virtue and knowledge as the patriarch.

A contemplation on Moses.

And again, another Moses appears. In the time when the passions hold sway, when the devil, the intelligible Pharaoh, is tyrannizing, so that the worse naturally prevails over the better, the carnal rises up against the spiritual, and every pious thought is destroyed, he is born according to God by his own choice. He is placed in the ark of true ascesis, secured [?] outwardly in the flesh by moral ways and inwardly in the soul by divine thoughts, and until the time [?] of his taking up natural contemplations he consents to live under sense, the daughter of the intelligible Pharaoh. Then, with a genuine zeal for divine goods, he kills the Egyptian mind of the flesh and hides it under the sand, by which I mean the condition that is barren of evils. In that condition, even if the enemy sows the weed of vice, it does not naturally grow, because of the poverty of spirit that dwells there inwardly, which both produces and preserves dispassion. By divine command this poverty sets a limit to the sea of bitter and truly briny vice, which is made wild by the spirits of wickedness and tossed [?] by wave upon wave of temptations, as it is written: "He who sets the sand as a boundary for the sea, and says to it, 'Thus far you shall come, and you shall not pass beyond, but within you your waves shall be broken.'"
