And the thoughts that still bend down toward the earth and seek the enjoyment that comes from it, for which the irascible part naturally fights and tyrannizes and thrusts aside discerning reason, he leads like sheep, as a skilled shepherd, through the desert, the state deprived of passions, matter and pleasures, to the mountain of the knowledge of God, which is seen on the height of the mind. Dwelling there diligently through the contemplations that befit the spirit, after abandoning the mind's attachment to sensible things (for this, I think, is what the number [?] of forty years signifies), he will be deemed worthy to become, in understanding, a spectator and hearer of the ineffable and supernatural divine fire that dwells in the essence of beings as in a bush. I mean God the Word, who shone forth in the last times from the bush of the holy Virgin and conversed with us through flesh. He brings to such a mystery the bare foot of his mind, wholly free of human reasonings as of dead sandals. He turns away from inquiry the seeing faculty of the mind, as one turns away one's face, and through faith alone, in the manner of hearing, he opens the soul's obedience to receive the mystery. From him he receives strong and invincible power against the evil powers,

and with great authority separates what is according to nature from what is contrary to nature, the spiritual from the carnal, and the intelligible and holy [?] from the material and sensible, far surpassing the power that tries to make the free a slave.

Another brief contemplation on the same.

To put it in a word: one who has not gone under the yoke of sin, nor drowned himself in the muddy stream of the passions of desire, nor consented to be fed by sense, the fountain of pleasures, but has rather killed the mind of the flesh, which tyrannizes the nobility of the soul; who has risen above all perishable things and fled this deceiving world as from an Egypt, the world that crushes the most clear-sighted mind with bodily cares; who, communing with himself in stillness and in diligent leisure, has been ineffably taught through the scientific contemplation of beings the wise economy of the providence that divinely governs the universe [?]; and from there, through mystical theology, which is entrusted to the pure mind alone, through prayer, in an ineffable ecstasy, has communed wordlessly with God in the unknowing as in a thick darkness; and who has engraved himself inwardly, in the mind, with the doctrines of piety, and outwardly with the graces of the virtues, as Moses did the tablets, by the finger of God, the Holy Spirit; or, to put it in the words of Scripture, one who has chosen to suffer hardship with the people of God rather than to have the passing enjoyment of sin, and has judged the reproach of Christ more precious than the treasures of Egypt, that is, has willingly chosen labors for virtue in place of passing and perishable wealth and glory: such a one has become a spiritual Moses. He contends not with a visible Pharaoh, but with an invisible tyrant, the murderer of souls and author of vice, the devil, and with the evil powers around him. He is drawn up in battle against them in the realm of the mind, together with the rod he carries in his hand, by which I mean the power of reason in practice.

A contemplation on how one can imitate the saints before the Law and after the Law, and on the identity of the natural and the written law as they pass over into one another.

In the same way, each of us who wishes can transfer all the saints into himself, being spiritually formed after each of them from what is written about him typologically in the narrative ("These things happened to them typologically," says the divine Apostle, "but they were written for our instruction, on whom the ends of the ages have come"). He is formed after the saints of old before the Law by piously gaining knowledge of God from the creation of the world, and by being taught to achieve the virtues from the providence that wisely governs the universe, like those very saints before the Law. They naturally inscribed beforehand in themselves, in the spirit, the written law in all its parts, and so were fittingly set forth as a model of piety

and virtue for those under the Law (for "Look," it says, "to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you in travail"). And he is formed after those under the Law by being led up through the commandments, with a pious understanding, to the knowledge of God who dictated them, and by adorning himself through noble action with the fitting forms of the virtues. He is taught that the natural law is the same as the written law when it is wisely diversified through symbols in practice, and conversely that the written law is the same as the natural when, in those who are worthy in virtue and knowledge, it becomes uniform and simple and free of symbols through reason and contemplation. So it was with those very saints under the Law who, once the Spirit had removed the letter like a veil, were shown spiritually to possess the natural law.

That the saints under the Law too, understanding the Law spiritually, foresaw the grace [to come] through it.

For all of them foresaw expressly that there would be another worship besides that of the Law, and proclaimed in advance the perfection of the most godlike life that would appear in it [?], a life suited and most proper to nature, needing nothing external for its perfection, as is clear to all who are not ignorant of the divine oracles given through the Law and the Prophets. David and Hezekiah in particular, besides the others, each foreshadowed this by an enacted drama in his own person [?]: the one by propitiating God for his sin [?] with respect to the Law, the other by being honored by God with an addition of life under an ordinance other than the Law.

That one who genuinely follows Christ in disposition through the virtues comes to be above both the written and the natural law.

Nothing, I think, prevents one who has been trained beforehand in these laws, I mean the natural and the written, in a God-loving manner, from coming to be above them in a manner befitting God. Without them, through sincere faith, he genuinely follows the Word alone, who leads to the highest good, and in his thought does not touch at all any object, reasoning or concept under which the nature and knowledge of all that in any way is thought and exists fall and appear. So it is fitting for one who has resolved to follow genuinely Jesus, who has passed through the heavens, to be able, by the showing of the divine light, to receive comprehensively the true [knowledge?] of beings, as far as is possible for a human being.

A contemplation of the way in which one who has become obedient to God in all things will come to be above the natural and the written law.

The whole nature of beings is divided into intelligible and sensible things. The former are called, and are, eternal, since they received the beginning of their being in eternity, and the latter temporal, since they were made in time. The former fall under understanding, the latter under sense, because of the indissoluble power of the natural property of relation that binds them to one another. (For the relation of those who understand to what is understood, and of those who perceive to what is perceived, is strong. And the human being, consisting of soul and body, through his natural relation and property toward each of the two parts of creation in turn, both is circumscribed and circumscribes, the one by essence, the other by power: he is divided by his own parts toward these, and he draws these to himself in union through his own parts. For he is naturally circumscribed by intelligible and sensible things, as being soul and body, and naturally circumscribes them in power, as one who understands and perceives. But God is simply and without limit above all beings, both those that contain and those that are contained, and above the nature of the things without which these do not exist, I mean time, eternity and place, by which the universe is enclosed, since he is entirely without relation to anything.) If this is so, then whoever has wisely discerned how one must love God, who transcends reason and knowledge and absolutely every [?] relation of any kind and nature, will pass beyond all sensible and intelligible things and all time, eternity and place without attachment. Finally, having supernaturally stripped himself of all activity of sense, reason and mind, he will ineffably and unknowably attain the divine delight that is above reason and mind, in the manner and according to the principle known to God, who bestows such grace, and to those deemed worthy to receive [?] it from God. He no longer carries along with him anything natural or written, since everything that can be spoken or known has been entirely surpassed by him and reduced to silence.

A contemplation on the Gospel text about the man who fell among robbers.

And perhaps this is what is spent beyond the two denarii, which were given by the Lord at the inn for the healing of the man who fell among robbers to the one ordered to take care of him, and which the Lord generously promised to repay on his return: the complete removal of beings that comes about through faith in the perfect (for the Lord says, "Whoever does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple"). By this removal, taking all things away from himself, or, to put it more properly, himself from all things, the one who [has shown?] himself ever a lover of wisdom

[?]…having [?], he is deemed worthy to be with God alone, having received the adoption shown forth in the Gospel, after the example of the holy and blessed apostles. They stripped themselves completely of everything they had and clung wholly to God the Word alone, saying, "Behold, we have left everything and followed you." He is the Maker of nature and the Giver of the help that comes through the law. And having gained him, that is, the Lord, as the one and only light of truth in place of law and nature, they rightly received an unerring knowledge of all the things that come after God. For the knowledge of the things he has made is, properly speaking, naturally revealed together with him. Just as all bodies are clearly revealed along with the sensible sun when it rises, so God, the intelligible sun of righteousness, when he rises upon the mind, wills that the true principles of all things, both intelligible and sensible, be revealed together with himself, in the measure that he knows creation can contain him. This is shown at the Lord's transfiguration on the mountain by the bright garments, which were displayed together with the light of his face. This display, I think, gathers to God the knowledge of the things that come after him and surround him. For the eye cannot perceive sensible things without light, and the mind cannot receive spiritual contemplation without the knowledge of God. In the one case light gives sight its perception of visible things, and in the other the knowledge of God grants the mind its knowledge of intelligible things. Contemplation of the manner in which Adam's [?] came about.

Because the forefather Adam did not fix the eye of his soul on this divine light, he was rightly left like a blind man in the darkness of ignorance, groping willingly with both hands at the refuse of matter. He bent his whole self toward sense alone and gave himself over to it. Through sense he took in the destructive venom of the most bitter beast, and he did not even enjoy sense itself as he wished. He had tried to possess the things of God without God, before God, and not in accordance with God, as he should not have done, and this was impossible. He trusted sense as his counselor more than God, though sense had already let in the serpent. Sense held out to him the fruit of the forbidden tree, which he had been taught beforehand was joined with death. By making it the first fruits of his eating, he exchanged his life for a life suited to that fruit, and so fashioned for himself a living death for the whole time of the present age. For if death is the corruption of what comes into being, and the body that comes into being through the influx of food is always naturally corrupting, dissipated by that very flow, then through the things in which Adam believed life consisted he always kept death flourishing, for himself and for us. Had he obeyed God rather than his consort and been nourished from the tree of life, he would not have lost the immortality given to him, which is always preserved by participation in life,

since every life is naturally preserved by its own proper food. And the food of that blessed life is the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world, as the truthful Word declared about himself in the Gospels. Because the first man did not wish to be nourished by it, he was rightly deprived of the divine life and laid hold of another life, one that gives birth to death. In this life he put on himself an irrational form, darkened the inconceivable beauty of the divine, and handed over the whole of nature as food for death. Through this life death lives throughout this whole span of time, making us its food, while we never live, since we are always being devoured by it through corruption. That from the unstable cycle of the present life the saints were taught that there is another life, true and divine and always the same.

The saints wisely perceived how ineffectual this life is, one thing following upon another. They were taught, as was fitting, that this is not the life God first intended to give human beings. They were taught in a mystical way that there is another life, divine and always the same, which they understood that God, being good, must first of all have created as befitted him. Through wisdom and by the grace of the Spirit, as far as is possible for human beings subject to death, they lifted the eye of the soul toward that life and received inwardly the divine longing for it. They rightly judged that they must put away this present life if they were to lay hold of that one purely and as was due. And since a life cannot be put away without death, they devised as its death the casting off of fleshly affection, through which death had entered into life. In this way, by devising a death for death, they would cease to live for death. They died the death that is precious in the sight of the Lord, the death that is truly the death of death. It can corrupt corruption, and it gives the worthy entry into the blessed life and into incorruption. For I do not think it right even to call the end of this present life death. It is rather deliverance from death, separation from corruption, freedom from slavery, cessation of turmoil, the abolition of wars, the passing away of confusion, the withdrawal of darkness, relief from toil, silence after meaningless din, calm after seething, a covering for shame, escape from the passions, the obliteration of sin, and, to sum it up, the end of all evils. The saints achieved these things through voluntary mortification and so showed themselves strangers and sojourners in this life. They fought nobly against the world and the body and the revolts that arise from them. They stifled the deception that arises from both through the senses' entanglement with sensible things, and so kept the dignity of the soul unenslaved. And they were quite right to do so, judging it lawful and just that the lesser should be led

by the better, rather than that the better should be shackled by the worse. This is indeed a divine law, implanted in those who choose to embrace the life that first and foremost befits rational beings. Through frugality that life closely [?] imitates the angels' freedom from need and their ease. That the saints did not practice either natural contemplation or practical mystagogy in the way we do.

But let us return to the order of our discussion. Let us examine, as far as we are able, what remains to be said about the transfiguration, and fit it to what we have already contemplated. In this way the saints' excellence in all things and their genuine detachment from the flesh and from matter may be seen. We will also see that they did not contemplate [?] creation as we do, in a material and earthbound way, using only sense, surfaces and shapes for the [?] of the blessed knowledge of God, along with letters and syllables, from which comes stumbling and error in judging the truth. They contemplated it with the mind alone, a mind most pure and freed from all material mist. If, then, we wish to judge piously, examining the principles of sensible things in an intellectual way, we will see the saints walking rightly along a straight path to the unerring knowledge of God and of divine things. A broader contemplation of the transfiguration. It was said above that through the radiant brightness of the Lord's face on the mountain, the thrice-blessed apostles were led by the hand in a mystical way, ineffable and unknowable, toward what is wholly incomprehensible to all beings. They learned that the light which appeared to their senses was a symbol of the power and glory of the hidden mystery. Here the ray of the light that appeared overcame the activity of their eyes and remained beyond what their eyes could take in. In the same way, God there surpasses every power and activity of mind, leaving no imprint of any kind on the mind that tries to understand him. Through the white garments they were taught at one and the same time, in a manner befitting God, two things: the magnificence that is in creatures, in proportion to the principles according to which they were made, and the mystagogy that is in the words of holy Scripture, according to their meaning. For together with the knowledge of God, the power of Scripture according to the Spirit and the wisdom and knowledge in creatures according to the same Spirit are revealed, and through these he himself in turn is manifested in due proportion. Through Moses and Elijah, who were with him on either side (for this is what remains to be examined in the [?]), they received through true [?] contemplation many modes [?], according to many aspects of the mysteries whose types had been set forth beforehand.

1. First, through Moses and Elijah [?] they grasped that the word of the law and the word of the prophets must by all means be with God the Word, since they both come from him and speak about him, and are set firmly around him. 2. Next, through the same two they were taught that wisdom and goodness are with him. Wisdom, because by it the Word prescribes what must be done and forbids what must not be done; Moses was its type, for we believe that the grace of lawgiving belongs to wisdom. Goodness, because by it the Word exhorts those who have slipped away from the divine life and turns them back to it; Elijah was its type, displaying in himself the whole prophetic gift. For the distinctive mark of divine goodness is to turn back the erring with love for humanity, and we know the prophets to be its heralds. 3. Or they learned knowledge and correction. Knowledge, because the Word gives human beings the knowledge of good and evil. "I have set before your face," he says, "life and death," so that they may choose the one and flee the other, and not fall through ignorance into the worse as if it were good. Moses is declared to have done this, prefiguring in himself the symbols of the truth. Correction, because the Word punishes the indifference of those who freely make use of opposites, as Israel did, whose instructor the great Elijah became, and who mix indiscriminately things that cannot be mixed. As the Word, he also brings the folly and hardness of heart of those wholly given over to evil to awareness and perception. 4. Or they learned practice and contemplation. Practice destroys vice. Through the display of virtues it cuts off from the world entirely, in their disposition, those whom it leads, as Moses cut Israel off from Egypt, and it trains them to be led obediently by the divine laws of the Spirit. Contemplation snatches people away from matter and form, as the chariot of fire snatched away Elijah. Through knowledge it brings to God and unites with him those who are in no way weighed down by the flesh, because they have set aside the law of the flesh, and who are not inflamed in any way by pride at their achievements, because of the dew of poverty of spirit joined to true virtues. 5. Or again, they learned that there are mysteries with the Word concerning marriage and celibacy. They learned this through Moses, who was not prevented by marriage from becoming a lover of divine glory, and through Elijah, who remained entirely pure of marital union. For the Word and God proclaims that he mystically adopts as his own those who govern these things by reason, according to the divinely given laws concerning them. 6. Or through the same two they were fully assured in faith that the Word is Lord of life and death.

7. Or they learned through the same two that all live to God and that no one at all is dead in his sight, except the one who has put himself to death through sin and cut himself off from the Word by willingly inclining toward the passions. 8. Or again they were enlightened to see that the types of the mysteries exist with reference to the Word, who is the truth, and are gathered together into him as the beginning and end of the whole work of the law and the prophets. 9. Or they were enlightened to see that all things that come after God and from God, that is, the nature of beings and time, are with God, and are revealed together with him, as far as possible, when he truly appears as their cause and maker. Of these Moses would be the type of time. He is so not only as the teacher of time and of its numbering (for he was the first to number the time from the creation of the world), and as one who became the leader of a worship bound to time. He is so also because he did not enter bodily into the rest together with those to whom he was a guide before the divine good news. Time is like this too: in its motion it does not arrive or enter together with those whom it naturally conveys to the divine life of the age to come. For time has as its successor Joshua, that is, Jesus, who is the successor of all time and every age. Yet the principles of time still remain in God in another way, as is mystically shown by the law given through Moses in the desert entering the land together with those who received it as their possession. For time is age when it ceases from motion, and age is time when it is carried along by motion and measured. So age, to put it in the form of a definition, is time deprived of motion, and time is age measured by motion. Elijah would be the type of nature. He is so not only because he kept the principles of nature in himself unharmed, and kept the disposition of his will toward them free from any change caused by passion. He is so also because, like a natural law, he instructed through judgment those who use nature in a way contrary to nature. For nature too is like this: it punishes those who try to corrupt it in proportion to the unnatural course they pursue. They no longer naturally possess the whole power of nature, since they have already been diminished in their natural integrity, and they are punished for this, having unwillingly and foolishly brought upon themselves, by inclining toward non-being, the [?] of being.

10. Perhaps someone who says that through Moses and Elijah the intelligible and the sensible creation are shown to hold fast to the Creator Word will not miss the truth. Of these Moses stands for the sensible creation, since he was subject to birth and corruption, as the history about him shows by recording his birth and his death. Sensible creation is like this too, having a known beginning of its coming-into-being and

[?] BOOK. expecting a fixed end in corruption. Elijah stands for the intelligible creation, since the history about him neither reveals his birth, though he was born, nor determines that corruption through death is to be expected, though he will die. The intelligible creation is like this too. It has no beginning of its coming-into-being that is evident to human beings, though it did come into being, had a beginning and was brought from non-being into being. Nor does it await an end of its being determined by corruption, for it naturally possesses indestructibility, having received it from God, who willed to create it so. [?] Another great and divine mystery, I think, appears to us from the divine transfiguration, more splendid than those already mentioned. For I think that the God-befitting visions on the mountain at the transfiguration mystically teach the two general modes of theology. The first is the prior mode, simple and without cause. Through complete negation alone it truly affirms the divine, and through silence it fittingly glorifies the divine transcendence. The second follows the first and is composite. Through affirmation it magnificently [?] the divine from its effects. By these, as far as human beings can know, [?] concerning God and divine things [?] hovering [?] principles, teaching that every symbol beyond sense belongs to the first mode, and that the magnificent works perceived by the senses are gathered [?] into the second. For from the symbols beyond sense we believe only that the truth beyond reason and mind exists. We do not dare in any way to examine what it is, how, of what kind, where or when, nor do we entertain the thought, since we refuse the impiety of the attempt. But from the things perceived by sense we form, as far as is possible for us and only in concept, faint conjectures of the knowledge of God. We say that he is all the things that we have come to know him to be, as their cause, from his works. That the Lord became a type of himself in his dispensation in the flesh. Let us examine whether the symbol of each of these modes is not present, well and wisely, in that divine transfiguration of the Lord. For [?] he consented, through boundless love for humanity, to be created like us without change, and to become a type and symbol of himself. He showed himself symbolically from himself, and through himself appearing he led the whole of creation by the hand to himself, who is hidden invisibly in every way. And [?] of the invisible one, beyond all things, hidden in mystery, who cannot be understood or spoken of in any way at all by any being [?]

The light of the Lord's face, then, which overcame human [?], [was a symbol] for the blessed apostles of mystical theology by way of negation. According to this theology the blessed and holy Godhead is in its essence beyond ineffable and beyond unknowable, and infinitely raised above all infinity. It leaves not even a bare trace of comprehension to those who come after it. Nor does it permit any being to conceive how and in what way the same Godhead is both monad and triad, since the uncreated cannot be contained by creation, nor the infinite comprehended by finite things. Contemplation of the Lord's shining garments. The affirmative mode is divided into activity, providence and judgment. The mode according to activity, which from the beauty and greatness of creatures teaches that God is the creator of all things, is shown through the Lord's bright garments, which the Word [?] displayed as the visible creatures. Contemplation of Moses. The mode according to providence is signified through Moses. For providence lovingly delivers from error those who have been caught by vice, and wisely varies for human beings the ways [?] of departing from material, corruptible and bodily things toward divine, immaterial and incorporeal ones, and knowingly establishes them firmly in the divine laws. Contemplation of Elijah. The mode of judgment is indicated through Elijah. For judgment, by word and deed, punishes some as they deserve and cares for others, since it is fitted to each appropriately according to the underlying matter and [?] of virtue or vice. In the present passage of holy Scripture, Moses and Elijah, as those above all who sketched divine things typologically in their own persons, each in his own time historically [?] all these things we have contemplated, things resembling what has been said by way of contemplation. Contemplation of the conversation of Moses and Elijah with the Lord at the transfiguration. From their talking with the Lord and

speaking of the departure he was to fulfil in Jerusalem, the apostles were taught not only the fulfilment, in him, of the mysteries proclaimed beforehand through the law and the prophets. Perhaps they were also taught that no being whatever can grasp the end of God's ineffable will concerning the universe and of the divine dispensations that serve it. They can grasp only his great providence and judgment, through which the universe hastens in good order toward the end foreknown to God alone. All were equally ignorant of this end: what it is, how, of what kind, and when. Only the saints, who had purified the soul by the virtues and had turned its whole intellectual inclination toward divine things, truly knew that it will be, and only that. They heard, so to speak, the universal nature of visible things itself all but shouting aloud, through the modes by which it naturally holds together, the end of its present good order.

Natural contemplation showing that the world must necessarily have an end. They surveyed the present world as knowledgeably as possible. In the bodies fitted together in it in various ways they wisely unfolded in thought the principle folded up within them. And they found that some of these bodies are sensible, some perceptive [?], and some universal, but that all are contained by all and turned about by the alternation of the qualitative property of each. For perceptive things are contained by nature in sensible things, and sensible things are contained by perceptive things through sensation, as things perceived. And again, universals are turned about by particulars through alteration, and particulars by universals through dissolution, and so they are corrupted. The corruption of the one comes about through the generation of the others. For the coming together of universals with one another, which produces the generation of particulars, is their mutual corruption through alteration. And the dissolution of particulars back into universals through the loosing of their bond, which brings about their corruption, is the persistence and generation of universals. They learned that this is how the sensible world is constituted: through the mutual corruption and alteration of the bodies in it, from which and in which it subsists. Consequently they were taught that its consummation must necessarily come in due sequence, because the property of the bodies of which it is universally composed is by nature unstable, subject to alteration, and moved and turned now one way and now another. They reasoned rightly that it is not possible, nor even a mark of rational understanding, to call everlasting what is not always the same, without change or any alteration whatever, but is scattered and turned about in countless ways.

[Natural?] contemplation of the age to come, and of what the chasm between God and human beings is, and what Lazarus [?] and the bosom of the patriarch are. Having risen from there above visible things,

[?] they nobly conjectured the absolute end of all things, in which nothing among beings is any longer carried along or carrying, nor is there any movement at all of anything, because an ineffable fixity has set bounds to the course and movement of things that are carried along and moved. Longing to reach this in mind while still clothed in corruptible flesh, they wisely crossed the chasm between God and human beings, having willingly died to the flesh and the world in their attachment. For the truly fearful and great chasm between God and human beings is affection and attachment to the body and to this world. Lazarus nobly and gladly embraced being deprived of these things, as both his sickness and his poverty show: the one brought about his estrangement from the world, the other his estrangement from the body. So he was counted worthy to receive rest in the bosom of Abraham, and left outside that relief the rich man who had clung to these things. The rich man gained nothing else from his life in the flesh except endless punishment for it. He no longer has the present life, which alone he loved and embraced, since by nature it cannot be held onto in [?]. Nor can he share in the life to come, toward which he remained utterly idle and without love, since by nature it unites itself only with those who have loved it wholly, and who for longing of it have readily and gladly endured every hardship. When we hear "the bosom of Abraham," we will understand God, who appeared to us in the flesh from the seed of Abraham. He is truly the giver of all things. To all who are worthy of grace he distributes himself without division, as if in various portions, in proportion to the quality and quantity of each one's virtue. Yet he is in no way divided along with those who partake of him, because the reality of his unity is by nature undivided. And again, because of the differing worth of those who partake, he paradoxically appears distinctly in their participations, in an ineffable union (the Word knows how). No one who delights in the luxury of the flesh, and takes more pleasure in the deceit of the world than in his blessed glory, will be able to cross over to him. Nor will someone defeated by the world, who wickedly exults in it, stand with the One who has conquered the world. For divine justice (166a) judged it unfitting that those who limit human life to this present life, who pride themselves on wealth, bodily health and other honours, who judge this alone to be blessedness and set the goods of the soul at nothing, should share in the divine and eternal goods, which they did not [?] at all. Through their great [?] concerning [?], they failed to recognize how far the virtues surpass wealth, health and the other passing goods. Contemplation on the virtues. For the virtues alone make a person blessed, whether together with the other goods or by themselves. Together with the others, [?]

they do so by breadth, as one of those wise in divine matters said; alone and by themselves, they do so by circumscription. For some beings are conceived by circumscription, like a length of two cubits, and others by breadth, like a heap. If you take two measures from a heap, what is left is still a heap. In the same way, if you take away the goods of the body and the external goods from blessedness considered by breadth, and leave only the virtues, blessedness still remains complete. For virtue is sufficient by itself to make its possessor happy. So every wicked person who lacks the virtues is wretched, even if he has every one of the so-called goods of the earth. And every good person is blessed, even if he is deprived of all goods on earth, because he has the splendour of virtue, with which Lazarus [?] rests in the bosom of Abraham and rejoices.

Another contemplation on "If you are crucified as a thief." And again: the right-minded thief is the one who has been counted worthy (167a) to be crucified with Christ by the complete and total expulsion of the passions. He is crucified with him on the right, that is, he goes through every virtue with reason and knowledge, keeps his life free of offence to all people, and has no movement at all that, through harshness, is out of tune with the gentleness of the Word. The ungrateful thief is the one who, for the sake of glory or larger gains, deceitfully plays the part of the virtuous life in his outward manners. Toward outsiders he pursues one single thing, flattering speech, in place of all virtue and knowledge, while toward those close to him he is crooked in mind [?] and hard to deal with. When such a person blasphemes the way of God, he must certainly be silenced with understanding. For perhaps, at the admonition of the one who rebukes him, he will stop slandering the word by his own conduct, as happened on the cross to the thief who boldly uttered blasphemy. For when someone does not answer back the one who rebuked him, his silence is a sign that he accepts what was said. So in whichever of the ways described we are crucified with Christ, let us strive, while we are here, to win the favour of the Word who is crucified with us. And let us receive his unlying promise of rest in a conscience cleansed of the thoughts that wound it. For "today" indicates the present day of this age ("Today," he says, "you will be with me in paradise"), and "tomorrow" indicates the day of the age to come. On that day we must expect no forgiveness of sins, only the repayment that each person deserves for the life he has lived.

[?] higher than the high [?], more wonderful than the wonderful [?]. And again, the first [Sunday] [?] is a symbol of the natural resurrection and incorruption, while the second bears the image of the deification by grace that is to come. The enjoyment of good things is more honourable than a state free of evils. The state of perfection in true knowledge is more honourable than a choice made healthy by virtue. And transformation toward God by grace, in deification, is more honourable than natural incorruption. The first Sunday bears the type of the lesser and the second is the symbol of the greater. So it was fitting that the teacher, led by the Spirit, called the new Sunday higher than the high. Natural contemplation, by which the saints were taught about God from created things. In this way the saints contemplated creation: its good order and proportion, and the use that each thing provides to the whole. They saw that all things have been made perfect, wisely and providentially, according to the principle by which they were made, and that [?] could not be well in any other way than they now are, needing no addition or subtraction to be better. So they were taught about the Creator from his works. In the same way they observed the permanence, order and position of the things that have come to be, and the way they are governed, by which each thing stands in its own species, unconfused and free of all mixing. They observed the course of the stars, which always proceeds in the same way and never varies at all, and the cycle of the year, which comes round in good order by the return [?] of the same things from the same place to the same place. And they observed the [?] balance of nights and days, each growing and shrinking in turn, with neither more nor less increase or decrease falling to them. From all this they understood that there is a provider of beings, whom [?] God and Creator of all things [?].

Natural contemplation showing that the world has a beginning and a coming-into-being, as does everything else after God. For who, seeing the beauty and greatness of God's creatures, would not at once think of him as their source, as the beginning, cause and Maker of beings? Who would not run up in thought to him alone and leave these things below, since by nature they cannot contain the whole ascent of the mind? Such a person longs to grasp directly the One he came to know through the works as intermediaries, and his own error that the world is without beginning

he will readily reject. For he truly reasons that everything that is moved has certainly also begun its motion. And no motion is without a beginning, since none is without a cause either. (168a) For motion has the mover as its beginning, and as its cause the end which calls and draws it, toward which it moves. Now the mover is the beginning of every motion of every moved thing, and the end toward which the moved thing is carried is its cause (for nothing moves without a cause). And nothing among beings is unmoved except the first mover (for the first mover is certainly unmoved, since it is also without beginning). So nothing among beings is without beginning, since nothing is unmoved. For all things that exist in any way are moved, except the single cause that is unmoved and above all things. Intellectual and rational beings are moved by way of knowledge and understanding, since they are not knowledge itself or understanding itself. For their knowledge and understanding are not their essence. They are habits observed in their essence, which arise from right judgment by intellect and reason (I mean their constitutive powers). Contemplation on the contraction and expansion of essence, quality and quantity, because of which these cannot be without beginning. Essence spoken of simply is not only moved by generation and corruption, as is the essence of things subject to generation and corruption. The essence of all beings has been moved and is moved by the principle and mode of expansion and contraction. For it is moved from the most general genus, through the more general genera, into the species through which and into which it is naturally divided, and it proceeds as far as the most specific species. There its expansion ends, setting a lower limit to its being. And it is gathered again from the most specific species, retracing its steps through the more general (168b) up to the most general genus. There its contraction ends, setting an upper limit to its being. So, being circumscribed from both sides, I mean from above and from below, it is shown to have a beginning and an end, and it cannot admit the principle of infinity at all. Likewise with quantity. It is not only the quantity of things subject to generation and corruption that is moved by increase and decrease, in every way in which this can be observed. All quantity of all things is moved by the principle of relaxation and intensification. It takes specific form by expanding into particular differences and is circumscribed, since it cannot be [?] poured out without limit. And it is gathered again, retracing its steps, setting aside the form belonging to those differences but not its own connatural form. Similarly with quality. It is not only the quality of things subject to generation and corruption that is moved by alteration. All quality of all things is moved by the changeability and [?] of its differences, and so admits expansion and contraction. And no one in his right mind would say that what is naturally

scattered and gathered, in principle or in activity, is entirely unmoved. And if it is not unmoved, it is not without beginning either. And if it is not without beginning, it is clearly not ungenerated either. Just as such a person knows that what is moved has begun its motion, so he understands that what has come into being has begun its coming into being, and has received both its being and its motion from the one and only ungenerated and unmoved. And what has begun as regards the coming-into-being of its being can in no way be without beginning [?].

Demonstration that every being apart from God is certainly in place, and therefore necessarily also in time, and that what is in place is certainly in time and has begun to be. (169a) I will pass over the argument that the very being of beings, which they have in a certain way and not simply, is the first form of circumscription, and is a strong and weighty proof that beings have begun in essence and in coming-to-be. Who does not know that for everything that exists in any way whatever, except the divine alone [?], which properly exists even beyond being itself, the "where" is conceived in advance, and that the "when" is necessarily conceived along with it in every respect? For it is not possible to conceive of the "where" with the "when" removed from it. These belong together [?], since each is something without which the other cannot exist. Nor is the "when", which by nature is conceived along with the "where", ever separated from it. That all things are under the "where," being in place, is shown as follows. The universe itself is not beyond the universe, for it would be both irrational and impossible to declare that the universe itself lies beyond its own totality. Rather, it has its circumscription from itself and within itself, after the infinite power of the cause of all things which circumscribes everything: its own outermost boundary is its limit. This is also the place of the universe, as some define place when they say: "Place is the circumference outside the universe," or "the position outside the universe," or "the limit of the container in which the contained is contained." And it will be shown along with this that they are under the "when," since they are certainly in time. For all things that have being after God have being not simply but in a certain way, and for this reason they are not without beginning. For everything that admits the principle of "how" in any way at all, even if it now is, once was not. That is why, when we say that the Divine is, we do not say that it is in a certain way. (169b) And for this reason we say both "Is" and "Was" of it simply, without limit and absolutely. For the Divine cannot be grasped by any word or thought, and so even when we predicate being of it, we do not say that it is. For being comes from it, but it is not being itself. It is beyond even being itself, whether being is spoken of and conceived as being in a certain way or as being simply. But if beings have being in a certain way and not simply, then just as they are under the "where" because of position and the limit

of the natural principles in them, so they will certainly also admit being under the "when" because of their beginning. Demonstration that whatever has its being in a quantity of number cannot be infinite, and so is not without beginning either. And again: the essence of all things cannot be infinite, since all things are many. For the quantity of the many beings in number is its limit, circumscribing the principle both of its being and of its manner of being, for the essence of all things is not unbounded. Clearly, then, the hypostasis of each individual will not be without circumscription either, since they are circumscribed by one another in number and in essence according to principle. And if no being is free from circumscription, then clearly all beings, each in proportion to itself, have received both being "when" and being "where." For without these nothing at all will be able to exist: not essence, not quantity, not quality, not relation, not action, not passion, not motion, not habit, nor any of the other things by which those expert in these matters encompass the universe. So no being is without beginning if something else can be conceived before it (170a), and no being is uncircumscribed if something else can be conceived along with it. And if no being is without beginning or uncircumscribed, as the argument has shown by following the nature of beings consistently, then there certainly was a time when each being was not. And if it was not, it certainly came into being, since it was not. For it is not possible both to be and to come to be without change and alteration. If it was and also came to be, then either it changed, passing in its coming-to-be into what it was not, or it was altered, showing an addition of [?] that it had lacked. And whatever changes or is altered, or lacks form, cannot be perfect in itself. What is not perfect in itself will certainly need something else to give it perfection. Such a thing is perfect, but not perfect in itself, because it has perfection not by nature but by participation. And what needs something else for its perfection will need it much more for its very being. For, as they say, essence is superior to form. Suppose that this being was able to provide essence to itself, or simply to have it, as they themselves wish to claim. How then was it not sufficient to have simply, or to provide to itself, the lesser thing, I mean form? Some call this being essence and some call it matter: those who dare to attribute beginninglessness to things that come after God and from God (we do not dispute the name). But if it was not sufficient to provide itself with the lesser thing, or simply to have it, how could it have the greater thing, I mean being itself, either simply or from itself, when it is incapable of having the lesser? If matter has in no way been able to have the lesser thing from itself (170b), much more

will it be unable to have being itself from itself, whether simply or in a certain way. So matter, which as has been shown is too weak to have the lesser thing, I mean form, could never have the greater thing, I mean being itself, in any way at all. And if so, both being and form have certainly been given by God to beings, since they exist. And if all essence, both matter and every form, is from God, no one who is not entirely bereft of sound reasoning would allow himself to say that matter is without beginning or ungenerated, knowing that God is the maker and creator of beings. Demonstration that nothing which is moved, or which has something else differing from it in essence contemplated along with it from eternity, can be infinite; that the dyad is neither a beginning nor without beginning; and that the monad alone is properly a beginning and without beginning. And again: if matter existed, as some say, then clearly it did not come to be. And if it did not come to be, it is not moved either. And if it is not moved, it did not begin to be either. And if it did not begin to be, it is certainly without beginning. And if it is without beginning, it is also infinite. And if it is infinite, it is certainly also unmoved (for the infinite is certainly unmoved, since what is not bounded has nowhere to move). And if so, there are certainly two infinite, beginningless and unmoved realities, God and matter, which is impossible. For a dyad can be neither infinite, nor without beginning, nor unmoved, nor indeed the beginning of anything at all, since it is circumscribed by union and by division. It is circumscribed by union because its existence is a composition of monads, which contain it as parts and into which it can be cut as into parts. (Nothing that is divisible or being divided, or composite or being composed, whether by nature or by position or in any other conceivable way, can be infinite, nor indeed can division or composition spoken of simply, since none of these is simple and single. Nor can anything that is countable, counted or counted together with something, or anything that is not free from every relation whatever. For all these things are contemplated in relation, while the infinite is without relation, since nothing at all is joined to it by relation.) And it is circumscribed by division because it is moved by number, from which it began and by which it is contained, since it does not have its being or its freedom from relation by nature. For every dyad, and every monad that contributes to it as a part, exists by number, through which the monads in it take uncircumscribedness away from one another. And no one with any share of reason at all would say that something is infinite if something different from it in essence is contemplated or observed along with it from eternity. He would know that his whole argument about the infinite would collapse if he held this view. For the infinite is infinite in every principle and mode: in essence, in power, in activity, and at both limits, I mean the upper and the lower, that is, at the beginning and the end. For the infinite cannot be contained in its essence, it is [?] in its power, and in its

activity it is uncircumscribed. It is without beginning from above and without end from below, and, to put it simply and more truly, it is unlimited in every respect, since nothing at all can be conceived along with it in any of the modes listed. (171b) For whatever the principle or mode in which we say that something else, differing from it in essence, can be set alongside it, we thereby take away from it the whole principle of its complete infinity. If something cannot be infinite when something else differing in essence coexists with it from eternity, a dyad can in no way be infinite. For the monads in it, coexisting side by side, limit one another. Neither allows the other to be seen without limit, since each has the other lying beside it rather than surpassing it, and so they rightly take the principle of infinity away from one another. If, as has been shown, a dyad cannot be infinite, it is clearly not without beginning either, for the beginning of every dyad is the monad. And if it is not without beginning, it is not unmoved either, for it is moved by number, receiving its being from monads by union and into them by division. And if it is not unmoved, it cannot be the beginning of anything else either. For what is moved is not a beginning but comes from a beginning, namely the mover. The monad alone is properly unmoved, since it is neither number nor countable nor counted (for the monad is neither part nor whole nor relation). It is properly without beginning, since it has nothing older than itself from which it might be moved and receive its being as monad. It is properly infinite, since it has nothing coexisting with it or counted together with it. And it is properly a beginning, since it is the cause of all number, of all that is counted and of all that is countable, as being exempt from all relation and from every part and whole. It is so properly and truly, (172a) primarily, solely and simply, and not in a certain way, being the first and only monad. Yet in saying this we do not signify the blessed Godhead itself as it is. The Godhead is infinitely, in every principle and mode, utterly inaccessible and unapproachable to every mind, every word and every name. Rather, we provide ourselves with a firm rule of faith in it, one that is within our reach and suited to us. For the divine word does not use this name, I mean the name of monad, as if it fully represented the divine and blessed essence. It uses it to indicate the essence's complete simplicity, which is beyond all quantity, all quality and every relation of any kind, so that we may know that it is not some whole made of parts, nor some part of a whole. For the Godhead is above all division, composition and part, since it is without quantity. It is removed from all existence by position [?] and from every notion that defines how it is, since it is without quality. It is free and unbound from every connection and kinship with anything else, since it is without relation, having nothing before it, with it or after it, as being beyond all things, and [?] none of beings

…arranged according to no principle or manner. Perhaps it was with this in mind that the great and divine Dionysius says: “Therefore the Godhead beyond all things, though hymned as Monad and Triad, is neither a monad nor a triad as known by us or by any other being. But so that we may truly celebrate both its supra-unity and its divine fecundity, we have named the One beyond all names with the triadic and unitary divine name, and the One beyond being with the names of beings.” So no one who has resolved to live piously in truth will ever be able to say that a dyad or a multiplicity is without beginning, or that it is the principle of anything at all. For through every contemplative power and knowledge that accords with reason and mind, God will appear to him as the one who is beyond all infinity and [related] in no way whatever to any being, except that he is known through faith alone, and this from his works: known to exist, but not known in what he is. He alone is maker and creator of every age and time and of all things in age and time. Such a person will conceive nothing at all as existing from eternity together with him in any way whatsoever, knowing that, of things that have coexisted with one another in their existence from eternity, neither can be the maker of the other. For it is utterly illogical and impossible, and to those who have sense ridiculous, that among things which have being at the same time one should be made the maker of another. Rather, he will accept that all things came into being from God, who always is, out of what is not, completely and wholly and not partially or imperfectly, as wisely brought forth from a cause infinite in knowledge and infinite in power. He will accept that all things subsist in him, guarded and held together as in an all-sovereign foundation, and that all things turn back to him as to their proper end, as the great Dionysius the Areopagite says somewhere. A demonstrative contemplation showing that God's providence extends over all things by nature. He will also be persuaded that God is provider of beings, through the very things by which he was taught that he is God, judging it just and reasonable that the guardian and caretaker of beings should be none other than their creator alone. For the very permanence of beings, their order, position and motion, the way the extremes cohere with one another through the means without harming one another through their contrariety, the convergence of the parts toward the wholes, the thorough union of the wholes with the parts, and the…

…unmixed distinction of the parts from one another according to the particular difference of each, their unconfused union according to their unvarying identity within the wholes, the combination and distinction of all things with all things (not to speak of each one individually), and the succession of all things and of each according to its species, always preserved, with nothing whatever corrupting the proper principle of its nature or being confused with another or confusing another: all this shows clearly that all things must be held together by the providence of God who made them. For it is not possible that God, being good, should not be wholly beneficent, nor that being beneficent he should not be wholly provident. Therefore, caring for beings in a manner befitting God, he wisely bestows his care upon them just as he bestows their being. For providence, according to the God-bearing Fathers, is the care that comes from God to beings. They also define it thus: providence is the will of God through which all beings receive their fitting direction. And if it is God's will (to use the teachers' own words), it is entirely necessary that whatever happens should happen according to right reason, admitting no better order. So whoever has chosen to have truth as his guide will be led to say, in every way, that the one whom he truly knew as maker of beings is also their provider, and none other than he who made beings. Even in animals, when we approach beings by rational inquiry, we find a reflection of our own intellectual nature that, in no ignoble way, images what is beyond reason. For when we see them caring by nature for their own offspring according to kind, we too take courage and piously define for ourselves, with pious boldness, the doctrine that God alone is the provider of all beings. He provides not for some and not for others, as some of the outside philosophers held, but for all together, according to one unvarying will of goodness, for universals and particulars alike. For we know that if all particulars were destroyed through not receiving providence and fitting protection, the universals too would be destroyed with them, since universals by nature consist of particulars. We set before ourselves the logical demonstration of this, which by a reasonable conversion leads rightly to the truth. For if universals subsist in particulars, and in no way possess a principle of being and subsisting by themselves, it is surely clear to everyone that when the particulars are destroyed the universals will not stand either. For parts exist and subsist in wholes, and wholes in parts. No argument will contradict this. Indeed, as though bound by the truth, these philosophers themselves unwillingly proclaim the power of providence, and by the very things they have eagerly argued establish that it pervades all things. For in saying that only universals are guided by providence, they have unwittingly said that there is providence of particulars too, being led of necessity toward the truth that they are striving to flee. For if…

…they say that universals are deemed worthy of providence for the sake of their permanence, they imply that the particulars, in which the permanence and subsistence of the universals lie, are much more worthy of it. For these are introduced together because of their natural, indissoluble relation to one another. When one is preserved in its permanence, the other is not excluded from this protection; and again, if one fails to receive protection for its permanence, it follows that the other does not receive it either. Besides, the claim that God does not provide for all beings is made in three ways: they say either that he does not know the method of providence, or that he does not will it, or that he is not able. But according to the common notions of all, God, being good and beyond good, always wills what is good, and wills it for all. Being wise and beyond wise, or rather the source of all wisdom, he knows fully what is beneficial. Being powerful, or rather infinite in power, he accomplishes in all things, in a manner befitting God, what he knows and wills as good and beneficial, since he is good and wise and powerful. He pervades all things visible and invisible, universal and particular, small and great, and all that have being in any essence of whatever kind, relaxing nothing of his infinity in goodness, wisdom and power. And he preserves all things, each according to the principle of its being, both in themselves and in relation to one another, in the indissoluble relational harmony and permanence of all. And what of this: do we not see that nature itself, by itself, is clearly a teacher of God's providence over all things? For nature itself gives no small proof that the knowledge of providence has been sown in us by nature, when, untaught, it pushes us as it were toward God through prayer and prepares us in sudden crises to seek salvation from him. For when we are suddenly seized by necessity, we call upon God involuntarily, before we have even thought, as though providence itself were drawing us to itself without any reasoning, outrunning the swiftness of our intellectual power and showing that divine help is stronger than all things. Nature would not lead us involuntarily toward something that does not exist by nature. And everything that follows naturally upon anything, as is clear to all, has a strong and invincible [?] in regard to…

…needs and pursuits, and the very reasonings of the soul, which are almost infinite, and changing along with everything that happens each day and hour (for man is a quickly turning creature, rapidly changing with the times and his needs), it is altogether necessary that providence too, [?] having comprehended all particulars by circumscription, should appear varied, diverse and manifold. It must extend itself along with the incomprehensible multitude of things and fit itself appropriately to each one, in every matter and thought, down even to the bare movements that arise in soul and body. If, then, the difference among particulars is incomprehensible, and the principle of the providence suited to them is fittingly infinite, still, just because the principle of providence over particulars is infinite and unknown to us, we must not make our own ignorance into a denial of the all-wise care of beings. Rather, we must simply and without scrutiny praise and accept all the works of providence as befitting God and beneficial, and believe that what happens happens well, even if its principle is beyond our reach. When I say “all the works of providence,” I do not mean the things wrongly done by us through what is in our own power, for these are wholly alien to the principle of providence. Now, as for the meaning indicated by this great teacher concerning the power and grace of the saints in reason and contemplation, I have run through it, as far as possible, by what has been said, and as it were tracked it, conjecturally and not assertively (for our mind falls far short of the measure of the truth in him). I offer the following merely as a surmise. A different contemplation of the material dyad handed down by the saints, and what the unity understood in the Trinity is. By “rising above the material dyad because of the unity understood in the Trinity,” I surmise that he means that the saints rose above matter and form, of which bodies consist. Or else he meant that, having as it were passed through the flesh and matter, they were united with God and deemed worthy to be mingled with the purest light. That is, they put off the soul's relation to the flesh, and through the flesh to matter, or, to speak generally, the natural affinity of all sense-perceiving essence to what is sensible, and laid genuine hold on the divine longing alone, because of the unity understood, as I said, in the Trinity. For knowing that the soul lies between God and matter and has powers that unite it to both, I mean the mind toward God and sense toward matter, they utterly shook off sense together with sensible things, as regards its relational activity in their disposition, and by the mind alone ineffably…

…[achieved] affinity with God. Seeing the soul united wholly to him, the whole of him, without confusion, as an image of the archetype according to mind, reason and spirit, and bearing his resemblance by likeness as far as is attainable, they were mystically taught the unity understood in the Trinity. Or perhaps the teacher called anger and desire the material dyad, because they are powers bound up with matter and belonging to the passible part of the soul. They rebel against reason and are able to scatter the mind among many things, unless one yokes them to himself from the beginning, leading them with knowledge. If anyone should master them and persuade them to be borne fittingly where they ought, yoked as servants to the dominion of reason, or even abandon them completely and leave them behind, and hold only to the unwavering, knowing enchantment of love through reason and contemplation; and if he has been drawn together out of the many into one single, pure, simple and undivided movement of the most virile power of longing, by which he has philosophically fixed for himself a stability around God, incomprehensibly, in the sameness of longing's perpetual motion: then such a one is truly blessed. He has attained not only the true and blessed [?] toward the holy Trinity, but also the union understood in the holy Trinity, having become simple, undivided and uniform in power in relation to that which is simple and undivided in essence. Through the habit of the virtues he imitates, as far as attainable, the goodness that is likewise [?], and through the grace of the God to whom he has been united he has laid aside the particularity of the powers that are divided by nature. An explanation of the passible part of the soul and its general divisions and subdivisions. The passible part of the soul, as they say, is divided into what obeys reason and what does not obey reason. What does not obey reason they divide into the nutritive, which they call natural, and the [?], which they call vital. Neither of these is led by obedience to reason. It is called disobedient to reason because it is not of a nature to be led by reason: growing, being healthy, or living is not up to us. What obeys reason is divided into two, the desiring and the spirited. They call it obedient to reason because in virtuous people it is naturally led by reason and subject to it. The desiring part, again, they divide into pleasure and pain: desire that attains its object produces pleasure, and desire that fails produces pain. Again, in another way, they say that desire when divided produces four species in all, itself included: desire, pleasure, fear and pain. For since some beings are good and others bad, and these are either present or future, they call an expected good desire and a present good pleasure, and again an expected evil fear and a present evil pain. So pleasure and desire exist and are seen [?]…

…in relation to good things, whether truly existing or only supposed, while pain and fear exist in relation to bad things. Again, they divide pain into four: grief, distress, envy and pity. Grief, they say, is pain that produces speechlessness in those in whom it arises, because it penetrates deep into the reasoning faculty. Distress is pain that weighs one down and troubles one over unwanted events. Envy is pain at the good things of others, and pity is pain at the evils of others. They said that all pain is evil by its own nature. For even if the virtuous man is pained at the evils of others because he is merciful, this is not primarily by his intention but consequently, by circumstance. But the contemplative remains impassible even in these things, having joined himself to God and estranged himself from present things. Fear, again, they divide into six: hesitation, modesty, shame, consternation, amazement and anxiety. Hesitation, they say, is fear of an action to come; modesty is fear in expectation of blame; shame is fear over a disgraceful deed already done; consternation is fear arising from a great image in the imagination; amazement is fear arising from great things heard, which deprives one of sensation; and anxiety is fear of falling short, that is, of failure, for it is when we fear failing that we are anxious. Some also call it cowardice. Anger, again, they say is a boiling of the blood around the heart from a desire to inflict pain in return. This too they divide into three: wrath, which some have called bile and choler, resentment and rancor. Wrath, they say, is anger that has its beginning and movement toward action, or anger in action. Bile is retaliation against the one who caused pain carried out through someone else; choler is the pursuit of the offender by the injured person himself. Resentment (mēnis) is anger grown old; it is so called from its “remaining” (menein) and being retained in the memory. Rancor (kotos) is anger watching for an opportunity for revenge; this too is so called from “lying in wait” (keisthai). They also divide each of these into many others. If anyone wished to commit these to writing with exact examination, he would amass a long discourse and spend much time, so that because of its length it would be unbearable for its readers. It is truly a great and marvellous thing, needing much attention and effort, and above all divine help, to be able, first, to master the material dyad of innate powers, I mean anger and desire, together with their subdivisions (and blessed is he who has been able to lead them readily wherever reason sees fit), until, by means of moral philosophy, he has been purified of his former thoughts through practical [virtue].

A contemplation from Scripture showing that the gnostic must not join the [?] of wisdom to the law of nature, and what the addition of the letter alpha to the name of Abraham means. And then to rise above them and reject them completely, as that great Abraham did Hagar and Ishmael, once the reasoning faculty, like that Isaac, was already able to be exercised in divine spectacles. He was taught by the divine voice conveyed through knowledge that the divine offspring of the mind, born of the free knowledge that is according to the Spirit, cannot, if joined to the servile seed of the flesh, attain the blessed promise. That promise is the grace of deification laid up in hope for those who love the Lord, which he had already received typologically, mystically through faith, in the word concerning the monad.

Perhaps that great Moses too was taught this at the beginning of his gnostic training, instructed by the divine voice when he approached to see the light mystically appearing in the bush. It said, “Loose the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” This shows, I think, that the soul must be loosed in its disposition from all bodily things when it is about to make its gnostic journey through contemplation toward the understanding of supramundane realities, and that through putting off the sandals it must have complete estrangement from its former life in relation to the flesh. A contemplation on the parts of the sacrifices. Perhaps the same most divine Moses again indicated this in the ordinances of the sacrifices, when he commanded that the fat, the kidneys, the breast and the lobe of the liver be removed from the victims. This means that the generic powers of the passions in us, I mean anger and desire, the truly material dyad, together with their activities, must be removed and melted away by the divine fire of the mystical power of knowledge. Desire is signified by the kidneys, and its activity, that is pleasure, by the fat or suet; anger…

…by the breast, and its activity by the lobe of the liver, where the bitter and most pungent bile is lodged. A brief contemplation on the various kinds of leprosy in the Law. I think he wisely suggests this again, through symbolic riddles, in the passage about leprosy, where he divides the infection of leprosy into four kinds: white, greenish, yellow and dark. By these the spirited and the desiring parts are shown divided into their species. Desire is shown by the white and the greenish to be divided into pleasure and pain; anger, by the yellow and the dark, is divided into wrath and resentment and the hidden villainy of hypocrisy. For these, as they say, are the first kinds of the passions under them, and the most fundamental of all the offspring of anger and desire. As long as the sick soul is [held] by them, it cannot be within the camp of those deemed worthy of the divine. A contemplation on Phinehas and those he slew. I think that admirable Phinehas too alludes to this by his zeal. For by piercing the Midianite woman together with the Israelite, he showed mystically, through the spear, that by the power of the high-priestly word matter must be utterly destroyed from the soul together with form, desire together with anger, and alien pleasure together with passionate reasoning. For anger holds the place of form in relation to desire, since by drawing near to it, it gives motion to desire, which in itself is motionless; and reasoning holds the place of form in relation to pleasure, since it is of a nature to give form to pleasure, which according to its own principle is formless and shapeless. The very meaning of the names shows this too. For the Midianite woman is named Cozbi, which means “my tickling,” and the Israelite Zimri, which means “my song,” that is, “my elevation.” So when the reasoning faculty of the soul has turned aside from divine study and gazing, and, being elevated, becomes entwined with the material tickling of the flesh in the chamber of sin, it surely needs the zealous high-priestly word, to destroy those who have been so wickedly joined with one another and to turn away the divine wrath that is coming upon them. A contemplation on “Do not give what is holy to the dogs,” and on the apostles' needing to carry neither staff nor bag nor sandals. The Lord himself too, as it seems to me, indicated this, in one place where he says, “Do not give what is…

"…what is holy to the dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine." By "what is holy" he perhaps means the intellect in us, as an image of the divine glory. He commanded that it must not be wrongly allowed to be disturbed as the movements of anger bark at it. By "pearls" he means its divine and brilliant thoughts, which naturally adorn everything precious, and he urged that we must keep them unsullied and free from the unclean passions of material desire. This also [?] in what he says to his holy disciples when he sends them out to preach about [?]. He prescribes that they should travel lightly and without superfluity, and among other things he says: "Take no bag for the road, nor staff, nor sandals for your feet." For whoever has set out on the lofty journey of knowledge must be free from material weight and pure of every passionate disposition of desire and anger, as the bag and the staff show: the one signifies desire, the other anger. Above all, such a person must be stripped bare of the wickedness of hypocrisy. Like a sandal, hypocrisy covers the footprint of one's life and hides the passionate state of the soul under a counterfeit of gentleness. The Pharisees foolishly put it on, having the form of godliness but not godliness, and thought they would escape notice; but they were refuted by the Word and taught otherwise.

A Contemplation on the Moonstruck Boy.

It was again from this material pair, I mean anger and desire, that the Lord, I think, set free the moonstruck boy. Or rather, when the evil demon wanted to destroy him by fire, which is anger, and by water, which is desire, the Lord checked and put an end to the raging madness. (For the relation of people overcome by material things to the things that come to be and pass away differs in no way from the moon.) The demon who stirs up the passions seizes on this relation, casts the mind as if into water and fire, into desire and anger, and does not stop choking it [?] until God the Word comes. Then he drives out the material and evil spirit, by which the old and [?] man is characterized, and frees the possessed person from its evil tyranny, restoring and granting him his natural self-control, through which the new man, created according to God, is shown forth. So all the saints, genuinely holding fast to the divine [?] word, passed through this age without setting the footprint of the soul on any of its delights. For they gazed very intently [?] at the highest principles concerning God that are attainable by human beings, I mean his goodness and his love. Moved by these, God [?] to give being to the things that are and to grant them well-being (if motion in the case of God, who alone is unmoved, [?]

may lawfully be spoken of, and we should not rather speak of will, which moves all things, brings them into being and holds them together, but is itself in no way moved). On these the saints also wisely modelled themselves. Imitating well, they bore the characteristic of the hidden and invisible beauty of the divine majesty and made it visible through the virtues. That is why they became good, God-loving and loving toward humanity, compassionate and merciful, and were shown to have one and the same disposition of love toward the whole human race. Through this love they held firmly, all their lives, to humility, the most excellent form of all the virtues, which guards what is good and destroys its contraries. So they were never captured by any of the troubling temptations, either the voluntary ones that depend on us or the involuntary ones that do not. The uprisings of the former they withered through self-control; the assaults of the latter they shook off through endurance. Though they were assailed from two sides, by glory and by dishonor, they remained unshaken and immovable toward both. Insults did not wound them, because of their voluntary lowliness. Nor did they accept glory, because of their surpassing embrace of poverty. So anger had no mastery over them, nor envy, nor strife, nor hypocrisy, nor guile.
