Neither did that dissembling, thievish affection which, under a counterfeit appearance, deceitfully draws one off toward something else, the most destructive of all the passions. Neither did desire for the things in this life that seem splendid, nor anything else from the evil host of the passions, nor threats brandished by enemies, nor any manner of death. That is why they were rightly judged blessed by both God and humans. By the grace of God's great gift, they made themselves manifest images of the ineffable and resplendent glory that is yet to be revealed. And so, rejoicing in the principles of the virtues as in what is familiar to them, or rather in God, for whose sake they endured dying every day, they would be united with him. In him the principles of all good things pre-exist, as in an ever-flowing spring, in a single, simple and unified embrace of all things. Toward him he draws all who use the powers given them for this purpose well and in accordance with nature.

From the forty-second oration of the Theologian, on what he said in mentioning the blessed Job, at the words: "But the rest are small things, and were arranged for the sake of the small."

I think he is comparing the bodily goods given to Job after his trials with the declaration God made to him. He calls them "small" because they can in no way be compared with the eternal goods. And he says they were "arranged for the sake of the small", plainly meaning those who are small in contemplative understanding. These people are easily scandalized in discussions of providence and judgment, and with regard to godliness itself…

…arranged for the sake of the small.

From the same oration, at the words: "He cleanses the temple of the God-hucksters and Christ-traffickers, though not with a woven whip; he does it with persuasive speech."

In these words this celebrated teacher does not show our Lord and God to be harsher than the blessed father Athanasius, as some have supposed. God forbid! Nor is he flattering Saint Athanasius when he says that the one used a whip and the other a word to cleanse the temple of the [?]. On that reading, according to those who say this, we would have to suppose one of two things. Either our Lord and God did not know the gentler method of healing, or Saint Athanasius did not know the ways of spiritual care and practiced an untimely kindness. The truth is this. When the discerning reason that judges what we have done is stirred within us, it acts like a [?] living [?] and produces a repentance that matches our offenses. Through it Christ, God and Word, always strikes us when we sin, using as a kind of woven whip our very conscience, which is woven together out of improper thoughts and deeds. Saint Athanasius, on the other hand, led those who stumbled gently toward correction, since he too was clothed in the weakness of the flesh. I think that is why this godly-minded teacher used these words in this way.

By the same author, from the oration delivered extempore against the Eunomians, at the words: "For there are, there are some whose ears and tongue itch."

Those who have spent their leisure on words and know their precise meanings, and have won no ordinary fame for it, say that each thing must be given a fitting word. That word should represent the distinctive property of what is signified, unmixed with anything else, in whatever way it happens to be said…

…and rising up against things that have long been familiar and stay the same, as if they were stale, well-trodden and worthless, while gladly welcoming newer things instead, even if these happen to be false and bring no benefit that reaches the soul. It is above all for the sake of this benefit that every pious word and saving labor is sung, written and practiced. The one is armed against ignorance, the other against pleasure. The word aims to cut away the maimings that ignorance inflicts on the soul. By doing so it brings those who delight in learning for this reason, and who possess the truth through knowledge, into kinship with God. It sends the mind beyond things seen and things thought, enchants it with an ineffable love of the divine beauty, and nails it there by longing, so that the mind cannot be carried anywhere else, or rather does not even bear to be able to. The labor aims to knock out the nails of attachment to pleasure. Since the ancient disobedience, the soul's longing and striving for God have been fastened by these nails onto matter and corruptible things. The labor frees those held fast by vice, makes them genuine disciples of virtue, and renders the soul's attachment to the good unshakeable against everything that seems to hinder it. It does this by teaching two things. Against pleasure it teaches self-control. Pleasure deceitfully fawns on us through the improper things that are in our power, softens the firmness of the will, and persuades it to prefer the present to the future and the visible to the intelligible. For laying aside fear and cowardice it teaches endurance, and the courage that is perfected through endurance. This courage is a state that neither yields to nor is conquered by any pleasure from things in our power or any pain from things not in our power. It is needed because those [?] suggest that things not in our power are irreparable and beyond human strength, and they contrive to overpower sober reason by force, by bringing frightening things upon it. The teacher called the people he is speaking about "itching in ear and tongue" because every word is naturally spoken and uttered through the tongue and heard and learned through the ear. But we may also take the phrase "itching in ear and tongue" in another sense. Perhaps it refers to those who are eager to hear and speak only for the sake of blame, slander or abuse against others. They think it a mark of dignity to exalt themselves ignorantly against every word and every person. Before the one they suspect and envy has said anything, they are already quivering in spirit. They push their soul forward, as it were, and make ready their ear and tongue to hunt down some syllable or word. They do this not to take pleasure in it, but to disparage him and have material for their wagging tongues against him. This is what the enemies of the truth at that time did to this holy man. They leapt ahead and rose up against what was being said before it had even been said, like warhorses and racehorses which, even before the contests and the trumpet, prick their ears up straight. [Apparatus: 83 ἐνεσχημένους [?] cod.; 33 διὰ τῶν cod. Gud.]

They strike the ground with their feet, paw at it with their hooves, rouse themselves before the race, and often run ahead of the whip that drives them. But no blame attaches to horses [?], because they are naturally without reason, when they do not wait for the proper moments of the contest that the sound of the trumpet and the stroke of the whip signal. For such men, however, no blame can be devised that matches their wickedness. Their work and their pursuit is the practice of falsehood and opposition to the truth. Such men may fittingly be called "itching in ear and tongue". A very acrid and thick humor lurking deep in the body often gets irritated by scratching and breaks out onto the surface. In the same way, the hidden disposition of those who abuse what is well said provokes them to seize an occasion, above all to make public the wickedness in their soul. And the further this disposition comes out, the more firmly it holds the depths, when one would naturally have expected it to be emptied. For when the disposition of wicked people comes out through their deeds, it does not leave the depths. It madly spreads over everything outside while never leaving its place in the soul.

From the same oration, at the words: "Like a flower in winter, entirely out of season, and men's adornment on women or women's adornment on men, or geometry in mourning."

The teacher says these things to introduce good order in every word and deed, through which the principle of the propriety of each thing and of all things naturally shows itself pure. He does this by listing incongruous things. Through them he wants to teach the bold and disorderly to be orderly and reverent. Such people know no order in anything, least of all in discourse about God. Instead they boldly mix and confuse with one another all things that are distinct. Some things belong to what has no nature, and so no order either: a flower seen in winter, men's adornment put on a woman, women's adornment on men, and what we might call geometry joined to mourning. The flower makes an innovation in time and departs from its proper place. The adornment counterfeits nature by appearing crosswise on man and woman, and overturns the order that belongs to them by nature. The third forces into one things that cannot exist together, I mean joy and mourning, and so it utterly corrupts and destroys them. If that is so, how much more will discourse about God be unsightly and unseemly, and not at all worthy to be heard about God, when it is uttered at random, by just anyone, and when and where it is not fitting! In that case, I think, people of sense must treat timeliness as being as important as God is incomparably preeminent above all things [?]. Geometry, however, is out of keeping with mourning, says

the teacher. What has puzzled you more, I think, can be explained in ways such as these. First, people who have conquered a land by military force divide it up by geometry when they wish to rule it by the law of kingship. For those who pursue only present goods, it is a matter of joy, indeed the greatest joy, to have become victors and to have gained a great deal of wealth all at once, and for them any sort of mourning is impossible. Second, experts in these matters say that compelling syllogisms belong especially to geometry. So anyone who reasons with a mourner and tries to show him that he is mourning irrationally will rightly seem tactless and blind to what is fitting. Or perhaps one could say that it is unfitting for the mourner himself to reason, contriving by plausible arguments to persuade himself that he has not suffered the misfortune that has really and truly befallen him. Or else that reasoning is wholly contrary to mourning itself, that is, to its nature. For just as the mourner who reasons is driven out of his mourning, so mourning ceases to be mourning when it is turned into a syllogism. A man who has lost the one in whom he placed his hopes of succession considers everything here superfluous from then on. In this way perhaps one might say that these reflections are not unreasonable, since one knows that joy and mourning cannot coincide at the same time. Clearly, the productive cause of each does not take its occasions from the same principles. A trustworthy witness to this is the holy and godly-minded Dionysius the Areopagite, who writes as follows about the way angels are depicted: "The geometrical and builders' instruments signify the founding, building and perfecting, and whatever else belongs to the providence that lifts up secondary beings and turns them back." All these point to a cheerful way of life, to which mourning is entirely contrary and therefore out of keeping. If the passage can also be taken another way, I think it would not be out of place to add to what has been said the saying of Jesus son of Sirach, which runs: "Music in mourning: an untimely tale." Those who have studied these matters say that music comprises all the disciplines, of which geometry is one. For this reason, I think, the teacher agreed with the author of that saying and said that geometry is out of keeping with mourning. And if someone asks, "Why have you passed over the other disciplines and taken this one alone as out of keeping with mourning?" we answer that he [chose?] this one because it suits all the interpretations given above. Besides, the others are included along with this single one by synecdoche. Let this much be said, as far as I am concerned. But if anyone finds a better explanation, I will acknowledge my gratitude, having received from him knowledge of what I did not know.

…free of [?]. Through this, the forms and shapes of sense perception are naturally led, by way of the power of reason, into principles of every kind. And the variety of the manifold principles in beings [?] the difference of the power of reason is gathered into a single-formed, simple and undifferentiated understanding. In this understanding consists the knowledge that is called partless, without quantity and unified. Whoever has done this has truly formed an image, as far as is possible for a human being, of the maker, sustainer and originator of visible things, through those things and the good order in them. He has come to know God, though not as to what his essence and hypostasis are, for that is impossible [?]. … the passage of sense perception in the shape of position, form, impression and imagination. And, if I do not seem excessive to anyone, he has come wholly outside even the difference that lies in the principles of beings. He has placed himself as a kind of boundary between God and all things after God. God transcends him and remains wholly untouched, admitting no understanding of himself. The others are left behind by his new abundance [?] of intellectual knowledge and appear more obscure and lower than his conception, because he has firmly and truly conceived, above them, that [God] in some way is [?]. These things, it seems to me, are what the teacher hints at through "sight" and "natural law" in the reason he gives. He does not, as some have thought, treat sight and natural law as the same thing. Both are active with regard to the same things, but they can be distinguished from each other in concept. Sight rests, without reason, only on contact with visible things and cannot go any further. Natural law both investigates these things with the reason joined to it and goes beyond them, well and wisely, with the mind. It is above all in this way that natural law has introduced, through sight, the notion of and the faith that God exists. So he called "sight" the bare application of sense perception to sensible things, without qualification, since it is not proper to sense perception as such to infer one thing from another. And he called "natural law" the natural activity of mind and reason that takes place through sense perception,

through which the ascent from lesser things to the better takes place step by step, with careful examination. The teacher said that visible things are moved and borne along without moving. He meant that, in terms of the principle by which they came to be, they have their nature, power, activity, order and permanence unchangeably. They do not depart in any way from their natural property, or change into something else, or become confused. Yet they are moved in terms of flux and efflux: by growth and diminution in quantity, by alteration in quality, and, properly speaking, by succession from one another, as earlier things always give way to those that come after. To put it simply and briefly: all beings are entirely stable and unmoved in terms of the principle by which they subsist and exist. But in terms of the principle of the things observed about them, by which the economy of this universe clearly consists and is carried on, they are all plainly moved and [?]. They say that motion is not the same as being borne along. Motion, they say, belongs rather to things subject to generation and corruption, since the things observed about them admit of more and less (though it can properly be said of all created things together). Being borne along, by contrast, is the tireless revolution of the substance that moves in a circle. I do not know whether one can safely say outright that this revolution belongs to a substance that acts naturally upon the universe or to one that is acted upon. But properly speaking, being borne along belongs to what is acted upon. For no being is entirely self-moving, since none is uncaused. Whatever is not uncaused is certainly moved through a cause. It is clearly moved to its natural motion by the cause through which and toward which it moves. For nothing that is moved is moved in any way without a cause. The beginning of all natural motion is the coming into being of the things that are moved, and the beginning of their coming into being is God, as the author of their coming into being. The end of the natural coming into being of created things is rest. Infinity brings this rest about once finite things have been passed through. In infinity, because there is no interval, all motion of things moved by nature ceases [?]. It no longer has anywhere, any way or anything toward which to be moved, since it has as its end, as its cause, God, who sets the bounds and is himself the infinity that bounds all motion. So God is the beginning and end of all the coming into being and motion of beings: they came into being from him, are moved through him, and will come to rest in him. Coming into being is conceived as prior to all natural motion of beings, and motion as prior by nature to all rest. Since coming into being is by nature conceived before motion, and rest by nature after motion, it is clearly impossible for coming into being and rest to exist at the same time. Motion lies between them and naturally keeps them apart. For rest is not the natural activity of the coming into being of things that are moved. It is the end of the power or activity that belongs to that coming into being, or however one may wish to put it.

For the things that have come into being came into being through an activity, and every activity is directed toward some end, so that it may not be incomplete. Whatever lacks the end of its natural activities is not complete either, and the end of natural activities is the rest of motion toward the cause of the things that have come into being. Let us take one example, so that from it we may understand how motion works in all beings. The soul is an intellectual and rational substance, and it both thinks and reasons. Its power is the intellect, its motion is the act of thinking, and its activity is the concept. The concept is the limit of the thinking of both the one who thinks and the thing that is thought, because it marks off the relation of the two extremes to each other. When the soul thinks, it stops thinking about the thing it has thought once it has thought it. For what has properly been thought once no longer calls out [?] the soul's power toward being thought, since each concept in this way receives rest from the particular thinking of what was thought in that concept [?]. So when the soul has passed in its thinking through all the concepts of all things that are thought, both sensible and intelligible, it ceases. Just as it ceases from all the things it has thought, so it ceases from all thinking and from all relation to all sensible and intelligible things, since there is nothing left for it to think at all once it has thought everything that can naturally be thought. After this it will be united to God beyond intellect, reason and knowledge, without thinking, without knowing and without words, by a simple apprehension. It will not think at all, nor will it reason about God. For God is not one of the things that are thought, such that the soul could think of him through some relation. Rather it is united to him in a simple union, without relation and beyond thinking, by an unspeakable and inexplicable principle. This principle is known only to God, who gives this ineffable grace to those worthy of it, and perhaps [?] to those who will later experience it. That will happen when all things are free from change and from all alteration, and the motion of beings in every respect [?] has received as its limit the infinity that is around God, in which all moving things receive rest. For the infinity is around God, but it is not God, who incomparably transcends even this. So I think the one who teaches the pre-existence of souls justly deserves the greatest blame. He decrees a wholly unmoved henad of rational beings, mixing in Hellenic fashion things that cannot be mixed, and he says that the rest of rational beings exists at the same time as their coming into being. But the true account does not allow us to conceive coming into being before rest, since according to him it is by nature unmoved. Nor can we conceive rest after an unmoved coming into being, nor conceive rest together with coming into being. For rest is not a power of coming into being, such that it could be conceived together with the coming into being of things that have come to be. It is the end of the activity, according to their power, of the coming into being of things that have come to be. To put it simply and briefly, rest belongs among relative terms, and it is spoken of in relation not to coming into being but to motion. It admits a contrast with motion, but it admits no reference at all to coming into being, with which it has no contrast. Whenever I hear 'rest', I understand [?] the cessation of motion. But if the existence of [rational beings?] does not by position [?]

[admit?] coming into being and rest, then the one who decrees this clearly falsifies the account of truth and teaches a henad of rational beings that is unmoved [?] together with its coming into being and pre-existing. But someone might ask: 'How is God called rest, when he has no motion conceived before him?' First, I say that the Creator and creation are not the same, so that whatever can belong to one cannot necessarily be observed in the same way in the other. If it could, the natural difference between them would never be evident. Second, strictly speaking, God neither moves at all nor stands still, since this is proper to things that are limited by nature and have a beginning of being. Nor does he do or undergo anything whatsoever of all the things that are seen [?], thought and said about him, because by nature he is beyond all motion and rest and is in no way subject [?] to our categories [?]. [?] For we must say that no being acts by its nature in an absolute way, so that we do not foolishly introduce among the things after God something that has no cause. Rather, by nature it is moved to act [?], and it acts in the way it is naturally disposed to act when moved.

From the same oration, on the words: 'But if he is incorporeal, not even this yet presents his essence, any more than "unbegotten" does, or "without beginning", or "unchangeable", or "incorruptible", or anything else that is said to belong to God or to be about God.' The teacher says this against those who wickedly present the Son as utterly unlike the Father because they think that 'unbegotten' is the Father's essence. I think he aims his argument at them and teaches them from similar cases what they ought to recognize. He wants them, driven by the truth toward piety, to agree with us willingly that 'unbegotten' indicates that the Father has no generation. They should realize that if they force 'unbegotten' to be the essence of God, then to stay consistent they will be compelled to say that 'incorporeal' is also necessarily the essence of God. The same would go for 'without beginning', 'immortal', 'unchangeable', 'incorruptible', and everything else God is said to be by privative negation because of his transcendence. They would then be shown to hold that God has many essences and not one. Or, to speak more properly and truly, they would be shown to be sick with Hellenic polytheism. Ashamed to say this, since it is impious, they will surely abandon their folly, even against their will. For privative or negating terms that are observed about something are not the very thing about which they are observed. Otherwise they would surely be among the terms that signify what something is, as being that very thing, rather than terms that signify what it is not [?]. And if that were so, they would turn out to be the definition of the thing

about which they are said, which is absurd and impossible. For the definitions of things are not compiled from what the things are not, but from what they are. They unfold the concise summary of the things, which is their name. So nothing at all of what is said to belong to God or to be about God can ever be God's essence, since none of it can display what that very thing is. None of it is an affirmation that fits God alone, free of relation and free of activity directed toward something [?].

From the same oration, on the words: 'For it is not enough to say "body" or "begotten" in order to present and make clear the thing to which these belong. One must also state what underlies them, if what is thought is to be presented completely and adequately. For this thing that is embodied and perishes is either a man or an ox or a horse.' The saint saw that the heretics had only one aim: to drag the superessential nature down to their own level, foolishly. They were trying to use technical methods to master, as they imagined, a power that cannot be mastered and that no creature can contain, by bringing it within the grasp of their own knowledge. So throughout the whole oration he preferred to speak of God through privations and negations, and he allowed no positive statement or affirmation whatever. Otherwise they would seize on it like shameless dogs and madly sink their venomous teeth into the word of truth. They would take any positive statement about God that was granted to them as an excuse to propose anything at all, to reason falsely, and so to carry their own project through. For this reason he declares that God is not a body, nor an immaterial body, nor embodied in any way. He is not in the universe, nor in any part of the universe, nor above the universe. Put simply, he is nothing whatever, in anything, in any manner at all, among the things that are seen or contained or spoken or thought or can in any way be known, as is true [?]. In this way he beats away from them every notion that claims to comprehend what God's essence is. Then he leads them toward piety in a way more likely to shame them. He wants to show that the investigation of secondary things, which are incomparably far from God, gives no license to dare even to think anything at all about God, still less to say it. So he says these things. He also says them to confirm what he had already told them by privation and negation. He wants them to recognize from this that even the exact comprehension of the lowest things among beings [?] exceeds the power of our rational activity. Then they would check the reckless impulse of their boldness about far greater things, having learned in small things the weakness

of their nature. Suppose we examine an element, or, say, a man or a horse or an ox. For complete comprehension it is not enough to call the element a body, or to call the man or the ox or the horse merely begotten or perishable. We must also present what underlies these, which is begotten, perishes and has been given qualities. That subject is in no way body or generation or corruption. Otherwise it would necessarily follow that if something is a body, it is also an element, and if something is begotten or perishable, it is a man or an ox or a horse. But it is not true that whatever is a body is necessarily also an element or a man or an ox or a horse. If something is an element, it is necessarily also a body, but if something is a body, it is not necessarily also an element. Nor is whatever is a body, or begotten, or perishable necessarily also a man. Otherwise absolutely everything that [is begotten?] would necessarily be a man. If something is a man, it is necessarily also body, begotten and perishing. But if something is body or begotten or perishable, it is not necessarily also a man. That simply does not follow, for then the man would necessarily also be an element, an ox, a horse, and everything else that is embodied, begotten and perishing. Particulars are never predicated of universals, nor species of genera, nor contained things of the things that contain them. For this reason universals do not convert with particulars, nor genera with species, nor common things with peculiar ones, nor, in short, containing things with contained ones. So according to the account just given, the same must be understood of the ox, the horse and anything else whatever. It is not enough for complete knowledge of things to list the many features observed about them: body, being begotten, perishing, and everything else of this kind that belongs to the subject. If we are to present what is thought completely and without omission, we must also show what the subject of these features is, the thing on which they rest like a foundation. For we can say 'man' or 'ox' or 'horse'. These are not body itself but embodied, and they are not generation and corruption themselves but things that are begotten and perish. So body, generation and corruption clearly belong to the living creatures, but the living creatures are not body, generation and corruption. So no being whatever is, in its very being, what the sum of the things we think and say about it is and is called. It is something other than these, the thing to which they belong. It holds them together, but it is in no way held together by them. For the thing to which these belong and of which they are said is not made of them, nor is it them or one of them. It is not made of some of them or of one of them, and it is not in them, or in some of them, or in one of them. Therefore let every soul that is used to leaping boldly upon the things of God with every kind of argument stop doing so in vain [?]. In small things it has learned its own

weakness [?]. Let it reverence in silence alone the being of the divine essence, which is ineffable, beyond thought and beyond all knowledge. For, as the saint taught earlier, 'not even in small measure' is 'the exact understanding of creation' truly contained by our knowledge. Let me too dwell a little on this point and marvel at how unsearchable is the wisdom that is above all things. Which of the very wise, trusting in logical methods and relying on demonstrations that do not exist, could survey with reason the greatness of beings and come to know, state and present any of the following? What are the principles first implanted in the existence of each being, by which each being exists and has its nature? By them it has been given form, shape and composition, and has power, acts and is acted upon. I need not mention its differences and particular features in quantity and quality, relation, place, time, position, motion and state. Our rational power is magnificently fitted by nature to expand in countless ways in these respects, into intellect, thinking, notion, thought, reflection, the inner word, and the spoken and uttered word, that is, voice and cry, and then to gather itself back again. And that is apart from its differences and particular features in science and art, as in quantity, quality and the rest, as listed above. Who knows the principles of beings as they are and as they differ, as I said? They have an unmoved rest, namely their natural motion, which never shifts from one into another, so that they have rest in motion and, most paradoxically, motion in rest. What is the bond between contraries that makes up one world, and what is the manner of its orderly and unconfused motion and governance? Again, what is the intertwining of contraries through composition in the mixture of our bodies? It leads things that are opposed by nature into friendly cohabitation. Through the mean it tames the harshness of the extremes and makes them pass through one another without harm. And it makes the interpenetration of the extremes in the mixture the means by which composite things are preserved. How does each of these exist, what is it, where does it carry or where is it carried, and for what purpose did it come to be, or carry, or is it carried? And this is not only a question of the principles by which these things primarily exist, as was said. It is also a question of the countless ways, in conception and in act, in which they are divided and united with themselves and with one another. Again, what is the principle of the essence, nature, form, shape, composition, power, activity and passivity of each thing? And again, what is the universal principle that joins the extremes to one another through the mean at the limit of each? Through it, intellect and the thing thought are joined and held together by each other through the act of thinking that stands between them. This act is a relation that unites the divided terms around the concept that arises from both. So nothing at all

BOOK OF AMBIGUA [?]. is shown in this respect to be free of circumscription among the things that come after God. In the same way, all sensible things and all sensing things are joined through sensation, which is a relation common to the divided extremes. Through it the sensing things apprehend, and through it the sensible things fall under the sensing ones. This happens around the sense organ, in which the limit of the power of each in the relation is established, and around which the extremes are naturally united to each other through the relation that stands between them. When we try to investigate the principles of these things, or of any one of them, we remain utterly powerless and speechless. We have nothing on which to rest the mind with precision except the divine power. And this, I think, is what the saint meant when he said, training our intellect for piety: 'Not even in small measure is the exact understanding of creation [possible].' Then there is the phrase: 'But much more than these, the nature that is above these things and from which these things come is ungraspable and incomprehensible.' The words 'ungraspable and incomprehensible' must be taken as applying both to creation and to the nature that is above these things and from which these things, that is, the creatures, come. The words added next, 'not that it is, but what it is', anticipate an objection. The person against whom the argument is aimed might attack him, saying, 'If what we worship is wholly ungraspable, then the proclamation of the Christians is empty, and faith too is empty, since it rests on nothing [?].' So the saint says these things to forestall the malicious argument or man. He did not say that this nature, which is under discussion, is ungraspable as to the fact that it exists, but as to what it is. To confirm the argument he adds: 'For it is very different to be persuaded that something exists and to know what it is.' That is, there is a great difference between being persuaded that something exists and having an exact comprehension of its essence. So, he says, we have spoken fairly in saying that the divine essence is ungraspable. Do not maliciously twist the statement to mean that we present it as ungraspable with respect to its very existence, and then conclude from this that we profess complete atheism. A little later he says: 'For what will you suppose the divine to be, if you trust in logical methods at all?' That is, if you think that by running around with reason you can shut up what you are seeking inside some form of knowledge. 'A body?' That is, is it then a body? 'And how could the infinite, the boundless, the shapeless, the intangible and the invisible be a body?' To make this clear, understand it as follows. Common notions have established that the divine is infinite, that is, that it has no limit. Being limited is proper to what is marked off by four limits: point, line, surface and solid, (1) [?], ch. [?], p. 499 [?].

[?] And it is also proper to what is marked off by three dimensions, length, breadth and depth, and through these by six limits, each dimension being bounded by two. Length is bounded by up and down, breadth by right and left, and depth by the front limit and the back. Again, the same common notions [hold] that God is boundless. That is, he admits no detailed unfolding [by which?] the subject stands, nor indeed any beginning in [?] or in [?]. Moreover, he is shapeless: for example, he is not spherical or square or [?]. And indeed he is intangible [?] and invisible, since he does not fall under sense (these are properties of bodies). [?] To suppose from such likenesses that the divine is [a body?] [?] would also mean that it must be divided into as many parts as it is composed of as a body. But the divine is entirely without parts, because it is entirely without quantity. It is entirely without quantity because it is entirely without quality. It is entirely without quality because it is entirely simple. It is entirely simple because it [?] has no extension. It has no extension at all because it is infinite. It is entirely infinite because it is entirely unmoved, for what has nowhere to move to never moves. It is entirely unmoved because it is entirely without beginning. It has nothing before it and greater than it, nor anything equal to it, nor anything after it that could be measured alongside it and contain it. It is entirely without beginning because it is entirely unbegotten. It is entirely unbegotten because it is entirely one and utterly alone. It is entirely one and [alone?] because it is entirely without relation. For this reason it is altogether unutterable and unknowable. It is the only limit of all the knowledge of those who are moved toward it rightly and in a way befitting God, and the only true knowledge of it [?] is that it is not known.

[?] he led away [?], saying: For if someone says that he knows [God?] as [God] knows himself, [?] and he extended [?] where the [knower?] must be [?], it is altogether necessary for them [?] to have complete comprehension of what is known, and [?] of none of beings at all thus [?]

[?] … what could be more absurd than not to say that it is somewhere, or even to be unable to say [where it is]? And as for the premise of the argument, what could be more [?] … (for what could that be which is not at all somewhere?) Or else that it is altogether [somewhere]: the logic of the argument compels them by necessity to say [?] … and for this reason that the divine exists, but what it is, and how it exists, cannot be [?]. For if, from the fact that the divine is unknowable in its essence, how much more will the divine itself, whatever it is in its essence, be unknown? Therefore, if we are pious, we must of necessity confess [?] that what is not known is not somewhere either. For this reason, I think, the teacher, going along with Eunomius and his followers [?] … the reversal, perhaps setting down [?] … the word, and leaving us to understand that what is not altogether somewhere is called “nowhere.” For we say that God is, and is nowhere, in that his existence is not circumscribed as though in a place; and that he altogether is, in that he has no need whatever of the totality of beings in order to be. Without them he both is and will be [?], and always is. For he does not have beings as his position [?], since he existed before beings were. For if, among us, among things that are not altogether [?] … being belongs only [?] to this corruptible thing, which it would be truer and more proper to call never-being, what would one say about the ineffable, unknowable and uncontainable power, which is always the same and unchanging?

From the same oration, on the words: “Whether it was some daytime vision, or a truthful dream by night [?], or an impression on the governing faculty, which converses with things to come as though they were present.”

This blessed [teacher], having been utterly purified through practical philosophy of the things by which human nature is apt to be defiled, and having had his mind wholly shaped by the Holy Spirit [?] through his applications to divine contemplations, by true initiation in knowledge, as one who had experienced the same things as the holy prophets, enumerated for us in these words the kinds of prophecy. If one must dare at all to approach words spoken so magnificently and with such inspiration, words that surpass the capacity of all who are not such as the teacher himself was, and if it is useful [?] to do so, it must be done by conjecture and not by firm assertion. I think, then, to speak conjecturally, that by [“daytime vision”] he meant the seeing and hearing by the saints of words and things formed spiritually, as though perceived through the senses. For it is not lawful to say that in divine matters the wondrous object must altogether be present in order to give shape to the

imagination; rather, that paradoxically and supernaturally, with no person present and no audible voices striking through the air, [God] sets the imagination to work, so that the one being initiated into divine things truly hears and sees. For all imagination is of things present or of things past; of things that have not yet come to be there is none at all. For imagination is a relation that mediates by itself between the extremes. By extremes I mean the one who imagines and the thing imagined, from which, through imagination in the middle, which is the relation between the extremes, the image arises. The image is the limit of activity and passivity: of the activity of the one imagining and of the passivity of the thing imagined, the extremes being joined to each other through imagination in the middle, since their relation consists in it. For all things that apprehend something in some respect are said to act, and all things that fall under others in some respect are said to be acted upon. Things that apprehend, then, act by nature, and things apprehended are acted upon by nature, and the limit of their passivity and activity is their mutual contact [?] in the middle. For this reason I do not think it fitting to suppose that in divine matters the thing imagined must be present, since what is already materially present in its own hypostasis is no longer something yet to come, and at the same time it is not believed to be divine, having nothing beyond the natural course of things. For if we, imagining at night in sleep, both see and hear, often when there is no one speaking or being seen, much more will the saints truly experience this, with God acting in them while they are awake [?], that which we are accustomed by the law of nature to experience in sleep.

By “truthful vision by night” I take him to mean either the precise knowledge of future things that arises in the soul during sleep by [divine revelation?], as with Joseph and Daniel, or some vision of divine things which, because of the utmost dispassion that comes from great purity, falls even under the bodily eyes of the saints.

By “impression on the governing faculty” I think he means the types of future things which appear to the saints by way of reflection, as in an image [?], through the simple and undivided apprehension of the intellect.

I have said these things about these matters conjecturally and with some daring, not for the sake of [?] … but because of the command of the one who ordered me. If anyone among those who have received grace in these matters [?] …, let him not blame me for my rashness, but rather accept [?] my obedience, even if the present discourse has no power to express the clarity [?] of the things proposed.

From the same oration, on the words: “[?] … whether it was a progress, or an ascent, or an assumption.”

As those who have wisely studied the divine words say [?] …

[?] … that names, to put it summarily, are some of essence, some of relation, and some of grace or of perdition. Of essence, as when they say “man”; of relation, as when they say “good,” or “holy,” or “wise man,” or the opposite, “wicked man,” or “foolish,” or “impure.” (For relation, by presenting how each of the things that are divided diametrically by opposites stands toward something, rightly names them from the inner habit of choice they possess.) Of grace, when a man is named “God” in Scripture: the man who has become obedient to God in all things, according to the words “I said, You are gods,” having neither by nature nor by relation the being and being called God, but becoming and being named so by adoption and grace. For the grace of adoption is wholly without relation [?] …, having in nature no power whatever that is receptive of it, since then it would no longer be grace, but the manifestation of an activity in keeping with a natural power. And so, again, what comes about would not be paradoxical if deification took place according to a receptive power of nature. For deification would then reasonably be the work of nature and not the gift of God, and such a person would be able to be God by nature and to be called so in the proper sense. For the natural power of each being is nothing other than the unswerving movement of nature toward activity. And how deification could make the one deified go out of himself, if it were itself contained within the bounds of nature, I cannot see. In the same way, from the opposite side, they call “perdition,” “Hades,” “sons of perdition” and the like those who have by their own choice given subsistence in themselves to non-being, and have become wholly like it in their ways.

I think, then, that this holy and great teacher, bearing in mind what has been said, set out the rapture of the holy Apostle in these terms, fittingly assigning to each the appropriate word. Therefore I suppose that by “progress” he means the dispassion that comes from virtue as a settled habit, which placed the holy Apostle outside natural necessity; by it he chose to have no relation of choice toward nature, as one who had gone outside even the natural activity of the senses, or rather had transformed it into a spiritual habit. By “ascent” he means the leaving behind of all sensible things, no longer acting upon them or being acted upon by them through the senses, and the passing beyond even the natural contemplation of them in the Spirit through knowledge. By “assumption” he means the abiding and settling in God that came to him after these things, which the teacher fittingly called “assumption,” showing that the Apostle underwent the assumption rather than performed it. For assumption is something undergone by the one assumed, but an activity of the one who assumes. So the Apostle, who was master [?] of these natural and relational names, transcended designation according to both nature and relation, having come to be above nature [?], virtue and human knowledge.

[?] … but rather [?] … of the divine name, of which he came to share the designation by grace, becoming and being called God by the assumption, in place of the natural and relational name otherwise belonging to him [?].

Or again, thus: “progress” is the complete denial of nature through virtue; “ascent” is the passing beyond the things in which nature exists, I mean place and time, in which the subsistence of beings lies; “assumption” is the restoration by grace to him from whom and through whom and to whom are all things, as to the end of all things.

Or to put it another way: “progress” is the Apostle's going ahead, as teacher, of his disciples into virtue through practical philosophy; for in everything the teacher must go before his disciples toward the performance of their duties. “Ascent” is the scientific apprehension, through natural contemplation, of the principles (logoi) in beings. “Assumption” is the pious and ineffable initiation into true theological wisdom.

By the “third heaven” I conjecture are meant the bounds that circumscribe practical philosophy, natural contemplation and theological mystagogy, that is, their highest principles, or their limits. For there is a certain measure of comprehension of virtue and of nature, and of the theology concerning both, fitted by God to each being proportionately to its nature; and the blessed Apostle came to be within these bounds and limits, having passed, as far as was attainable, through the principles of the things mentioned. For if heaven is the circumscription of the things naturally separated off within it and the boundary of all things that fall under the senses, then clearly, according to the anagogical sense, every end that circumscribes the principles concerning some virtue or knowledge, as the boundary of what is bounded and the limit of what is circumscribed, is figuratively called “heaven.”

Or again, perhaps Scripture calls the “third heaven” the three orders of holy angels above us, ranged in succession upward, which holy Paul perhaps reached, being initiated into their affirmations by negating the knowledge proper to himself, and imitating their habits by the transcendent privation of his own. For every rational nature, according to its own order and power, receives [?] and imitates the cognitive habits and positions, that is, the affirmations, of the essence and order above it, privatively, by the subtractive negations proper to itself. The affirmation in knowledge of the higher is the negation of the lower, and conversely the negation in knowledge of the lower is the affirmation of the higher, and so it proceeds apophatically up to the nature and order highest of all by transcendence. After all orders and powers this is succeeded by the immediate negation in knowledge concerning God, which is affirmed by no being whatever, since there is no longer any boundary or limit encompassing this negation. For just as intelligible things are the negation of sensible things [according to ?], so too in the essences [and powers?] that fill the world above, the transcendences of the first [orders], in their [nearness?] to God [?] …

… are known [?] by those after them through privation. For just as what we cannot understand is intelligible to the holy angels above us, so too what the holy angels above us do not understand is intelligible to the holy angels above them; and so in succession, from power to power, the mind ascends and is raised up, and passing through all orders and powers, comes to rest in the ineffable, the inconceivable and the altogether unknowable. If, then, according to Dionysius the Areopagite, negations are true in divine matters, while affirmations are unfitting to the hiddenness of the ineffable, it was fitting that the divine Apostle, having negated the understanding of all the knowledge proper to himself and having risen above every relation to beings, was, as he said, neither in the body, since his senses were not active, nor again out of the body, since his intellect was not idle, at the time of the rapture that befell him. In it he received, inexpressibly and unknowably, by a supramundane initiation, certain words, which he honored with silence and kept wholly unspoken, since neither mind can conceive them, nor tongue speak them, nor hearing receive them.

As those who have experience say, the perfect practice of virtue in what was called “progress” is produced [?] by right faith and unadulterated fear of God; the unerring contemplation in the ascent by firm hope and unimpaired understanding; and the deification in the “assumption” by perfect love and a mind that, by transcendence, has wholly and willingly become blind to beings. And again they say that the work of practical philosophy is to render the mind pure of every passionate imagining; that of natural contemplation, to make it knowledgeable of all true knowledge in beings, according to the cause by which they exist; and that of theological mystagogy, to make it like God and equal to him, as far as attainable, by grace in its settled habit, so that because of this transcendence it is no longer conscious of anything at all that comes after God.

From the same oration, on the words: “Nor could the lower world have contained him, John, the forerunner of the Word, the great …”

It would be fitting for me too, as I behold the greatness of the wisdom given by God to this holy and great teacher of truth, to say to him what David, the most illustrious of prophets and kings, uttered by inspiration to God when struck with amazement at the infinity of his majesty in all things: “Your knowledge is too wonderful for me;

it is too strong; I cannot attain to it.” And rightly so, since he circumscribed the uncircumscribed power by wonder alone, having nowhere else to rest the restless footing of the soul concerning unattainable things. So I too, as I said, should be content to gain sanctification from wondering at the understanding of the wise teacher, and not to inquire curiously how and for what reason, contrary to the history, the teacher interchanges the names which the divine voice mystically assigned to the saints, calling John, the son of thunder, “forerunner” here. But since the reward of obedience is great, especially as the commandment bids us obey those who lead us, and to be at leisure and to know and to search the Scriptures and to meditate on the divine law day and night, I recognized that this lies among the things that are good; and fearing the danger of sloth and disobedience, I will speak conjecturally about these matters as best I can, trusting in the prayers of you who commanded me.

I think, then, that what this God-bearing teacher said contrary to the history, putting the Forerunner of Christ in place of the son of thunder, cannot be reconciled otherwise than through contemplation. For contemplation alone harmonizes things that seem to be opposed to each other in the history, since it shows forth incorporeally the truth in all things, which is simple by nature and is not thickened along with words or bodies. Just as the great John the Baptist was called forerunner in relation to the one truly expected; and voice in relation to the Word, since he went before to announce him; and lamp in relation to the sun, as an artificial, conferred and temporary light in relation to the natural, essential, unartificial, eternal and inextinguishable light; and, I think, also as repentance proclaiming the righteousness that by nature existed before it but came after it by the divine dispensation; so too here, I think, this godly-minded teacher, by calling the great apostle John “forerunner” contrary to the history, wishes to hint that John too, in his Gospel, is the forerunner of a more mystical and greater Word signified through him, [which cannot] be imprinted in letters or spoken by the voice of a fleshly tongue. For the writing of the holy Gospels is an elementary introduction relative to [the manifestation granted] each time to those who are raised up through them, and [who rise spiritually above their bodily way of thinking ?], or to the [manifestation ?] to come hereafter [?], at the consummation of things in motion. For just as the law was an elementary introduction for those who through it were trained toward Christ, the Word in the flesh, and were gathered by the Gospel at his [first] coming, so too the holy Gospel is an elementary introduction for those who through it are trained toward Christ, the Word in the spirit, and are gathered into the world to come at his second [coming]. For since the same [Word] is flesh and spirit,

becoming this or that according to each person's proportion of knowledge, [so is] every word that falls under sounds and letters. And I dare say that every thought that can be imprinted on the mind differs in no way from an elementary introduction that points to what lies beyond it. This is why the Gospels are four in number, being accessible for the time being to those who are still subject to the senses and to corruption. For the elements of this world are just as many, and again there are four virtues, of which the spiritual world of the understanding is composed. Thus the Word of truth circumscribes both the intelligible world within us for the time being and the world in which we are, and joins them to each other in union without confusion, and again distinguishes them from each other without division, by the likenesses between the elements that make them up. For what the ether, that is, the fiery element, is in the sensible world, as they say, prudence is in the world of the understanding: an illuminating habit that reveals the spiritual principles proper to each being, unerringly showing forth through them the cause in all things, and drawing the soul's desire toward the divine. What air is in the sensible world, courage is in the world of the understanding: a habit of movement, both sustaining and active of the innate life in the Spirit, and [sharpening ?] the soul's perpetual movement around the divine. What water is in the sensible world, temperance is in the world of the understanding: a habit that produces life-giving fruitfulness in the Spirit and engenders the never-dissolving erotic attraction of desire toward the divine. And what [earth ?] is in the sensible world, justice is [in the world of the understanding ?]: a habit that generates, according to their form, all the principles in beings, that distributes life-giving bounty in the Spirit equally to each, and that is the immovable settling of one's footing in the good by its position.

The Gospel according to Matthew, then, mystically holds the place of earth and justice, as it gives a more natural account; that according to Mark of water and temperance, as it begins from John's baptism and the repentance he preached, in which temperance consists; that according to Luke of air and courage, as it is more extensive [?] and packed with more narratives; and that according to John of ether and prudence, as it is the highest of all and introduces simply and mystically faith and understanding concerning God.

They also say, in another way, that the four holy Gospels are a symbol of faith, and of practical, natural and theological philosophy. Matthew is a symbol of faith, since it introduces the unbelieving Magi worshipping with gifts; Mark of practical philosophy, since it begins its teaching from repentance, by which every action is made virtuous; Luke of natural philosophy, since it has a more discursive exposition of the Word, and the narr[ative] of the teaching …

…if in the modes [?], and of the [?]; the Gospel according to John, from which and into which it began and ended in a manner befitting God. [11?] Again, just as the sensible world, according to its nature, gives elementary training to the five senses, falling under them [?] and guiding them toward the comprehension of itself, so also the world of the virtues, which belongs to the intellect, falls under the powers of the [soul?] and trains them toward the spirit. It makes them uniform by having them move around it alone, and it supports them [?] with its own apprehensions. They say, too, that the bodily senses themselves, according to the more divine principle that befits them, give elementary training to the powers of the soul. They gently train these powers toward activity through their own apprehensions of the principles in beings. Through these principles, as through letters, God the Word is read by those [?] who seek the truth. Hence they also called the senses exemplary images of the soul's powers, since each sense, together with its organ, that is, its sense-organ, has by nature been assigned beforehand [?] to each power of the soul by some more [?] principle. They say that sight is the image of the intellectual power, that is, of the mind; hearing of the rational power, that is, of reason; smell of the spirited power; taste of the desiring power; and touch of the vital power. To put it more simply and clearly: the image of the mind is sight, that is, the eye; the image of reason is hearing, that is, the ear; the image of the spirited part is smell, that is, the nose; the image of desire is taste; and the image of life is touch. Riding on these by nature, through its own powers and according to the law of God who wisely created all things, the soul is conveyed in various ways toward sensible things. If it uses the senses well, gathering through its own powers the manifold principles of beings, and is able wisely to carry over into itself all that is seen, in which God lies hidden and is proclaimed in silence, then by its own choice it creates in the intellect a most beautiful spiritual world. It combines the four generic virtues with one another like elements to build the world that is brought to completion from them intelligibly, in the spirit. It establishes each virtue by interweaving the activity of its own powers with the senses. Prudence, for example, comes from the cognitive and scientific activity of the intellectual and rational powers interwoven with the senses of sight and hearing, concerning their proper objects. Courage comes from the [?], that is, the nostril, in which, as they say, the spirited breath dwells, [?] concerning the [?] sensible object, of the utmost evenness of activity. Temperance comes from the interweaving of the [?] [?]

[?] of the desiring power with the sense of taste, a measured use concerning its proper sensible object. Justice comes from the equal, orderly and harmonious distribution, in activity, of the vital power through touch, which is present in all things and concerns nearly all sensible objects. From these four generic virtues, in turn, the soul is taught to make by combination two more generic virtues, namely wisdom and meekness: wisdom as the limit of things known, and meekness as the limit of things done. From prudence and justice it makes wisdom, since wisdom is the cause that holds together the knowledge belonging to prudence and the understanding belonging to justice, and for this reason it is, as I said, the limit of things known. From courage and temperance it makes meekness, which is nothing other than a complete immobility of [anger?] and desire toward what is contrary to nature, which some have called dispassion; for this reason it is the end of things done. These again it gathers into the most generic of all the virtues, I mean love. Love draws out of themselves those that come from it, [leads up?] those that pass through it, unites those that began, moved and came to rest in it, and above all else deifies. Thus the soul, moving wisely and acting according to the God-perfected principle by which it both exists and came to be, apprehends sensible things profitably through the senses and makes its own the spiritual principles in them. It takes up the senses themselves, already made rational by the abundance of reason, as rational vehicles of its own powers. It joins the powers themselves to the virtues, and itself, through the virtues, to the more divine principles within them. It joins the more divine principles of the virtues to the spiritual mind hidden invisibly within them. Then the spiritual mind of [?] the more divine principles in the virtues thrusts aside every natural and volitional relation that the soul has to present things and gives the soul, simple and whole, to the whole God. God embraces it entirely, together with the body naturally joined to it, and makes them like himself in due proportion. As a result, he who by nature never appears of himself to any being in any way can appear whole, without circumscription, through the whole of it. Perhaps this is what this blessed and great teacher had in mind when he spoke of the resurrection in the Funeral Oration for his brother Caesarius: 'A little later, having received back also its kindred flesh,' clearly speaking of the soul, 'with which it philosophized about the things of that world, from the [earth?] which both gave it and was entrusted with it, in the way known to God who bound these together and loosed them, it makes the flesh co-heir of the glory of that world. And just as the flesh shared in its hardships because of their union, so the soul shares its own delights with it, having taken it wholly up into itself and become one with it, and spirit, and mind, and God, when what is mortal and

transient has been swallowed up by life.' For just as, because of the [?] of corruption, the soul was swallowed up by the [flesh?] and became known through its activities, and the knowledge of God was swallowed up by the soul through complete ignorance, so that it was not known even whether God exists, so it will surely be at the time of the resurrection. In the reversal that will rightly [?] come about in the Holy Spirit through the grace of God made flesh, the flesh will be swallowed up by the soul in the spirit, and the soul by God, who is the truly existing life. The soul will then have him alone appearing wholly through all things. Simply put, the God-befitting grace of the resurrection will in the future show all that is ours in the reverse of the present condition in which we now exist and live. Just as death, having prevailed, swallowed us here because of sin, so it will justly be swallowed up, made weak because of grace. These things follow if, as has been said, the soul uses its own powers well and, according to God's purpose, carries the sensible world over to God [?] with understanding, through the spiritual principles in it. But if it uses them badly and views [?] the present world contrary to the proper principle, it plainly falls into dishonorable passions. In the future it will fittingly be cast away from the divine glory, receiving as a fearful condemnation for endless ages its estrangement in relation to God. Under this [?] it cannot say that it suffers unjustly, since it has as its accuser the disposition that brought [the evil?] into being, of which it can never be ignorant. But we must bring our discourse back to the matter before us.

For when the evangelist said, 'There are also many other things that Jesus did; if every one of them were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself could contain the books that would be written,' he showed us that what he had written is a kind of preparatory levelling of the road for the more perfect Word, which cannot yet be contained. In this sense, then, anyone who calls the holy evangelist John a forerunner will not miss the truth, since in the Gospel he composed he prepares the way for the mind to receive the more perfect Word. For this reason the teacher also calls him, who thundered spiritual things, a great voice of the truth. Thunder is a voice that only strikes the hearers with astonishment and makes nothing clear, as is the case with the elementary word. For every word written by God for human beings in this age is a forerunner of the more perfect Word. That Word is signified through it in the spirit, without writing, to the intellect, and will be made manifest later. The written word has the truth signified within itself, yet it does not show that truth unveiled [?] and naked. Thus, I think, when the meaning of the whole divine Scripture is piously levelled in this way, it will be shown to have nothing difficult or uneven because of the apparent contradictions in the historical narrative. For every one of the saints of old, according to

some true principle, was a forerunner of the mystery signified and prefigured through him, proclaiming its archetypes in advance by what he suffered, did and said. That is why they are blamelessly taken in place of one another, all for all and each for each. In the usage of Scripture they are named in place of the books they wrote, and the books in place of them. The Lord shows this clearly when he makes John the Baptist Elijah and calls him so. This may be because of their equal habit of virtue, as the teachers say, their purity of mind in all things and the rigour of their way of life, or because the same power of grace was in both, or for some other hidden reason. He who said it, being God, would know, and so would those whom he makes wise in such mysteries. Again, he called the Law 'Moses' and the prophetic books 'the prophets', where he brought in the patriarch Abraham saying to the rich man tormented in Gehenna, 'They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.' There he set forth the men themselves, Moses, I mean, and the prophets, in place of the divine books they wrote. And this is no wonder. For if the one proclaimed through them is one, they can all be understood as one, like the one they proclaim. Each can piously be taken for all, and all for all, both those who ministered to the mystery of the Old Covenant and those entrusted with the preaching of the grace of the Gospel. Therefore, just as the great John the Baptist can piously be taken for the whole [?] that is [forerunner?] of the New Covenant and of the worship belonging to it, so John, truly the great evangelist, can justly be taken for the whole New Covenant and the worship belonging to it. The New Covenant is itself the forerunner of the mystical hiddenness of the ineffable good things in the age to come. John is a forerunning voice of the more divine Word that will be clearly spoken, and an image of the truth that is to be revealed. For the whole mystery of our salvation was wisely arranged through shadow, image and truth. 'The Law had a shadow,' as the divine Apostle says, 'of the good things to come, not the very image of the realities.' Through this shadow the Word educated those under the Law in a way suited to them, by a faint reflection of the true things, so as to prepare them to receive the Gospel. The Gospel, by contrast, possesses an image of the true things, and from now on clearly holds all [?] who have acquired a likeness to the good things to come. Through hope the Word makes them ready, by receiving the archetype of the true things, to be given soul and to become living images of Christ. They become the same as he is by grace rather than a mere likeness, perhaps even the Lord himself, if the statement does not seem [too bold?] to some. He is now called by the God-bearing teacher a forerunner of himself, because, in proportion to those who receive him under

both the Old and the New Covenant, [he reveals?] himself and runs ahead of himself through enigmas, voices and types. Through these he leads to the truth that is without them. The Lord's own words bear witness to this, where he said, 'I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.' He was pointing to the teaching about himself that would come to them through the divine Spirit, higher than the teaching that preceded it, yet itself lower than the one that would follow. Hence he fittingly added: 'But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will guide you into all the truth.' And [?] what he says elsewhere: 'Behold, I am with you all the days until the end of the age.' This does not mean that after that he would no longer be with them at all. It means that he would be known, according to their capacity, as higher than the lower way in which they had known him until then. For although he always remains the same in himself and admits no change from [?], nor any more or less, he becomes all things to all through the abundance of his goodness: lowly to the lowly, lofty to the lofty, and God by nature to those who are [deified?] through him. All the forms and mysteries of providence concerning humanity in the present age, however great they are, are therefore a kind of road-building and prefiguration of things to come. The Lord's word that could be contained until then, compared with the more mystical word that was to be given to the disciples, and his first coming compared with his second, is thus a forerunner of himself. He showed faintly in himself what suited the capacity of those who received him, but he did not then make manifest the mysteries he keeps silently and in secret with himself, because they are as yet entirely beyond what creation can contain. For, as has been said, everything that falls under letters and spoken words holds the place of a voice in relation to a clear word. This certainly includes the meaning understood from it, even if that meaning is spiritual, insofar as it falls in any [?] way under letters and utterance. For this reason this divine teacher has perhaps called 'John' all that Christ, who is God, spoke to the disciples, in relation to the ineffable mind or understanding, well and wisely [naming] the forerunning grace from that which receives it [?]…

From the same oration, on the words: 'But the word about God, the more perfect it is, the harder it is to attain, and the more apprehensions it involves, and the more laborious its solutions.' If the things that have come into being are many, they are also certainly different, since they are many. For it is impossible for many things not also to be different. If the many things are different, we must understand that the principles by which they exist in their essence are also different. In these principles, or rather through them, different things differ. For different things would not differ from one another if the principles by which they came into being had no difference. If, then, just as the senses, naturally

[?] apprehending sensible objects, necessarily form, as they receive them, many and different apprehensions of the objects that underlie and fall under them, so also the mind naturally apprehends all the principles in beings. In these principles, which are infinite, it contemplates the activities of God, and it draws many and, truly speaking, infinite distinctions among the divine activities it apprehends. It will then fittingly find its power feeble and its method at a loss in the scientific investigation of what is truly true. It cannot understand how God, who truly is none of the beings and in the proper sense is all things and beyond all things, is present in the principle of each individual thing and in all the principles together by which all things exist. According to the true account, every divine activity signifies through itself God, whole and without parts, in each thing according to the particular principle by which that thing is. Who, then, can understand and say precisely how God is wholly in all things in common and in each being particularly, without parts and without division? He is neither divided in various ways along with the infinite differences of the beings in which he is present as being, nor contracted into the particular existence of one thing, nor does he contract the differences of beings into the one unified wholeness [?] of all things. Rather, he is truly all in all, and he never departs from his own simplicity, which has no parts. The teacher therefore spoke well when he said that the apprehensions of the word about the Godhead are many, for from them we are taught only that God is, and that the solutions are more laborious, for from them, in turn, we learn what he is not. He said this to stop useless and harmful curiosity in those who think the divine can be grasped by the empty fabrications of their own minds, when not even the least of beings can truly be grasped according to the principle by which it is and exists. From the First Oration on the Son, on the words: 'For this reason the monad, moved from the beginning to a dyad, came to rest at a triad.' Everything that moves by nature certainly moves because of a cause, and everything that moves because of a cause certainly also exists because of a cause. Everything that exists and moves because of a cause certainly had, as the beginning of its being, the cause through which it exists and from which it was brought into being. As the end of its motion it has the same cause, through which it moves and toward which it hastens. Everything that both exists and moves because of a cause is also certainly created. If the end of what moves is the cause through which it moves, that cause is certainly the same as the cause through which it came into being and exists. There is therefore certainly one cause, as beginning and end, of whatever exists and moves by nature in any way. Through it everything that is and moves both exists and moves. For being an active power, it both makes the [Note 33: 'of each' in the Gudian codex.]

things that come into being in a manner befitting God and brings them forth as their beginning, and as their end it providentially draws the things that move and [?] defines them. If everything that moves and is created exists, moves and has come into being because of a cause, then whatever does not exist because of a cause is neither made nor, clearly, movable. For what has no cause of its being at all does not move. If what is uncaused is certainly also unmoved, then the divine is unmoved, since it has no cause whatever of its being and is itself the cause of all beings. How then, someone may ask, does this [great?] teacher present the divine as moving in the passage before us? We shall answer that he knew better than anyone the following. To use an example, the principle of each art remains entirely unmoved in itself, yet it takes form in each kind of thing that falls under that art. It is said to move because it moves the crafted object in accordance with itself, rather than because it appears to be moved. Or again, light is said to move when it moves sight toward seeing, since in the proper sense it is what moves all sight rather than what is moved. In the same way the divine, which is entirely unmoved in essence and nature because it is infinite, free of relation and unbounded, is present like a kind of scientific principle in the [substances?] of beings. It is said to move because it providentially moves each being according to the principle by which that being is naturally moved. As cause, it receives without being affected all that is predicated of the things it causes. [?] The God-revealing and great Areopagite, Saint Dionysius, inquired into this where he says: 'Why ever do [the theologians?] call the divine [?] sometimes eros and love, and sometimes the object of eros and the beloved?' He concludes the argument thus: 'Because by the one it is moved, and by the other it moves.' To put it more clearly: as eros and love, the divine is moved, and as the object of eros and the beloved, it moves toward itself all things that can receive eros and love. To say it more plainly still: it is moved because it produces an inward relation of eros and love in those who can receive these, and it moves because by nature it draws the longing of those who are moved toward it. And again: it moves and is moved, as thirsting to be thirsted for, longing to be longed for, and loving to be loved. In this way too the God-minded Gregory says: 'The monad, moved from the beginning to a dyad, came to rest at a triad.' For it is moved in the mind that can receive it, whether angelic or human, which carries out its inquiries about it through it and in it. To say it more clearly, at the first approach it teaches that mind, without division, the principle of the monad, so that no division may be brought into the first cause. Then it leads the mind further to receive its divine and ineffable fruitfulness. It tells the mind, mystically and secretly, that it must never think this Good barren of Word and Wisdom, or of sanctifying Power, which are consubstantial and subsist in their own right. This is so that the divine may not be supposed to be composed of these as of accidents, and may be believed always to be these. The Godhead, then, is said to be moved as the cause of the inquiry into the mode in which it exists. For without

[?] to attribute [?] to the Godhead is one of the impossible things. Again, it is said to be "moved" also because of the gradual revelation, in Holy Scripture, of the more perfect account of it.
