Scripture begins by confessing the Father, goes on to confess the Son together with him, and leads those who are being taught to accept the Holy Spirit along with the Father and the Son, and to worship together a perfect Trinity in a perfect Unity, that is, one essence, Godhead, power and activity in three hypostases.

From the same oration, on the words: "But willing, I think, is one thing and what is willed another; begetting and begotten; speaking and word, unless we are drunk. The former belong to the one who moves, the latter are, as it were, the motion. So what is willed does not come from the willing (for it does not necessarily follow), nor does the begotten come from the begetting, nor what is heard from the utterance. They come from the one who wills, begets and speaks. But the things of God are beyond all these; for him, begetting is perhaps the will to beget."

The Arians try every means to make their blasphemy against the Only-begotten easy to put across, and they say that the only-begotten Son comes from the will and not from the Father. The wise teacher says these things against them, and shows that from this point their whole device against the truth is easily undone. Take the powers of the soul, which one might perhaps call the completion of its essence. We say that they can be active in the essence in which they exist, but that they cannot by any means be moved to effective activity without the consent of the one who wills. Even if we granted, for the sake of argument, that they want to act of themselves by natural motion, they are still wholly unable to bring their own impulse into effective action without the inclination of the one who, so to speak, possesses them. For the work does not necessarily follow the power if the power lacks the inclination of the one whose power it is, which contributes to it the actual fulfillment of its activity, since by itself the power has no hypostasis (205a). So they put forward the will in vain, since it brings nothing about apart from the one who has it and wills. And this is what the teacher says: what is willed does not necessarily follow the willing, and the same holds for the other pairs, without the contribution of the subject in which these exist. So then, you people, if you judge divine things from examples among us, keep at least to your own premises and accept that things which coexist with one another in a mediating relation are entirely simultaneous. I mean the one who wills and what is willed, the one who begets and the begotten, with the relation between them,

that is, the willing and the begetting, existing together with one another. There is no seeing apart from the one who sees and what is seen, and no thinking apart from the thinker and what is thought. In the same way there is no begetting apart from the one who begets and the one begotten, and no willing apart from the one who wills and what is willed. For, as was shown, what is willed does not follow the willing without the contribution of the one who wills. But if these are among the things that are simultaneous by relation, since the relation in both cases is immovable, then even on your view the begotten Son existed simultaneously with the begetting Father, who is always Father through begetting. The Son admits no interval of time of any kind between himself and the Father who begets him. So the Son is no longer of the will; he is of the begetting Father. "And let these things," he says, "be said from examples among us; but the things of God are beyond all these, for him begetting is perhaps the will to beget." He left this open with the adverb "perhaps" because the begetting of the Son from the Father is beyond will as well. The Son is not mediated from the Father (205b) by a will, and the Father's will is in no way conceived before the Son, since the Father did not exist before the Son, any more than the mind exists before the word that comes from it, or light before its radiance. The Father and the Son, begotten from him without beginning, have their being together, and so they also have one will, simple and indivisible, just as they have one essence.

From the same oration, on the words: "Then what prevents me too from taking as my premise 'The Father is greater by nature,' then adding 'But what is by nature is not necessarily greater, nor Father,' and concluding 'The greater is not necessarily greater,' or 'The Father is not necessarily Father'?"

The teacher wisely defined the Father as greater by being the cause of the Son, since the Son is from the Father and the Father is not from the Son. The Arians then added the premise "the cause is by nature" and maliciously drew from it the conclusion "greater by nature." First he nobly refutes the conclusion they had drawn by false reasoning, saying: "I do not know whether they are deceiving themselves or the people they are addressing. For it is not simply the case that whatever is said of something will also be said of its subject; clearly it matters of what and what things are said." That is, he says, whatever is said of the cause as cause will not also be said of what is by nature. Take something said of a wise man or a king, as wise or as king. It is unreasonable to say it also of their subject, as men, and lawlessly to combine with the definition of the subjects' essence what is said of wisdom as wisdom and of kingship as kingship. These things have nothing at all in common with the principle of the essence (206a), and it is unreasonable to treat them as differences that constitute the essence and complete

its definition. Then, more wisely, he weaves against them a syllogism from their own premise and turns them against themselves. It goes like this: "Then what prevents me too from taking as my premise 'The Father is greater by nature,' then adding 'But what is by nature is not necessarily greater, nor Father,' and from this concluding 'The greater is not necessarily greater,' or 'The Father is not necessarily Father'?" To make the point clearer and more concise, let us lay it out schematically, if you agree, beginning from the opponents' attack and ending with the Father's teaching.

Premise of the Arians, or rather the Eunomians: "If the Father is cause of the Son by nature, and the Father is greater than the Son, then the Father is greater than the Son by nature."

Refutation by our holy father Gregory, who turns the opponents back by reducing their argument to absurdity: "If, as you say, the Father is greater than the Son by nature, but what is by nature is not necessarily greater nor Father, then the greater is not necessarily greater, or the Father is not necessarily Father."

In this way those who reject the truth are caught in their own devices and turned back. They are empty, and they have been emptily shaken out of piety. For in arguments of this kind the conclusions are constitutive of the premises and the premises define the conclusions. Those who think themselves wise have fallen into this through great ignorance.

"But let it be the name of an activity, if you like. Not even so will you catch us. This very thing would have produced the consubstantial, even if the supposition of an activity here is otherwise absurd."

Those whose tongue is sharpened like a razor against the truth asked, ostensibly as a question: "Is 'Father' the name of an essence or of an activity?" Their aim was this. If we said that "Father" is the name of an essence, they would conclude that the Son is of a different essence from the Father, on the ground that the same essence does not admit two different proper names (for if "Father" is the name of an essence, "Son" could never be a name of the same essence). If we said it is the name of an activity, they would show that we plainly confess the Son to be a creature of the Father, as the product of an activity. The teacher first went through the proper use of the term by way of rebuttal and told them directly that "Father" is the name neither of an essence nor of an activity, but of a relation, that is, of how the Father stands to the Son or the Son to the Father. Then, making a concession, he went on to say: "Let it be the name of an activity too, if that is your view," and he adds: "This very thing would have produced the consubstantial." How then does it produce the consubstantial? someone might ask, one of those who inquire very closely and cannot bear to be ignorant of anything useful. This can be cleared up as follows. They say that among beings there are, in general, two activities:

one brings forth naturally from beings things of the same kind, consubstantial and in every way identical with themselves. With this activity in mind, the teacher goes along with the chatterers in a reasonable way, so as to restrain them at least a little from blasphemy, and says: "But let 'Father' be, as you say," in keeping with the stated aim of the argument, "the name of an activity too." To this he adds: "This very thing the Father would have produced," that is, the consubstantial, as an activity that subsists in its own right and lives. In just this way the God-minded teachers of the truth have called the only-begotten Word of God and Son of the Father the living Word and the self-subsistent power and wisdom. The other activity, they say, produces things outside oneself. By it someone acts on something external (207a) and of a different essence, and makes something else, foreign to his own essence, out of pre-existing matter [?]. They say this activity is put together with expert knowledge in the arts. Of it the God-minded teacher says: "even if otherwise absurd" (that is, in the sense in which it was taken) "is the supposition of an activity here," and especially when it is applied to the Father and the Son. In their case the pious mind will not properly accept even the first kind, because the existence of the Only-begotten from the Father, together with the Father and in the Father, is ineffable and incomprehensible and beyond even this.

From the second oration on the Son, on the words: "He would be called God not of the Word but of the visible. For how could he be God of the one who is properly God? In the same way he is Father not of the visible but of the Word. For he was twofold, so that one title is used properly of both, the other not properly; the reverse of how it is with us. For God is properly our God, but not properly our Father."

"Properly" must be applied to both titles, "Father" and "God," since both can be said properly of Christ because of the one hypostasis. God is properly Father of Christ, since Christ is Son and God the Word and one of the Holy Trinity even after the incarnation. And God is again properly God of the same Christ, since Christ is truly man by reason of [?] the natures from which he is also constituted. "Not properly" [?] must be applied to "God" and to "Father," since neither can be said properly of Christ because of the natural difference between the natures from which and in which he is constituted. For what belongs to the whole by composition will never be properly predicated of one of its parts. "The reverse (207b) of how it is with us" means: conversely to how it is in our case. For when I

consider the difference of the natures and distinguish them in thought, I cannot apply "properly" to both, I mean to "Father" and to "God." For the Father is not properly God of the Word, and God is not properly Father of the flesh. "The reverse" means conversely, or reciprocally. "Properly" and "not properly" are taken in reference to the union and the one hypostasis on the one hand, and in reference to the difference of the natures and their distinction in thought on the other. The one hypostasis admits God, called properly God and Father as God and Father of Christ, for the reason already given. The essential difference of the natures, conversely, admits "not properly," as is the case with us. For God is properly our God, as he is also of the flesh [?], but not properly our Father, as he is not the Father of the Word's flesh either. So the attributes of the whole must be expressed in exchange with the parts, and those of the parts in exchange with the whole. Then the passage before us will be easy and clear to understand. To make the point clearer still: when Christ is considered as a hypostasis, "properly" must be applied to both, I mean to "God" and to "Father." When Christ's natures are considered according to the unconfused existence of the things in which and from which he is, "the reverse" must be applied, that is, "not properly," as it is with us. The teacher shows this clearly by adding: "And this is what causes the heretics' error: the joining of the names, the names being interchanged because of the blending. Here is a sign of it: when the natures (208a) are separated in thought, the names are divided along with them." That is, as long as you consider Christ as one hypostasis, the joining of the names by interchange is undivided. But when you separate in thought the natures that complete Christ's one hypostasis, you have divided the names along with the natures. Or again: since Christ is twofold in nature, both titles, "God" and "Father," are predicated of him. They are predicated properly when the names are spoken in correspondence with the natures, and not properly when what belongs by nature to each of the natures from which, in which and which he is, is given in exchange to the other because of the one hypostasis. The heretics of the past and of the present do not know how to do this, or rather, to put it more accurately, will not tolerate it, and so they do not shrink from blaspheming the only-begotten God the Word. Some bring him down to a creature because of his human attributes. Others confound the dispensation by denying the natures of which he is [?] constituted. Another man, very wise in divine things, when I asked him about this, said [?]: "'Properly' and 'not properly' with respect to both belong to the same category, the category of relation. Whether 'Father' or 'God,' or each of them, is applied to Christ, who is composed of two, it admits the opposites 'properly' and 'not properly.' If the Father is called God of Christ when the two natures are considered, he would be called so 'properly' of the creature, but 'not properly' of God the Word. In the same way he is [?] Father 'properly' of the Word, but of the
[?] Maximus [?] creature 'not properly,' just as it is with us." I judged the wise man's interpretation sound and thought it worth including in this writing. [?]

From the same oration, on the words: "He receives," that is, Christ receives, "life, or an inheritance, or the heritage of the nations, or authority over all flesh, or glory, or disciples, or whatever else is mentioned." To these the teacher adds: "This too belongs to the humanity," and then concludes: "But if you were to give it to God as well, it is not absurd. For you will give these things not as acquired, but as existing with him from the beginning, by reason of nature and not of grace."

I often puzzled over this by myself: how, and for what reason, as the teacher says, God is said to receive what he has by nature. Since I could not satisfy myself, I finally decided it would be good to ask a wise elder. He explained the matter with great expertise, saying something like this. Suppose someone who [?] the natures of beings were to say to [?] them: "Let us give to God omnipotence, wisdom, goodness and justice; and likewise to the creature servitude, obedience, being circumscribed, coming into existence from nothing, and whatever fits with these," since in our common notions the nature of each thing calls for its own properties. Whoever says "Let us give to God" is not supplying something that did not belong to him before, but what his nature has. Used this way, "Let us give" means, as it were, marking off the nature by what belongs to it from what does not. In the same way, understand piously that here too the teacher is saying, "But if we were to give it to God as well," meaning that the nature receives what belongs to it from those who distinguish things.

From the same oration, on the words: "For as we say it is impossible for God to be evil, or not to be."

I asked the wise elder mentioned above about this too. He said that "not to be" does not depend on what comes before it; otherwise the conclusion would be that God is evil. Read that way it says: "For as we say it is impossible for God to be evil, or not to be" evil, that is, it would mean he is evil, with "evil" understood with both clauses. For two negations produce one affirmation. "Impossible" is a negative, and joined with "not to be evil" it yields "to be evil." But that is not so. God forbid! Each clause

has its own sequence from its own beginning. The clause is cleared up like this: "For as we say it is impossible for God to be evil." Here one should put a stop, start again with a new thought, and add "or not to be," meaning "to be nonexistent."

From the same oration, on the words: "You have the titles of the Son. Walk through them: through the lofty ones loftily [?], through the bodily ones with compassion, or rather wholly in a godlike way, so that you may become God, having ascended from below, for the sake of him who came down from above for us."

Take someone who has enlightened his mind through lofty contemplation, according to the meaning of each of the divine names. He has led his mind up to the original, spiritual meaning of each name and has been transformed toward it. By his labors for virtue he has subjected the mindset of the flesh to the spirit, and has become obedient to the point of death. Such a person truly walks "through the divine titles" blamelessly in both spirit and flesh, making the divine journey that leads to God. He walks "loftily" through the lofty names, according to mystical contemplation, and "with compassion" through the bodily names, according to practical philosophy, as he hastens toward his portion above; "or rather wholly in a godlike way," since his action is also contemplative and [?] has its share of grace. And the teacher clearly states why such a person chose to be estranged from the flesh by his own choice, through the perfect circumcision of its natural movements. He chose it so that he too might become God by grace. In the flesh he has placed himself above matter through action, and in the mind above form through contemplation, matter and form being what the existence of beings consists of. In short, by the habit of virtue and knowledge he has become wholly immaterial and formless, for the sake of God the Word, who by nature is properly immaterial and formless and who for our sake truly came to be in matter and form like us, from us. Or again, "or rather wholly in a godlike way" may refer to the dispassion that arises from compassion toward God and neighbor in someone who has achieved the virtue and knowledge attainable by human beings. Such a person is ready to suffer to pay what others owe and readily lays down even his life, since he is entirely free from stains.

By the same author, from the oration on the Nativity, on the words: "The laws of nature are dissolved; the world above must be filled. Christ commands; let us not resist."

In truth, the dissolving of the laws of nature brought about the filling of the world above. Clearly

³³ The apograph reads "above the material according to the fl[esh]".

St Maximus [?]

had they not been dissolved, the world above would have remained deficient and unfilled. And what are the laws of nature that were dissolved? Birth through the sowing of seed and birth through corruption, I think. Neither of them marked in any way the true incarnation and perfect becoming-man of God. The conception was truly without seed and the birth wholly without corruption, pure and untouched. For this reason the Mother remained a Virgin even after giving birth to her child; through the childbirth she remained, if anything, even freer from what she might have suffered. This is both astonishing and beyond every law and principle of nature. God, who deigned to be born from her in the flesh, drew the bonds (210a) of virginity tighter for her as mother through the birth. It is a truly wondrous thing to see and to hear: that an infant was born and came forth without the bars of the mother's womb being opened. For it was truly necessary, necessary, that the Maker of nature, restoring nature through himself, should first dissolve the laws of nature. Through disobedience, sin had used these laws to condemn human beings to share with the irrational animals the same way of succeeding one another. In this way he would renew the laws of the first and truly divine creation, so that what man destroyed through his carelessness, since he was weak, God might restore through his love for humanity, since he is powerful. If, then, the laws of nature brought in by sin were dissolved in Christ, and every slavish revolt of the passions was entirely done away with through the coming of the Word, the world above must certainly be filled, as the teacher says. And let us not resist this. The old Adam under sin, a mere man, dissolved by his disobedience the first laws of nature in the spirit, and filled the world below with those born after him in the flesh for corruption, becoming the founder of a race in the likeness of his transgression. No one will dispute this. Much more, then, will the sinless new Adam, Christ God, who as Word dissolved the laws of irrationality brought into nature through sin, rightly fill the world above with those born after him in the Spirit for incorruption, becoming the founder of a race in the likeness of his obedience. And let no one doubt this who has had even a small sense of God's might and is not ignorant of its greatness. So then, the world above is filled (210b) with those born in the Spirit according to Christ. In this way the law of the flesh and of birth here below comes to its fitting end, and everything is reordered toward the world above.

Another interpretation of the same passage.

Since the teacher's words seem to me to have yet another meaning besides these, I must speak of that too, as far as is possible for us, with God guiding the account [?]. In the Gospels, the sole cause of all things

And my God Jesus, teaching in hidden fashion in parables, called man a sheep that had strayed from the divine hundred, a drachma lost from the divine ten, and a prodigal son who had foolishly run off from his father and broken the concord of the divine pair of brothers. He called him a sheep, I think, as one who is cared for, led and set in order, and who provides three useful things to his owner: wool, lambs and milk. So he is both nourished and nourishing by the principle and mode of natural contemplation; both clothed and clothing by the mode of ethical philosophy; and both enriched and enriching, by begetting what is like himself, in the mystery of true initiation. He called him a drachma as being splendid and royal, stamped by virtue of the image with the impress of the divine archetype, and receptive, so far as is attainable, of the whole of the divine beauty. He called him a son as heir of his father's goods and equal in honour to the father by the [?] that comes from grace. This man, as a sheep that had gone astray, God the Provider sought as a shepherd and found, and laying him on his own [shoulders?] he brought him back to the fold of his fellow sheep. As an image buried under the passions, which had [lost?] its lovely beauty, the Word, as [Wisdom?], found it, lighting his own flesh like a lamp with the light of his own divinity, and he makes the finding an occasion of great joy, since by it he filled up what was lacking in the divine ten. As a son made dead by sin and lost through ignorance of the true [God?], he received him on his return as a good father. He once more sets on him, with nothing lacking, the marks of his former dignity, and, greatest and most mystical of all, he sacrifices the fatted calf, whatever this calf and its astonishing sacrifice may be. (I think it is the highest, most hidden and most unknowable Word of the incomprehensible and unknown mode of the divine and ineffable providence, and his imparting of himself to beings in a manner worthy of God.) And he makes the son's return the crown of ineffable joy, having magnificently filled up the pair of sons, whatever that may be, and the ten drachmas before it, and the hundred sheep before that. [?] Let us, if you agree, pass over speaking of these things now. It will be more timely to set out elsewhere, God granting, the account of each number with careful elaboration. If, then, the good shepherd laid man on his shoulders as a sheep and brought him back to his fellows; and if the Lord and Saviour, as the Wisdom and Power of God the Father, found man through the incarnation as a drachma bearing the royal impress through the image; and if the good and all-compassionate Father received him on his return as a son, counted him among the heavenly powers and placed him in their ranks, and filled up what was lacking in each of the numbers in the heavens through the man who was saved,
then it is clear that Christ God filled the upper world, having himself, in a manner worthy of God, worked the [salvation?] of all in himself.

Let us also, if you will, consider the difficulty before us in another way. Those who have closely examined the nature of beings say that the law of each nature is the unwavering and unalterable permanence of the principle by which it exists and came to be. And this, I think, would be a good definition of the law of nature, as anyone with a share of reason will [agree?] on hearing it. If this is true, then clearly the law of nature necessarily keeps the principle of the nature inviolate, and in the same way it wholly preserves the nature's place, according to its position, unchanged. But he who wisely defined the subsistence of beings, species by species, by law, principle and nature is himself above nature and law, intellect and reason, place and motion. He acts on the things beneath nature in nothing according to nature. Rather, in a manner proper to himself, he takes up above nature the natural properties of the things beneath nature, and he both acts and suffers, while paradoxically preserving in both, in himself as he suffers and in the things he does, their natural unchangeability unmixed. So, truly moving down to us by his manifestation among us, he became perfect man, without moving from himself at all and without in any way experiencing circumscription in place. And he deified us perfectly, without taking away by alteration anything at all of our nature. He gave himself wholly, with nothing lacking, and took man wholly and entire in the ineffable and [unimpaired?] union, and he diminished nothing of the perfection of either. He is truly wholly God, the same one, and wholly man, the same one, and by his perfection in both of the things in which he truly is, he bears witness to his own changelessness and unalterability in both. In this way he dissolves the laws of nature, using nature above nature in the things that are according to nature.

Another contemplation, on: "The upper world must be filled." Christ, as man, is the firstfruits of our nature before God the Father, like the leaven of the whole lump. And he who as Word never departed from his abiding in the Father stands before God and the Father with respect to his humanity. If so, let us not doubt that we shall be, according to his request to the Father, where he himself, the firstfruits of our race, is. For just as he came down for our sake without alteration and became man like us, sin alone excepted, supernaturally dissolving the laws of nature, so we too, consequently, shall go up through him and become gods like him by the mystery of grace, changing nothing at all of our nature. And so, according to the wise teacher, the upper world is filled again as the members of the body are gathered to the head according to their worth. Each member, that is,

by its nearness in virtue, harmoniously takes the position fitting to it through the architecture of the Spirit, and helps to fill out the body of him who fills all in all, the body that fills all and is filled from all. The upper world, then, will certainly be filled, according to the teacher. This may happen, as has been said, by the spiritual rebirth of those born according to Christ. Or it may happen by the replenishing, accomplished in Christ and through Christ, of the mystical numbers in the heavens, by which I mean the divine hundred of rational sheep, the mystical ten of intellectual drachmas, and the honoured pair of sons. Or it may happen by the gathering of the members of the body to their own head and to their own firstfruits of the lump. It has already been filled in Christ, and it will be filled again later in those who are according to Christ, when they will be united with him in his resurrection also, having already been united with him in the likeness of his death through the same sufferings.

From the same oration, on: "A child was born to us, a Son was also given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulder; for he is lifted up with the cross."

The prophet Isaiah, in his reasoned word about the incarnate Word, said mystically: "whose rule is upon his shoulder." This great teacher, who had attached himself wholly through reason to the first Word, made plain concisely, as is his custom, what we must take this rule to be, saying: "for he is lifted up with the cross." But the cross admits many contemplations, according to the various ways of conceiving it. So it is worth asking in which sense the teacher here called the cross "rule." The cross is contemplated according to its shape, its composition, the property of its parts, its activity, and many other aspects, which are visible to those who love to behold divine things. According to its shape, the cross, when contemplated, indicates the power that holds together all things, those above and those below on either side, at their limits. According to its composition, it displays the being, providence and judgment of the power that governs the universe, or rather their manifestations, by which I mean wisdom, knowledge and virtue. Being and wisdom, as productive, are shown by the upright beam. Providence and knowledge, as preserving, are shown by the crossbeam. Judgment and virtue, as destructive of evil and as binding together things made and things preserved with their own principle and cause, are shown by the whole. According to the property of its parts, the cross shows by the

upright line God, who is always the same and never departs from his own permanence because of his [?] immovable foundation. By the crossbeam it indicates that the whole of creation depends entirely on God and has no other basis for being apart from God. According to its activity, it shows the inactivity and mortification of those fixed to it, and this, I think, is the mode of contemplation in which the teacher has here taken the prophetic word. (It is good to show the truth of things beyond us by examples drawn from our own world.) Each office has certain insignia by which those who receive them become manifest to all [?] as having received that office from the emperor. A magistrate, for example, has what are called codicils; another holds the so-called [?] by means of the sword; and another holds another office by some other token. They receive these from the emperor themselves and carry them in their own hands, but on going out they give them to their own servants to carry. In just this way our Master Jesus Christ, with respect to his humanity, received his own cross as the symbol of his own rule and went out bearing it on his shoulders. First he carried it himself, then he gave it to another, showing by this that whoever is entrusted with rule must first lead those guided by it and hold fast to what it prescribes (for so he will be readily heeded in his counsels), and only then command those entrusted to him to do the same. If the insignia of the rule of our Lord Jesus Christ is the cross, which he carried on his shoulders, it is fitting to learn what he wished to show mystically by arranging and enduring these things as he did. Those versed in symbols say that the shoulder is a token of practice, and the cross a token of dispassion, since it brings about mortification. Our Lord and God passed through both of the things these enigmas stand for, I mean practice and perfect dispassion, so that practice would not be corrupted by vainglory. Through these enigmas, by what he himself accomplished, he showed his subjects, all but crying aloud: "This is the symbol of my rule. Whoever of you, therefore, desires this rule, let him deny himself, take up his cross and follow me." That is, let him take up the practice that mortifies the passions. By this he showed his goodness and the [?] beauty of his generosity, for he longs for all to exercise this rule as he does. For when the God-bearing teacher says, "he is lifted up with the cross," I think he gives us this indication: as the rational nature of men is exalted through practice and the dispassion yoked to it,

Christ himself is clearly said to be lifted up with it. That is, the Christlike state in men is lifted up as it moves, in sequence and order [?], through dispassionate practice to the knowing contemplation of nature, and from that to theological mystagogy. This seems to me to be what the holy Areopagite, the great Dionysius, shows when he says: "But since the Divine is the beginning for holy [minds?], by which holy minds come to know themselves, he who runs up toward what is visible of his own nature will at the beginning see what he himself is, and will receive, as the first holy gift, the gift of looking up toward the light. He who has gazed well upon his own things with dispassionate eyes will [be freed?] from the lightless visitations of ignorance. While he is imperfect, he will not himself desire the most perfect illumination of God, but little by little he will be led up through the first things to those still higher, and, once perfected, he will be led up in due order and in holiness to the highest communion with the Thearchy." Thus, according to this great and God-bearing teacher, the only Most High is lifted up with the cross through us, as we are exalted in the Spirit after his example. We are exalted through practice and the dispassion joined to it to [natural?] knowledge, and [through it?], with [immaterial?] mind, to the mystical contemplation of divine things and initiation into them, and, I will boldly add, to participation in them.

From the same oration, on: "The Word becomes thick."

The God-bearing teacher says that the Word becomes thick in the following sense, I think. It may be that, being the simple and incorporeal Word who spiritually nourishes all the divine powers in heaven in their order, he deigned, through his presence in the flesh, to become thick, from us and for our sake, yet without sin. He deigned to set forth to us, in a manner suited to us, through words and examples, the teaching about ineffable things that surpasses all power of speech. (For he is said to have spoken all things in parables and to have explained nothing without a parable. Teachers like to use this method when their hearers do not attend [?] to what is said, and so to bring them to an awareness of what is said.) Or it may be that, having ineffably hidden himself for our sake in the principles of beings, he is signified proportionately through each visible thing as through certain letters. He is whole in all things at once, most full, and entire in each, whole and undiminished: undifferentiated amid things that differ and always the same, simple and uncompounded in composite things, without beginning in things subject to a beginning, invisible in visible things, and intangible in tangible things. Or it may be that for our sake, who are thick in understanding, he consented to be embodied for us and to be [expressed?] in letters and syl- [?]

lables and [sounds?], so that from all these he might little by little gather us to himself as we follow him, united in the Spirit, and lead us up to a simple and unconditioned conception of himself. He draws us together for his own sake into union with himself as far as he, for our sake, spread himself out by the principle of condescension.

From the same oration, on: "not from what is in him, but from what is around him, one impression gathered from one thing and another from another into a single image of the truth."

From what concerns the essence, that is, from the essence itself, God is never known as to what he is. For the conception of what he is lies beyond reach and is wholly inaccessible to all creation, visible and invisible alike. But from the things around the essence, God gives those who see some indication of himself: only that he is. And this happens when these things are contemplated rightly and piously. All the things around the essence indicate not what it is but what it is not, for example the unbegotten, the unoriginate, the infinite, the incorporeal, and all such things as are around the essence. They present its not being something, not its being something. Besides these there are also the principles of providence and judgment, by which the universe is wisely administered. Together with them, the harmonious contemplation of nature is also said to concern God, since it shows proportionately only that its creator is. The negations, then, stand opposite to the affirmations, but around God they are interwoven with one another in friendly fashion, each taking the other's part. The negations signify not what the Divine is but that it is not something, and so they are united with the affirmations around its being something, though it is not this. The affirmations show only that it is, but not [how?] it is this, and so they are united with the negations around its not being something, though it is this. Toward each other they show the contrariety that comes from opposition, but around God they show their affinity, through the coinciding of the extremes in each other.

From the same oration: "But since it did not suffice for Goodness to be moved only in contemplation of itself, but the good had to be poured out and to go forth, so that the objects of its benefaction might be more."

I asked the great and wise elder I have often mentioned about this. He said that by these words the great and God-bearing Gregory shows the following. The same God is alone in himself, as being one in the proper sense, with nothing at all different by nature conceived together with him, and he has in himself alone an incomprehensible, unoriginate, infinite and inconceivable permanence. From this, by an infinitely generous outpouring of goodness, he willed to bring beings from non-being and

give them subsistence, and also to impart himself proportionately and without defilement to all and to each, granting each the power to be and to endure. So says the holy and godlike great Dionysius the Areopagite, who declares that "the One is to be hymned of God" because he is exempt from all things. Having brought into being by goodness the whole ordered array of intelligible things and the beauty of visible things, he is present undiminished in each creature proportionately, according to an ineffable principle of wisdom, and yet in no way or manner is he held by the whole. In some he is present by an abundant, good-giving outpouring, in others moderately, and in others so that they can at least image him in some respect. And this, perhaps, in my foolishness, would be the good's being poured out and going forth: the one God being multiplied, in proportion to those who receive him, through the imparting of good things.

From the same oration, on: "He shares in a second communion, far more paradoxical than the first."

It was wonderful, I think, though not so wonderful, great as it was, that at the first fashioning, when human nature was pure, having been fashioned by the hand of God, God led it into communion with himself through the inbreathing, imparting to what was like him the divine beauty according to the image. It was far more wonderful that, when this nature had been defiled and had fled from God through the passions it had taken on, he consented to associate with it and to share in the worse, and that he, who is wholly unmixed with created things, heightened the wonder by the paradoxical union. Before, the nature had received oneness with God in no mode or principle of essence or hypostasis, the categories in which all beings are universally contemplated. But now, through the ineffable union, it has received oneness with him according to hypostasis. It preserves unchanged its own principle according to essence, different from the divine essence, with which, through the union, it has hypostatic oneness while remaining different. So by the principle of being, according to which it came to be and exists, it remains, properly possessing its own being, undiminished in every way. But by the principle of how it is, since it has received its subsistence divinely, it neither knows nor admits at all any inclination of movement toward anything else. In this way, then, the Word made a communion with human nature far more paradoxical than the former, uniting the very nature to himself essentially, in hypostasis.

From the same, on: "But now receive for me the conception, and leap, if not like John from the womb [?], then like David at the resting of the ark."

John the Great not only of repentance and of the [?]

…is an image of practical philosophy [?], of dispassion and of gnostic contemplation: of the first as herald and baptist, of the second as a hermit wholly separated from the world, and of the third as Levite, priest and forerunner of God the Word. He is also a symbol of unchangeableness in the settled state of these virtues [?], since from the womb until his death he kept the soul's tension in them unrelenting. David too is an image of confession, of practice and of contemplation, as one of the tribe of Judah, first a shepherd and later a king, and the destroyer of the foreigners. He is not, however, a symbol of unchangeableness in the state of these. For after coming to knowledge he fell, suffering something human, and did not keep his state of virtue and knowledge unchanged. Perhaps this is why it is not written that he leapt before the Word from the womb, as the great John did, but only after the complete destruction of the foreigners and the restoration of the ark, that is, after the passions had withdrawn and knowledge had returned. John, then, is a type of all who are born in the Spirit through repentance into virtue and knowledge, and who through progress keep that state unchanged to the end. David is a type of all who fall after coming to knowledge and who through repentance bring back to the soul the exultation of divine joy in virtue and knowledge. Being, then, [?] and having wisely drawn together by the Spirit the power of the word that could have been spread out at length, the great teacher compared the hearers of the divine oracles to the great John and David through the state of each. It is as though each person who lives in piety is wholly modeled [?] on one of these two, according to the mode that is fitting [?] in each case, and he were crying out plainly: "All of you who have received the divine Word of virtue and knowledge, conceived in you through repentance: either, like the great John, keep the soul's divine leaping toward him unchangeably in your state from beginning to end through progress, never coming under any form of evil or ignorance at all; or, like the blessed David, if something you did not will has befallen you in the divine race, strive diligently through repentance to bring virtue and knowledge back to yourselves by the tension of endurance and the exercise of divine words. Do not, through negligence, leave this divine ark within you, I mean the ark of virtue and knowledge, exposed to the passions, and so suffer what befell the priest Eli, falling backward by the gates of the temple at Shiloh and dying with the shoulder of your practice broken." This, I think, is what this blessed Father teaches more clearly in his oration on New Sunday, where he says: "We are commanded to sing a new song to the Lord, whether we are those who were dragged off by sin to Babylon and its evil

confusion and then were brought safely back to Jerusalem, who could not sing a divine song there, as in a foreign land, but here establish a new song and a new way of life; or whether we are those who have remained in the good and are making progress, having already accomplished some things and still accomplishing others by the Spirit who makes all things new." Having understood these things, as I conjecture in my folly, the teacher, I think, says: "Now receive my conception and leap, if not like John from the womb, then like David at the ark's coming to rest." In doing so he has drawn together the contemplation of what was said by the mode of contemplation according to dignity and genus. For those who carefully tend such mysteries, lovers of the spiritual principles within them and lovers of contemplation, say that the universal principle of scriptural contemplation, though it is one, is contemplated as spread out tenfold: by place, time, genus, person, and dignity or occupation; by practical, natural and theological philosophy; and by present and future, that is, by type and truth. Gathered together again, they say, it encloses the five within three modes, the three again within two, and the two within one principle that is wholly beyond number. That is, the modes of time, place, genus, person and dignity, which are five, it gathers into three, those of practical, natural and theological philosophy; these, being three, it gathers again into two, those signifying present and future; and these into the perfecting, simple and, as they say, all-embracing ineffable principle. From this principle, by procession, came the universal decad of the modes under which Scripture is contemplated, and into it, as into its origin, the same decad is gathered back anagogically into a monad by circumscription. The principle of Scripture is contemplated by time when it indicates "once", "was", "is", "will be", "before this", "the present", "after this", "at this time", "from the beginning", "the past", "the future", years, seasons, months, weeks, days and nights and their parts, and simply whatever is expressive of time. By place, when it signifies heaven and earth, air and sea, the inhabited world, its ends, countries, islands, cities, temples, villages, fields, mountains, ravines, roads, rivers, deserts, winepresses, threshing floors, vineyards, and simply whatever can characterize a place. By genus: universally, when it indicates angels or whatever belongs to the ordered ranks of intelligible beings in heaven, and also the sun and moon, stars, fire, and whatever is in the air, on the earth or in the sea, whether animals, zoophytes or plants, whatever is mined from the earth and is subject to human arts, and other such things; and particularly, when it names human beings, nations, peoples, tongues, tribes, clans and the like, with or without number. By person, when it calls by name this angel or that archangel, or the Seraphim, or any of the intelligible beings who dwell in heaven, or when it indicates by name Abraham or Isaac or Jacob, or anyone else whom Scripture sets down for praise or blame.

By dignity, when it speaks of a kingdom or a king, a shepherd or a flock, a priest or the priesthood, a farmer, a general or a master builder, and simply any other of the occupations by which the human race is divided. All these things which our account has shown to be contained in the five modes are constituted by essence, power and activity, the first divisions that apply to them. They either move or are moved, act or are acted upon, contemplate or are contemplated, speak or are spoken of, teach or are taught, receive encouragement or dissuasion; in short, as doing or as suffering, they introduce us in varied ways, by being interwoven with one another, to practical, natural and theological philosophy. Each of the things named is taken in many ways, for praise or for blame, by the conceptions formed about it in contemplation, and it brings to light the principles concerning it: what is to be done or not to be done, what is natural or unnatural, what is intelligible or unintelligible. For this, as I said, is the mode in each principle, as far as possible for someone who examines it intelligently in contemplation, so that by positing the principles that are to be done, natural and intelligible, and by removing the imaginings that are not to be done, unnatural and unintelligible, the pious may acquire practical, natural and theological philosophy, which is the same as to say love of God. These in turn are divided by present and future, as having shadow and truth, type and archetype. For however supernaturally and loftily it may be possible for a human being in this age, having reached the highest measure of virtue, knowledge and wisdom, to attain knowledge of divine things, that knowledge is in type and image of the archetypes. Truly, everything we now take to be truth is a type, a shadow and an image of the greater principle. The Word who is in all things, who in the present points toward the future and who is the maker of all things, is understood as in type and in truth, both being and appearing; yet he is beyond present and future and beyond type and truth, since nothing opposed to him is contemplated alongside him. But to truth something is opposed, namely falsehood. Therefore the Word toward whom all things [?] is beyond truth, and [?] as being man and God, and as truly beyond all humanity and divinity. Thus the first five modes, through the manifold contemplation of them, are gathered into practical, natural and theological philosophy; these again into present and future, that is, into type and truth; and present and future into the principle of all, that is, the Word who was in the beginning. He causes those who have become worthy of him to experience and see him, those who have diligently made their journey to him by the means described, and who, for his sake, have made the decad that came about for them into [?], shaking them free of every [?] and natural

and intelligible movement, and forming in them by grace, in their whole state, the divine property of the simplicity that belongs to God by nature. It should also be known that the principle of providence is sown in natural philosophy, and the principle of judgment in practical philosophy, according to the modes that befit them, in which they are revealed through the contemplation of things that are and things that come to be. Having understood these things, as was said, this God-minded teacher, I think, fittingly named the saints in question from the mode of contemplation by genus and dignity, and the great John also from the mode of place. So Saint John, as herald of repentance, is an image of practice; as a hermit, of dispassion; as Levite and priest, of gnostic contemplation; and as having leapt before the Word from the womb, he is a symbol of unchangeableness and of the settled state of virtue and knowledge. Saint David, as one of Judah and a shepherd, is an image of practical philosophy through confession, and as king of Israel he introduces contemplative mystagogy. Saint John's genus is the nation and tribe from which he came; his dignity, his preaching and priesthood; his place, the desert in which he lived. Likewise Saint David's genus is the nation and tribe, and his occupation, that is, his dignity, is shepherding and kingship. Thus each of them, contemplated in a manner proper to himself according to the fitting principle of the modes applied to him, shows without error the mystery signified through him.

From the same oration, on the passage: "If he flees into Egypt, eagerly go into exile with him; it is good to flee with Christ when he is persecuted. If he lingers in Egypt, call him out of Egypt, where he is rightly worshiped." Besides knowing that the Lord fled into Egypt, one must, I think, also know, as follows from this, by whom he was persecuted. The Lord flees, then, not simply into Egypt, but persecuted by Herod, who was at that time reigning over the land of Judea. Herod is interpreted, they say, as "[?]", "made of skin" and "nature". Egypt too is understood in many ways, according to the conceptions formed about it by the contemplative modes: sometimes as the present world, sometimes as the flesh, sometimes as sin, sometimes as ignorance, sometimes as affliction. It is chiefly in this last sense that it is now fitting to take the Lord's flight into Egypt. It is good, then, to flee into Egypt with Christ, that is, with the discerning [?] word within us. He is persecuted for the time being because of his infancy, on account of us who are still infants in relation to him, by the earthly mind that holds sway over us and reigns [?] through the passionate movements of the flesh. We flee with him into the

affliction of practice, until death is announced to us, through dispassion, of those who seek the soul of the most divine Word who is an infant within us, that is, of those who wish to put to death our God-perfected life according to the Word, and who rage to destroy our Christlike condition, that is, our settled state. Meanwhile the Word, through our unmixed [?] eagerness of choice, rides as on a light cloud into our Egypt, I mean the flesh, and shakes its movements and passions like idols made by hands, moving them from their seat and driving them wholly out of the soul, and once the images are cast off, he rightly transfers worship to himself. This is how we flee well with Christ when he is persecuted, receiving dispassion as a fine reward for fleeing with him through voluntary affliction. And again, we call Christ out of Egypt when, after the passions have withdrawn and been completely put to death, we do not allow the divine word of discernment within us to busy itself foolishly with stratagems against things that no longer exist, nor allow him to be known only as the Word in the flesh, whether in ourselves or in those who converse with us. Rather, having been well and faithfully trained beforehand through the virtues in the types belonging to the affliction of practical philosophy, let us ascend from these through contemplation to the knowledge of the things of which they are types and prefigurations, as if going up well from some Egypt into Judea and teaching those with us to go up as well. And let us pass from knowing Christ through practice as the Word in the flesh to the knowledge of his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father. Thus one flees well and piously with Christ when he is persecuted, and so calls him back again to contemplation and knowledge, passing over from practice and doing everything with the Word, through the Word, and for the Word. Do not be surprised that Egypt has now been taken to mean the affliction that belongs to virtue. Look carefully at what is recounted in the Old Testament: how Egypt not only oppressed Israel as they made bricks, but also tormented the Egyptians themselves to destruction through Moses' coming. For Egypt is interpreted, as I said, as affliction [?] and also as darkness. Every interpretation, by reasonable account, generally admits both a praiseworthy and a blameworthy sense of what it signifies through contemplation. If, then, when the flesh is in good condition and well fattened, the soul is tormented and darkened by the passions, as the state of the virtues and the illumination of knowledge withdraw, then in the same way, surely and reasonably, when the soul is guarded and made radiant by the divine beauty of the virtues and the illumination of knowledge, the outer man is destroyed, and the flesh, through the coming of the Word, casts off its natural vigor. Hidden in the flesh, or rather reigning in it, the dragon whose power is in the navel, like an invisible Pharaoh scattering what is good, used to creep through the soul, inflicting the bites of sin. But as the mind of the flesh is gradually extinguished by the hardship of practice, he

withdraws, wholly put to death, leaving, as is fitting, not even a trace of his former tyranny. So those who have gained freedom through Christ can cry out even before the general resurrection, because of the voluntary resurrection of their will that has already taken place in them: "Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O [Hades], is your victory?" By this they mean the pleasure of the flesh and the deception of the soul joined to it out of ignorance. Through these, before Christ, the all-defiled devil once held human nature in his power, piercing it unsparingly with the sting of pleasure and contentiously cutting it down [?] to destruction with the sword of deception. By the same author, from the oration on the Lights, on the passage: "If they had to be impious at all and fall away from the glory of God, being carried off to idols, works of art and things fashioned by hands, those who have sense should pray for nothing else against them than that they should worship such things and honor them in this way." When these words were read, some of the listeners [?] reproached the teacher, saying it is not right for people who have sense and have resolved to live according to the Gospel to pray against anyone that they should worship such things and honor them in this way. To them I say nothing of my own, but what I was taught about this by an elder who was wise in divine things and held the teaching of the Fathers in high regard. You people (for I shall speak to them as if they were present), our holy and blessed Father and teacher Gregory saw that the Greeks had from the outset been so irrationally led astray and so completely carried away from the conception of the God who truly is, and he goes through these things out of the law of compassion. His aim was that, through the irrationality and cheapness, or rather, to speak more precisely, the abomination of their objects of worship, and through the thorough refutation of those objects by argument [?], their ascent to right teaching might become very easy; and moreover that no one might be dragged by them into false belief, since the deception is plain and easily detected by everyone at first glance, not covering the hidden evil with anything that seems honorable. From the same oration, on the passage: "Where there is purification there is illumination, and illumination is the fulfillment of desire for those who long for the greatest things, or the Greatest, or what is beyond the great." Those versed in the divine mysteries know that where the soul is purified through the virtues, there the illumination of knowledge also appears, after a pious examination of beings, raising the soul to the understanding of the divine [?]

[Saint Maximus the Confessor] ...lifting the soul up and fastening its desire to the last of desirable things, which is God, who properly exists and is known in the greatest things, in the Greatest, and beyond the great. He is in the greatest things as in three hypostases, consubstantial and equal in power, unconfused by the precise and unchangeable property of each, I mean unbegottenness, begetting and procession. He is in the Greatest because the Godhead is one and the same in essence and is a monad. He is beyond the great because the divine is not circumscribed by any quantity, magnitude or size, nor contained within any limits. For every magnitude is limited, but the divine alone is without limit. As the great David says, "Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and of his greatness there is no limit", for it is bounded by no limitation. It is therefore also infinite, since no concept of any kind, whether of time or of nature, reaches it. It was by such concepts that those devoted to such matters devised the technical method of logical arguments, in which they took pride [?], and with which they were shown unfit for the discovery of truth, since they believed that whatever could not be captured by their own reasonings did not exist at all. The teacher shows that this is what he meant by using the same words elsewhere too. In his oration on the arrival of those from Egypt, discoursing theologically [?] about the uncreated and divine essence and the created nature that received a beginning of being, he says: "The one is called God and subsists in three greatest things: the cause, the creator and the perfecter, I mean the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit." And again, in his oration on Baptism, discussing the one and the same holy Godhead in three holy hypostases, he says: "Equal on every side, everywhere the same, like the one beauty and greatness of heaven, an infinite union in nature of three infinites." So the teacher has become his own interpreter for those who read his God-inspired words with care. From the same oration, on the passage: "Natures are made new, and God becomes man." The saints received many of the divine mysteries from those who became eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word and were initiated by them directly into the knowledge of beings, and these were handed down to them by succession from those who came before them. They say that the existence of all things that have come to be is divided by five divisions. The first of these, they say, is the one that divides created nature as a whole, which received its being through coming into existence, from uncreated nature. For they say that God, by his goodness, [?]

[?] the ordering of all beings, it did not become immediately evident to it who and of what sort he is; and they call the ignorance concerning this, which distinguishes creation from God, a division. For the division that separates these from each other by nature, and never admits union into one essence, since it cannot receive one and the same principle, they left unspoken. The second division is the one by which the whole of nature that has received its being through creation is divided by God into intelligible and sensible things. The third is the one by which sensible nature is divided into heaven and earth; the fourth, the one by which the earth is divided into paradise and the inhabited world; and the fifth, the one by which man is divided into male and female. Man was introduced into beings last, by way of generation and in a manner befitting the good, as a kind of workshop that binds the whole universe together, mediating naturally through himself among all the extremes of every division. By the relation his own parts bear to all the extremes, he clearly possesses by nature every power for union through the middle terms between all the extremes. Through this power the mode that is fulfilled according to the cause of the generation of divided things was to make manifest through itself the great mystery of the divine purpose: the union of the extremes among beings with one another, advancing harmoniously from the nearest to the farthest and from the lesser to the better in ordered ascent, and culminating in God. This is why man is introduced last among beings: as a kind of natural bond, he mediates through his own parts among the universal extremes and brings into one, in himself, things that stand naturally far apart from one another. In this way he would begin the union that gathers all things to God as their cause first from his own division. Then, advancing in sequence and order through the intermediates, he would reach his goal in God, the end of the lofty ascent that comes about through all things by way of union, in whom there is no division. Through a most dispassionate disposition toward divine virtue, he would shake off from nature entirely the property of male and female, which in no way depended on the primary principle of the divine purpose for the generation of man. So he would be shown to be, and would become, according to the divine purpose, simply a human being, not divided by the designation of male and female. That is the principle according to which he was originally made, not split into the segments that now attach to him, because of his perfect knowledge, as I said, of the principle according to which he exists. Then, uniting paradise and the inhabited world through his own holy conduct, he would make them one earth, not divided for him by the difference of its parts but rather gathered together, since he would suffer subjection to none of its parts. Then, uniting heaven and earth through an identity of life with the angels in every way according to virtue, as far as is attainable for human beings, he would make the sensible creation one, wholly undivided

in itself and not divided for him spatially by intervals at all. For he would have become light in spirit, held down to earth by no bodily weight and kept from no ascent to the heavens, because to the mind these things would be perfectly invisible as it hastened genuinely toward God. Wisely making its ascent to him step by step, as on an ordinary road, the mind would naturally use the point already reached as a step toward what lies beyond [?]. Then, besides these, uniting intelligible and sensible things through an equality with the angels in knowledge, he would make the whole creation one creation, not divided for him by knowledge and ignorance, since his knowing understanding of the principles in beings would have become equal to the angels', lacking nothing. Through this understanding the boundlessly generous outpouring of true wisdom comes upon the worthy, as far as is lawful, and then purely and without mediation grants them an unknowable and inexpressible conception of God. And finally, beyond all these, uniting created nature with the uncreated through love (O the wonder of God's love for us!), he would show them to be one and the same by the possession of grace. He would wholly interpenetrate God entirely and become all that God is, apart from identity of essence. He would receive God himself wholly in exchange for himself, and would gain God alone as the prize, as it were, of his ascent to God. For God is the end of the motion of things that move, and the firm and unmoving rest of those borne toward him, and he is the boundary and limit, undefined and infinite, of every definition, ordinance and law, of reason, mind and nature. Man, however, was not moved naturally, as he had been created, around the unmoved, his own beginning (I mean God). Instead he moved willingly and foolishly, contrary to nature, around the things beneath him, which God had commanded him to rule. He misused the natural power given him at his creation for the union of divided things, turning it instead to the division of things united, and so he came pitiably close to passing back into non-being. For this reason natures are made new: paradoxically and beyond nature, that which is wholly unmoved by nature is moved, so to speak, immovably around that which is moved by nature, and God becomes man in order to save lost man. Through himself he united the fissures of nature in the universe as a whole, and brought forth the universal principles of the particulars, by which the union of divided things naturally comes about. In this way he would fulfil the great counsel of God the Father, recapitulating all things in himself, the things in heaven and the things on earth, in whom they were also created. Indeed, beginning the universal union of all things to himself from our

division, he becomes a perfect human being, from us, for us, and like us. He has everything that is ours, lacking nothing, apart from sin, and for this he did not need the natural course of marriage at all. At the same time he showed, I think, that there was perhaps another way for humanity to multiply, foreknown by God, if the first man had kept the commandment and had not cast himself down to the level of beasts by misusing his own powers. He also drove out of nature the difference and division of male and female, which, as I said, he did not need at all in order to become man. And things one can perhaps exist without need not remain forever. For in Christ Jesus, says the divine Apostle, there is neither male nor female. Then, having sanctified our inhabited world by his own conduct as a man, after death he goes unhindered into paradise, as he truthfully promised the thief when he said: Today you will be with me in paradise. Then, since for him our inhabited world no longer differed from paradise, he appeared on it again after his resurrection from the dead and lived with the disciples. So he showed that the earth is one and undivided in itself, keeping the principle by which it exists free from the division caused by difference. Then, through his ascension into heaven, he clearly united heaven and earth. Entering heaven with this earthly body, which shares our nature and essence, he showed that the whole of sensible nature is one by its more universal principle, obscuring the property of the division that cuts it within itself. Then, besides these, he passed in order through all the divine and intelligible ranks in heaven with soul and body, that is, with our complete nature, and so united sensible and intelligible things. In himself he showed that the whole creation converges toward the one according to its most primordial and universal principle, wholly undivided and free of strife. And finally, beyond all these, according to the concept of his humanity he comes to God himself, having clearly appeared on our behalf, as it is written, before the face of God the Father as man. As Word he can never in any way be separated from the Father. As man he fulfilled, in deed and in truth and by unswerving obedience, all that he himself as God had foreordained to come about. He accomplished the whole counsel of God the Father on behalf of us, who by misuse had made useless the power given to us naturally for this from the beginning. First he united us to ourselves in himself by removing the difference of male and female, and instead of men and women, in whom the mode of division is most clearly seen,

Gal. 3:28. Luke 23:45. Baruch 3:58.

he showed us to be properly and truly human beings only, wholly formed according to him and bearing his image intact and entirely unadulterated, untouched in any way by any of the marks of corruption. With us and through us he embraced the whole creation, the extremes through the intermediates as his own parts, and bound them tightly to each other around himself: paradise and the inhabited world, heaven and earth, sensible and intelligible things. For like us he has body, sense, soul and mind. Through each of these, as through parts, he appropriated to each the extreme that is universally akin to it, in the manner described above, and so recapitulated all things in himself in a manner befitting God. He showed the whole creation to be one, like another human being, completed by the coming together of its parts and inclining toward itself in the totality of its existence. This accords with the one, simple, indeterminate and undifferentiated conception of its production from non-being, according to which the whole creation can receive one and the same wholly indistinguishable principle, since it has the "it was not" prior to its being. For according to the true principle, all things that come after God and have their being from God through generation coincide with one another in some respect at least, if not in every respect. For no being whatever, not even the most honourable and exalted, is by nature wholly freed from a generic relation to the very lowest [?]. Nor is the lowliest among beings wholly cut off from, or without a share in, a generic relation by nature to the most honourable [?]. For all things that are distinguished from one another by their own particular differences are united generically by universal and common identities, and are drawn together toward one and the same by some generic principle of nature. For example, genera, united with one another according to essence, possess oneness, identity and indivisibility. For none of the universal, containing and generic things is entirely divided along with the particular, contained and specific things. For what does not gather together things divided by nature, but is divided along with them and departs from its own singular unity, can no longer be generic. For every genus, according to its own principle, exists whole, indivisibly and singularly, in the wholes beneath it, and is seen generically as whole in each individual. Likewise species, freed through the genus from the variety that lies in difference, receive identity with one another. Individuals, which agree with one another according to species, become entirely one and the same with one another, being unvarying in nature [?] and free from all difference. Accidents, compared with one another according to their subject, possess unity and are in no way scattered in the subject. And a truthful witness to these things is the true speaker of God, the great and holy

Dionysius the Areopagite, who says in the chapter on the perfect and the one in his treatise On the Divine Names: "For there is no multiplicity that does not participate in some way in the one. What is many in its parts is one in the whole; what is many in its accidents is one in the subject; what is many in number or in powers is one in species; what is many in species is one in genus; what is many in processions is one in the source; and there is nothing among beings that does not participate in some way in the one." In short, to put it concisely, the principles of all divided and particular things are contained, as they say, in the principles of universal and generic things. The principles of the more generic and universal things are held together by wisdom, while the principles of particular things, variously held within those of the generic, are contained by prudence. By prudence they are first simplified and shed the symbolic variety in the underlying things, and then they are unified by wisdom, receiving natural union in identity with the more generic. And the Wisdom and Prudence of God the Father is the Lord Jesus Christ. He holds together the universals of beings by the power of wisdom and contains the parts that complete them by the prudence of understanding, since by nature he is the creator and provider of all. Through himself he brings into one what stands apart, dissolves the war among beings, and binds all things into peaceful friendship and undivided concord, the things in heaven and the things on earth, as the divine Apostle says.

Another contemplation on the same difficulty.

Natures are made new again. The divine nature, through goodness and immeasurable love for humanity, willingly and supernaturally submits to our fleshly birth. Our nature, paradoxically and by a law foreign to nature, cultivates without seed for the incarnate God a flesh rationally ensouled, in every respect the same as ours and unvarying, without sin. And, more paradoxical still, the law of virginity of the one who became his mother was in no way diminished by the birth. And it is properly an innovation not only that God the Word, already begotten ineffably and without beginning from God the Father, should be born in time according to the flesh, but also that our nature should provide flesh without seed, and that a virgin should give birth without corruption. Each of these makes its innovation evident, yet at the same time wholly conceals the ineffable and unknowable principle according to which it came about and also demonstrates it: it conceals it by the mode that is beyond nature and knowledge, and it demonstrates it by the principle of faith, by which everything beyond nature and knowledge is naturally grasped.

someone, as if interpreting the births, to say: "My Christ is seen to honour all these births in himself: the first by the first and life-giving inbreathing, the second by the incarnation and the baptism with which he himself was baptized, the third by the resurrection of which he himself was the firstfruits; for just as he became the firstborn among many brothers, so he also deigned to become the firstborn from the dead." How is it that in these words this God-minded teacher seems to have made a superfluous repetition of what he said before? For after speaking of a threefold birth, from bodies, from baptism and from resurrection, he added a fourth, as though he had forgotten, in a phrase that seems superfluous, by saying: "the first by the first and life-giving inbreathing." For he had not mentioned this one among the three births, yet he added it as though it had already been mentioned, saying: "the first by the first and life-giving inbreathing." How the teacher said this truly is surely known to one who has become like him in virtue and does not stand far from his wise knowledge of divine things. As far as I can understand, within the limits of my weak mind, I do not think the fourth birth he added is superfluous. Rather, it completes the birth from bodies set out earlier and interprets the divine principles and modes concerning it. He consented to become man for the sake of the creation of the first Adam, and did not disdain to be born on account of his transgression. Through creation he showed his condescension to the fallen; through birth he showed his voluntary self-emptying toward the condemned. By creation he was naturally brought into the same state as man through the life-giving inbreathing; receiving from it, as man, what is "in the image," he kept the freedom of sinlessness unsold and unstained. By birth according to the incarnation he voluntarily took on, through the form of a servant, man's likeness in corruption, and he consented by his will to be subject to the same natural passions as we are, without sin, as though liable to them, though he was sinless. For having [?] these in both respects, he was composed of the parts [?]

a perfectly new Adam, bearing in himself the first Adam undiminished in both respects. For he submitted by condescension to the law of Adam's creation before the transgression, and in being fashioned he naturally received sinlessness through the inbreathing, but he did not also take on incorruptibility. And from the birth that came after the transgression as a result of condemnation he naturally received passibility through his voluntary self-emptying, but he did not also take on the inclination to sin. So he becomes a new Adam, receiving the same sinless creation and submitting to the same passible birth. For he wove both perfectly together in himself, each in turn by the parts that belong to it, and through each other he powerfully healed both, by the absence of the extreme belonging to each. He made the second, dishonoured one saving and renewing for the first, honoured one, and established the first as constituting and preserving the second. By extremes I mean, in the case of creation, which is first and honoured, incorruptibility, as the source of sinlessness; and in the case of birth, which is second and dishonoured, the inclination to sin, as the cause of all passion and corruption. In the incarnation the Saviour did not take these into himself at all, but he accepted what came about because of them [?].
