He made birth saving for creation, paradoxically renewing the incorruptibility of creation through the suffering that belongs to birth. In turn, he made creation preserving for birth, sanctifying the passionate character of birth by the sinlessness that belongs to creation. So he would wholly restore creation, holding nature fast by its God-perfected principle, and wholly free from birth the nature that had fallen under it through sin, no longer held, like the other living creatures on earth, by the flowing manner of seed. So then, join creation, fashioning and inbreathing naturally with the incarnation and birth, and distinguish them from each other by conception alone. You will then find, according to the great teacher, that the fourth birth completes the birth from bodies, and that it is distinguished from it by conception alone, in the manner explained. I mean that it is the same as creation, which is conceived as naturally prior to the birth introduced afterwards, and to which belongs the first and [?]

To put it briefly: if you wish to grasp the precision of the teacher's words, ask what the principle of man's creation is, the one that precedes as cause and always remains within its own stability without departing from it. Then ask what the mode of his birth is, according to the educative dispensation on account of sin, which has as its goal the correction of the one being educated and his complete return to the principle of his creation. Then you will learn clearly how God, having become man, has become so perfectly in both respects [?],

wisely leading the mode belonging to the dispensation back to the principle of creation that he truly possessed. And then you will rightly marvel at the teacher's understanding: by dividing in conception what is joined in nature, he secretly made plain the whole principle of the most divine mystery concerning us. For by dividing in conception the birth from bodies between the life-giving inbreathing and the incarnation, he hinted at the difference between the mode of birth and the principle of creation. God laid hold of these for our sake. He renewed nature, or rather, to speak more truly, made it new, and restored it to the ancient beauty of incorruptibility through his holy flesh, taken from us and rationally ensouled. More than that, he generously granted it deification, from which it cannot possibly fall away, since it is present in the incarnate God himself as a soul is in a body. It interpenetrates him wholly and without confusion in the union, and in exchange for his manifestation through it, it received concealment to the same degree that he himself became manifest through it; and he was thought to have gone beyond his own natural hiddenness. And what is more paradoxical than this? Being God by nature, and deigning to become man by nature, he did not wholly transgress the natural boundaries of either nature through the other. Being wholly God, he remained so when he had wholly become man. Being God did not prevent him from becoming man, and becoming man did not diminish his being God. [?] ... or whatever other things [?] ... taking [?] without the underlying reality did he fulfil this [?]. Instead, he properly assumed human nature itself, in fact and in truth, and united it to himself hypostatically, without change, alteration, diminution or division, holding it fast and unfallen in the principle and definition of its essence. According to this, as this holy and great teacher says, he also honoured our birth from bodies by truly becoming man and being born. He did this to free us from the bonds of birth: from the law by which, sown like grass, we spring up out of condemnation because of sin, and from sharing with plants and irrational animals the same kinship in our coming into being. As the great Ezekiel, seer of great things, says somewhere, when he was initiated into the divine mysteries and taught the cause of the present dispensation concerning man, speaking as if to Jerusalem: Thus says the Lord to Jerusalem: Your root and your birth are from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite, and [?]

…your mother a Hittite. On the day you were born they did not tie your navel, nor were you washed in water, nor rubbed with salt, nor wrapped in swaddling clothes; and you were cast out on the face of the [?] field in the crookedness of your soul on the day you were born. And I passed by you, and saw you weltering in your blood, and I said to you: From your blood is your life; multiply; I have made you like the growth of the field." So the Lord, who heals nature of its condemnation to grow from seed like grass and to have its life from blood like the other animals, and who leads it back to the original grace of incorruption, came to set it free. He came to show it plainly the good toward which, though it was created for it in the beginning, it never moved at all. He came to trample down the evil toward which it was moved against nature through deception at the very moment of its creation, and so emptied out its whole power. He came to bind to himself the power of desire (of which the navel is a symbol), so that it might acquire a fixed and unchangeable habit that bears fruit in the good. He came to wash it in water, by which I mean to cleanse it of the defilements of ignorance in the sea of knowledge poured around it by grace. He came to rub it with salt and wrap it in swaddling clothes. That is, he firmly strengthened by the Spirit its natural activity toward the good for which it was made, and so made it pure and closed to the rot of the passions. Then, binding it tightly like swaddling bands in the covering of the true principles found in beings, he made it wholly incapable of dissolution. Another contemplation on the same passage. Perhaps the teacher's point in what he said is that the principle and mode of the coming into being of human nature are twofold, one belonging to the soul and the other to the body. So he divided birth from bodies, conceptually, into two births. He indicates that the soul is constituted ineffably from the divine and life-giving inbreathing. The body, he indicates, is formed at conception, together with the soul, from the underlying matter of the body from which it comes. For it is not right to say that the principle and mode of coming into being are identical, without any difference, in both cases, since these two are not the same as each other in essence. When things do not have the same being, their principle and mode of coming into being clearly differ from each other as well. Rather, it is right to think that the soul has one principle and mode, [?] according to which the body comes to be, exists, and remains unchangeably joined to the soul. (229a) A brief contemplation against those who say that souls exist before or after bodies. [?] For both of them, I mean soul and body, exist together, and the time of their coming into being is the same. Neither exists before or after the other in coming into being, as I said, lest the [form made] from

both, as a whole, [?] be dissolved. For then the principle of relation [?] would rightly [be destroyed] if one of them, as a part, had a subsistence of its own that was older, and had its union with the other entirely without natural relation. For this reason it could never naturally join with another by composition to complete the hypostasis of something else without being corrupted and altered into what it was not. For what subsists individually and on its own beforehand is not of a nature to be brought into another [?] hypostasis. And if what subsists beforehand does enter into composition with another to complete a different form, it must do so either according to nature or against nature. If according to nature, it will be seen never ceasing from composition with another to complete a different form, since the force of nature cannot depart from itself. By this reasoning the soul will never be conceived without the body, nor the body without the soul. [?] So by their excess their wisdom has been turned [?] into folly, driven by force toward the very thing they were eager to flee. But if either of these enters into composition with the other against nature, to complete a different form, it is wholly corrupted. It departs from the boundary of nature, becomes what it is not by nature, and changes into what it was not. And what could be more senseless than that? But let me return to the subject. (229b) The soul, then, as the teacher expressly says, does not come into being from underlying matter as bodies do. It comes into being by the will of God through the life-giving inbreathing, ineffably and unknowably, in a way known only to its creator. Receiving its being [?], it is brought at conception, together with the body, to the completion of one human being. The body comes into being at conception from the underlying matter of another body, that is, of the parents, and together with the soul it receives the composition by which it is one form with it. The teacher shows this more clearly elsewhere when he says: "According to the double power of the inbreathing, we all have both breath and the Holy Spirit breathed into us." At conception, then, we must assign conceptually the life-giving inbreathing and the Holy Spirit to the intellectual essence of the soul, and the enfleshment and the breath to the nature of the body, as the Fathers [?] say. The coming into being of our forefather Adam was also brought about mystically. The soul had one principle of being and one mode of coming into being, and the body clearly had another, as divine Scripture has magnificently taught us. It does not allow the soul and the body to share the same mode of coming into being and so be confused in nature. Then the principle of each one's essence, and the mode of its coming into being, would be unknown.

[?] But if the double power of the inbreathing accompanied Adam and came together with him in his coming into being, what might one say about the composite of both, I mean soul and body, in the incarnation [?] of our God and Savior Jesus Christ? As far as possible, this blend keeps a close resemblance to the first Adam. For the teacher himself says: "Just as God took the body from matter, which was newly made and clearly existed beforehand, and placed in it life from himself, which the Word knows as the intellectual soul and the image of God, and so created man," in the same way he took the body from the immaculate Virgin, as from undefiled earth. He placed in it life from himself, which the Word knows as the [?] soul and the image of God, and so created his own humanity, or rather himself, without change, by assuming flesh animated with intellect and reason. He who, as almighty, created us of his own will, would have made [?]…

In this sense, I think, the teacher says that our Lord and God honored [?] the threefold birth, that is, the general modes of our coming into being, well-being and ever-being. The first is the birth from bodies, through which we receive being. It is one birth of the composite, since its parts, I mean soul and body, exist together at the same time. But it is divided into two because each part comes into being in a different mode. The second is the birth from baptism, through which we richly receive well-being. The third is the birth from resurrection, through which we are transformed by grace into ever-being. We must therefore pay close attention to the teacher's words, because of those who maliciously attack what is well stated. He divided birth from bodies only conceptually, for the reason given. Then he states that the Lord received the life-giving spirit, the inbreathing, in his humanity at the same moment as conception, with no interval of time at all conceived before it, and not after conception. By this I mean the intellectual soul, together with the body taken from the immaculate Virgin. Against those who say that souls exist before bodies.

For some say, as I have already mentioned, that souls exist before bodies. Others say the contrary, that bodies exist before souls. But we travel the middle road as the royal road, following our Fathers. We speak neither of the soul or body existing first nor of either existing afterward. Rather, we speak of their coexistence. We guard against straying to either side, and turn neither to the left nor to the right at all, as Holy Scripture says. We are afraid of

what is the most fearful thing there is to fear. If we say that souls exist before bodies, and that bodies were devised to punish souls for a wickedness committed earlier by incorporeal beings, we would logically be supposing that wickedness alone is the cause of the outstanding magnificence of visible things. Yet it is through this magnificence that God is known and proclaimed in silence. We would be imposing on God a necessity to create, against his purpose, an essence in which he took no pleasure. Perhaps he did not even hold its principle hidden in himself from the beginning, before the ages, together with the others. To say that God holds the principles of essence of things that come into being against his purpose does not seem to me to belong to an intelligent mind. Nor does it belong to one with any real sense of the majesty of God, who is impassible and alone true. Nothing at all is new in the principles of beings that pre-exist in him, and least of all something against his purpose. For all things that in any way exist or will exist have been willed, conceived and foreknown by him in their essence beforehand. He gives essence and subsistence to each of the beings at the suitable and fitting time. When we see God making something, let us not think that he only then began to will it, conceive it and know it. Far from it! It would be truly full of absurdity if God now carried out as good what he had neither conceived nor known nor willed to exist from the beginning, before the ages. That would mean he had now conceived, willed and known it, or rather, to put it more properly, changed his mind. Not to mention that he would not even know how to make the things whose principles he did not hold beforehand. We believe instead that all things are always contained foreknowingly in the will of God, according to his infinite power. Nothing in any way is newly conceived by him and then receives being in its essence. Nor do I suppose that those who think piously should imagine that God learns about each thing by producing it into being. All these things are contained beforehand in him, by his infinite power, according to their own principles, in his foreknowledge. To us, however, the ages and times show each thing being created wisely at its appointed [?] and suitable time, and things are brought forth into being. So the divine Apostle explains about Levi: "For he was still in the loins of his father" before he came into being. Levi existed potentially in the patriarch Abraham, and at the appointed time he actually came into being through gestation. In this way the Apostle led us to understand and believe that all things come into being in sequence and order, according to the ineffable wisdom of God, at the foreknown time.

Consider, then, all things that exist in their essence: those that exist now and those that will exist, those that have come to be and those that will come to be, those that appear and those that will appear. Their principles pre-exist firmly in God. According to these principles all things exist, have come to be, and endure. They are ever drawing near to their own principles, set by God's purpose, through natural motion, and are held more closely to being according to the quality and degree of the motion and inclination of their free choice. They receive well-being through virtue and through holding a straight course toward the principle according to which they exist. Or they receive ill-being through vice and through motion contrary to that principle. In short, this depends on whether they possess or lack their natural power of participating in him. By nature he cannot be participated in at all. Yet through his infinite goodness he gives himself wholly by grace to all, the worthy and the unworthy alike, and he will grant the permanence of ever-being according to how each has disposed himself and what each is. For them, participating or not participating, in due proportion, in him who truly is, who is well and who ever is, brings an intensifying and increasing punishment for those unable to participate, and of enjoyment for those able to participate. For there is absolutely nothing among beings whose principle does not wholly pre-exist with God. And when the principles of things' essence pre-exist with God, their coming into being is clearly wholly in accordance with the divine purpose. And when things come into being in accordance with the divine purpose, their existence in essence remains immovable, never passing from being to non-being. And when the existence of things in essence, after their coming into being, cannot be moved from being to non-being, their principles are permanent and stable. Their sole source of being is Wisdom, through which they exist and from which they have the power to be able to be firmly. And when the principles of things exist permanently with God, the purpose of God, who made (232a) all things, concerning them is unfailing. For God's purpose is in no way enclosed by limits of time. Nor does it admit alteration from change by changing along with its objects. So the existences of these things are clearly and indisputably incorruptible. For either God made human bodies willingly, in accordance with his purpose, and because of him they remain wholly unable to fall into non-being, ever willing to be what was willed with reason and wisdom in accordance with his purpose; in that case there will be no complete passing away of bodies into non-being, as they [?] hold. Or he did not make them in accordance with his purpose. In that case he was tyrannized against his will and led by force to bring into being things whose principles he is not shown to have. And if, tyrannized, he came to make bodies against his purpose and against his will, then clearly reason and wisdom in no way guided their coming into being. For what comes into being against the divine purpose is wholly deprived of reason and wisdom and [?] "or that have come to be" is not in Gallandi's edition. [?] "and of enjoyment for those" [?] Gallandi's edition. "made" [?] "came" Gallandi's edition.

estranged from them. What is wholly deprived of reason and wisdom is evil alone, and its being is marked by non-existence. May it never happen to us even to think of God as its maker, still less to say so openly and dare to believe it, to our ruin. Who, then, tyrannized God, if he has been tyrannized (if it is right to say so at all), so that he made against his purpose what he did not will? And how can one who is tyrannized be God, if he is forced against his purpose to bring into being a genesis of things for destruction [?]? Let those who cherish this opinion dare to answer. They will either say that God made these things, and so commit the greatest blasphemy by imposing on him a necessity to make something against his purpose. Or they will say that he did not (232b) make them, and they will be caught being forced to introduce, like the Manichaeans, another principle that makes these things. For the doctrine of pre-existence belongs wholly to those who set up two opposed principles against each other. By the grace of the all-merciful God, the deep darkness of obscurity has seized these people and driven them into complete oblivion, since they cannot bear the light of the truth proclaimed by our holy Fathers. I pass over for now all that could be said, to keep the discourse in proportion. But I wonder how the mystery of Christ our true God does not shame them into eagerly shaking off this opinion. For the mystery of Christ is more mysterious than all divine mysteries. It is the defining limit of all perfection in every motion in all things, whether present or to come, and it stands above every limit and boundary. And this mystery teaches that the body taken from us, consubstantial with us and united to him hypostatically, exists and subsists with God the Word, who became incarnate and became perfectly human. With this body he was also taken up into the heavens, "far above every principality and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come." With it he sits beside God the Father, now and to infinite ages, having passed through all the heavens and come to be above all. And he will come again to transform the universe and remake its elements, and to save our souls and bodies, as we have believed and believe, and may we remain believing forever. (233a) Given all this, who is so daring and arrogant, knowing only how to fight [?] against what is plain and evident, as even to entertain the bare thought of a passing

of bodies into non-being at some time, through the progress of rational beings toward perfection, as they say? Such a person believes that the Lord himself, the God of all, is with a body now and forever. It is he who gives others the power to be able to progress. As the author of the salvation of all, he leads and calls all to his own glory, as far as the power of the incarnation allows, and he cleanses away the stains in all things. Surely he is not led by them, as if they were types of his perfection, to put off the body, if they would dare to conceive such a thing at all. For he alone is by nature most perfect and the maker of all perfection. He does not follow others toward perfection, nor is his perfection seen through progress. Nor does he wait with others to receive perfection, as if he would put off the nature of the body only when the highest progress prepares the rest to put off the body. In no way at all is he like any being that needs progress. Otherwise he would no longer be the author and Savior of those who are saved, since he would not have shown mystically, beforehand, in himself [?], the end of perfection meant for us. Instead he would appear as just one of those who are saved and led, himself needing another to show in himself the perfection toward which all who naturally share in reason press on. But it is not so. How could it be? The word of truth does not tolerate those who say such things. For the divine Apostle calls him the author and perfecter of our salvation. He became incarnate for our sake, so that he might consume our sin in himself, and [?] give himself as a type and model of virtuous conduct to all who believe in him. As a good and wise teacher, he first carried out in his own person, as a pattern for us, what must be said and done. He died, rose, and was taken up into the heavens, and he is seated with the body at the right hand of God the Father. He did this so that we too, when we die, may firmly hope to rise and to live a life wholly free of all death and all corruption. We hope to be taken up into the heavens, and to receive honor and glory in God the Father through the mediation of his Son, and to dwell with him in blessedness forever. But we are not to expect any putting off of the body at all, since the word of Holy Scripture does not teach us this. Nor have we seen this happen beforehand in the author of our salvation. For if it had pleased him that this too should happen, he himself would first have done it in himself, along with the rest. Out of love for humankind he subjected himself to these things for our sake and brought them to perfection in our condition, so that we might believe and hope for them as well. But if we tolerate

their saying this, how shall we believe, with this holy teacher, that what is united to God is also saved? "For," he says, writing to Cledonius, "what is united to God is also saved." And the body too was united to God the Word together with the soul. Therefore the body too will be saved together with the soul. Again, this divinely minded teacher says that the Word of God became flesh "so that he might both save the image and make the flesh immortal." If so, I cannot see how what is saved will perish, and (234a) how what is made immortal will die again. Or rather, to put it more properly, the flesh has been wholly deified, through the intellectual soul that mediates between the divinity and the body. It has received, ineffably and essentially, the whole hypostasis of the incarnate God the Word, present in it, who made it his own body and showed it to be so. If this doctrine too is contained in the mystery of the Church's faith, why was it not included with the others in the creed, the statement of the blameless faith of Christians? That creed was set out by our holy and blessed Fathers, who assembled at various times to confirm the divine doctrines of the holy catholic and apostolic Church of God. Let us leave it to the wise to answer. But I think it is enough for now to have said these things to these people by way of digression. Let us turn to the others. Against those who say that bodies exist before souls. [To say] that souls exist after bodies is easy, and anyone who wishes can say it. But to establish the claim by reason is very difficult and laborious, [?] while their effort is very easily refuted. For if what is deposited, as you say, as the starting point of human generation is wholly without soul, then clearly it has no share at all in vital power. For what is wholly deprived of any kind of soul lacks all vital activity. And if it has no share at all in soul and in the vital power and activity that come from soul, it is clearly dead. If we suppose it to be dead, it is neither nourished nor grows. It will not be able to subsist at all, nor to remain [?] without scattering and dissolving. This is confirmed by (234b) what happens with wounds in bodies. When physicians treat wounds and find dead flesh on the surface, they first consume it with drugs that eat it away. Only then do they apply the remedies that fill in what has been hollowed out of the wound, so that it may be restored, since the [?] of the living…

[?] of a body that has a nature which [?] and a power that both constitutes and restores its own condition; whereas what is dead does nothing of the kind at all, since it has once been made dead and is wholly deprived of vital power, and is for this reason inactive. And how will what is by nature prone to scatter and easily dissolved hold together, unless some vital power is conceived as underlying it beforehand like a foundation, naturally gathering and binding tightly around itself what is being scattered, the power in which it has been allotted to exist and to receive its form from the power that wisely crafts all things? For in whatever thing being truly belongs to the body after it is born, in that thing it would surely be rightly said to have also the beginning of its existence. For that by whose separation the body naturally dissolves is, clearly, that with which it would quite reasonably also have come into existence at its genesis. But if, hard-pressed by these arguments, you people say that what is deposited as the occasion of the human constitution is not entirely dead, but shares at least to some degree in a vital power, as clearly having a soul for such participation in power (for without soul there could never be any form of life whatever among things that fall under nature and are contained within the ever-moving revolution of heaven, while, by logical consequence, a form of life without soul is never possible at all), then whatever form of life you suppose the deposited seed to have at conception, you have displayed the property of nothing but some soul, which constitutes the substance in which it exists and marks off its difference from things that are not such. And if, pushed by the truth toward what is necessary, you say that the embryo also has a soul, it is consistent and fitting for you to say which soul it is, and of what kind, and how it is to be contemplated or described. If you affirm that it has only the nutritive and growing soul, then clearly, by this argument and on your view, the body that is nourished and grows will be that of a plant and not of a human being. And how a man will be father of a plant I cannot see, though I consider it at length, since the plant does not have its being by nature from a man at all. But if you assign to the embryo only the sensitive soul, the embryo will certainly be shown at conception to have the soul of a horse, or an ox, or some other creature of land or air, and on your view the man will not be by nature the father of a human being as regards its first constitution, but of some plant, as I said, or of one of the animals on the earth. What could be more absurd or more senseless than this? For to affirm that the proper definitions of existence do not coexist, without omission, with the first constitution of beings, according to the natural difference of each, is to confuse all things with one another and to insist that none of the beings is properly what it is and is said to be. And, what is the greater evil, it will certainly be shown to carry a most manifest and very great slander

against the divine wisdom and power. For if all beings whatsoever, before their genesis, have their perfection in their own logos according to God's foreknowledge, then clearly, when they are brought into genesis according to their own logos, they will at the same moment as they come to be have their perfection, without omission, in actuality itself. But if beings have perfection in foreknowledge, but imperfection in their production and genesis into being, then either they will not be the very things that were foreknown, but others in place of others, or this would be a plain and manifest weakness of the Creator, who would have been unable to present what he foreknew, in accordance with his foreknowledge, all at once and in its fullness in actuality at its genesis, as it naturally is in its essence. But if, wary of these refutations, you take refuge in that last resort, claiming that it is not right for what is in the image of God and divine (for so you call the intellectual soul) to coexist with flux and filthy pleasure, and you think it more seemly to say that it is introduced after the forty days from conception, you will plainly be seen to be accusing the Creator of nature, and will be shown to incur, fittingly, the fearful danger of the blasphemy that comes to light from this. For if marriage is evil, clearly so is the natural law of generation; and if such a natural law of generation is evil, then clearly he who made nature and gave it the law of generation would justly be accused on our part. Why then do we turn away from the followers of Mani and the heretics before him, who for this reason, and in a sense for this reason alone, posited two principles and denied the God who is over all, when we find you too saying the same thing, even if not by the same means? But if for this reason, out of a scruple born of shame, you decline to say that the rational and intellectual soul coexists with the body at conception, then you will not dare to say that the one born has the rational and intellectual soul either after forty days, or after the nine months of pregnancy, or even after birth, before the forty days of purification. For until then the newborn has no access to the temple of God, being defined by the law as unclean. So it remains, by reasonable argument, to suppose that until the days of purification are completed the newborn does not have the rational and intellectual soul, but the soul of some plant, as I said a little earlier, or of one of the irrational animals found among beings. But if your pretext for such an argument is that the great Moses wrote that one who strikes a pregnant woman is not required to pay the penalty if, through the blow, it happens that she miscarries the embryo before forty days, you should know that the wise Moses was not indicating the entry of the rational soul into the body at that time, but showing that the complete formation of what was conceived is accomplished then;

and so far he wrote this according to the plain sense. On top of all this, I am afraid to accept such an argument, lest the order of the argument, proceeding in sequence, justly make me liable to fearful charges, forcing me by the logic of the argument to say what it is not lawful to say: that our Lord and God, if indeed he truly deigned to become man like us without sin, became at his conception a man without soul and without mind, and remained so for forty days. Yet our holy Fathers and teachers, or rather the truth that speaks through them and is spoken by them, explicitly proclaim that together with the descent of God the Word at the conception, the Lord himself was timelessly united to flesh through the mediation of a rational soul [?], and did not receive a rational soul added later through the mediation of soulless flesh; and that he did not assume a body wholly without soul, or a soul without mind and without reason, but ineffably united to himself hypostatically the nature, complete and lacking nothing, constituted of rational soul and body together. Therefore I hold above all to the doctrine of coexistence, fittingly rejecting those who go to either extreme, opposed both to one another and to the mean. I have as advocate and unerring teacher of this doctrine the very Maker of nature, through his own mystery of incarnation: he who truly became man and confirmed through himself that the nature has its existence complete at the same moment as its being at genesis; who innovated only the innovation of nature, I mean conception through seed and birth through corruption, which nature drew upon itself after the transgression, when it fell away from the divine and spiritual increase into multitude; but not the logos of nature, according to which it is and naturally comes to be, subsisting, at the same moment as it exists, from rational soul and body.

On how innovation comes about while the things innovated remain unchanged in their nature.

For, generally speaking, every innovation naturally concerns the mode of the thing innovated, not the logos of its nature. That is why the logos, when innovated, corrupts the nature, since the nature no longer keeps unadulterated the logos according to which it exists; whereas the mode, when innovated, while the natural logos is clearly preserved, displays the power of a miracle, showing the nature being acted upon and acting beyond its own ordinance. The logos of human nature is to be soul and body, and that the nature is made up of rational soul and body; the mode is the order in which it naturally acts and is acted upon, which often changes and alters without at all changing the nature along with it.

So it is with every other thing as well, whenever God wills to make something new in his own creation, for the sake of his providence over those he cares for and to display the power that extends to all things and through all things. So indeed, working wonders from of old through the transformations of miracles and signs, he acted by way of innovation. He transferred the blessed Enoch and Elijah to another form of life than that in flesh subject to corruption, not by alteration of nature but by a change in its conduct and governance. He multiplied water in quantity to flood the wicked people on earth. He showed Noah, the first sailor, living unharmed in the ark among wild beasts. He honoured Abraham and Sarah, his great servants, with a child beyond their age and beyond the limit and time customarily set by nature for having children. He made fire move downward to flood the ungodly, without its natural logos being in any way diminished thereby. He kindled the bush with fire without consuming it, to summon his servant. He changed water in Egypt into the quality of blood without denying its nature at all, for it remained water by nature even after it was reddened. He accomplished the other miracles and signs there, to give the faithful hope of freedom from the evils that held them, and to give the unbelievers a perception of the power that punishes, so that they might cast off the hardness toward the divine that held them. He cut the sea with a rod and broke the continuity of the water, though it did not depart from its own nature, to give passage to those who were pursued for his sake and to check those who without cause were pursuing the noble and free. He sweetened water with wood, and rained down from heaven unploughed bread, strange and unknown, and suddenly cast up from the sea a multitude of birds for food, without their natural succession from one another, to comfort those suffering in the wilderness. He made the rock a mother of water, to confirm the faith of those who were deserting in the contests. He cut off a river so that a God-fearing people might cross dry-shod. Wondrously he held back the unhindered course of the sun and the moon, making the ever-moving nature of the heavens stand still, for the destruction of an ungodly dominion. [?]

he innovated: by assuming flesh through the mediation of an intellectual soul, [?] conceived without seed and truly born without corruption as perfect man, having had an intellectual soul together with the body from the very moment of his ineffable conception.

That every nature always has its perfection in its own logos.

For, generally speaking, every nature, intelligible and sensible, that is, simple and composite, never in any way receives the beginning of its genesis into being in part, nor indeed can it subsist from a half share. If it is a composite nature, it subsists whole and complete all at once together with its own complete parts, having no temporal interval of any kind either in relation to itself or between the parts of which it consists. And if it is a simple, that is an intelligible, nature, it likewise naturally subsists complete, all at once, together with its own logoi, complete and without omission, no time at all separating it from its own logoi. For there never was, nor is, nor will be any nature at all among beings existing according to its own logos as what it is not now; nor is it now, or will it be later, what it was not before. For in the case of things whose logoi had their perfection with God at the same moment as their being, their production and coming into substance according to their own logoi is wholly incapable of any addition or deficiency with respect to being what they are. But I think that what has now been said in this digression is sufficient against these people as well, so that one may not be easily swept into absurd opinions by those who place their trust in the technical persuasiveness of elegant arguments.

Why the teacher joined birth from baptism to the incarnation.

With what in view, and for what reason, the teacher joined to the incarnation the birth from baptism (for this still remains to be examined in the passage before us), I will say briefly, as I was taught, and as well as I can. Those who treat the divine oracles mystically, and, as is fitting, honour them with loftier contemplations, say that man was made in the beginning in the image of God, so that he might certainly be born by his own choice in the Spirit and receive in addition the likeness that would come to him through keeping the divine commandment; so that the same man might be a creature of God by nature, but a son of God and god through the Spirit by grace. For it was not possible for man, once created, to be shown otherwise to be a son of God and god through deification by grace, without first being born by his own choice in the Spirit, because of the self-moving and unmastered power naturally present in him.

This deifying, divine and immaterial birth the first man abandoned, by preferring to the intelligible goods, as yet unseen, what is pleasant and evident to the senses; and he was fittingly condemned to have the birth from bodies, which is involuntary, material and perishable. For God justly judged that he who willingly chose the worse instead of the better should exchange the free, impassible, self-chosen and pure birth for one that is passionate, servile and constrained, like that of the irrational and senseless beasts on the earth, and should exchange the divine and inalienable honour of being with God for a dishonourable consortium with the senseless beasts. Wishing to free man from this and lead him back to his divine inheritance, the Word who created human nature truly becomes man from men, and is born bodily without sin for man's sake, and is baptized, willingly undergoing on our behalf the spiritual birth unto adoption, he who is God by essence and Son of God by nature, in order to abolish the birth from bodies. Since, then, for our sake he who made us, the Son and Word, who alone shares one Godhead and one glory with the Father and the Spirit, truly becomes man like us and from us, and is born bodily without sin, and, though God by nature, consents to undergo on our behalf the birth from baptism unto spiritual adoption, for this reason, I think, the teacher joined the birth from baptism to the incarnation, as having been devised for the abolition and dissolution of the birth from bodies. For what Adam willingly abandoned (I mean the birth from the Spirit unto deification), and so was condemned to be born bodily unto corruption, this he who alone is free and sinless mystically restored, the birth in the Spirit. Good and loving toward mankind, he became man by his own will in our fall, willingly shared our condemnation, and consented to be born with the birth from bodies, in which lay the power of our condemnation; and, loosing in himself on our behalf the bonds of bodily birth, he has given us, through birth in the Spirit by our own will, the power to become children of God instead of flesh and blood, to those who believe in his name. So incarnation and bodily birth came first to the Lord on account of my condemnation, and in this way the birth in the Spirit through baptism, which had been abandoned, followed, for my salvation by grace and my recall, or, to put it more clearly, my refashioning. For God was joining together in me the logos of my being and the logos of my well-being, and making one again the cut and division I had made between them, and through them driving me on toward the logos of ever-being, according to which man no longer carries and is carried along, since the economy of visible things will have brought its being carried along to an end [?] through the great and common resurrection, which begets

man into immortality, in an unchangeable existence: man, for whose sake the nature of visible things received its being through genesis, and with whom it will receive by grace freedom from corruption in its essence. But, if you agree, let us briefly recall the force of what has been said and sum it up. We have the bodily birth of our Saviour conceptually distinguished into the original logos of nature and the one that now exists in us, in which nature ended up; and again into the natural logos of genesis and the mode of birth; and further into the different modes of the essential genesis of soul and body; and in addition into the conception without seed and the birth without corruption. It is up to you, then, as just judges, to approve the better of the approaches set out.

Of the same, from the same oration, on: 'Why do you seek remedies that will do no good? Why wait for the critical sweat, when perhaps the sweat of departure is at hand?'

The teacher set down this saying, as the blessed elder used to say, against those who defer baptism, who put off baptism for love of pleasure in the hope that they will live. And he says: 'Why must you learn of your departure' (that is, from life) 'from someone else, instead of considering it as already present? Why do you seek remedies that will do no good? Why wait for the critical sweat, when perhaps the sweat of departure is at hand?' For the sons of physicians say that four days are critical in fevers: the fourth, the seventh, the ninth and the eleventh, and perhaps also the thirteenth. On these days, if they find the patient's body moist with sweat, as they put it, they take it as a sign that the one lying ill will live. So that the sick man may not wait for this sweat and ill-advisedly defer baptism, thinking he has a span of years ahead of him, the teacher very wisely advises the sufferer not to trust in this sweat and lean on it in vain, since instead of it the sweat of departure may come, which proclaims the end of the present life. Otherwise, as I said, the sick man, deceived on account of this sweat, may unawares be estranged from the manifest, divine and everlasting life, and be found clinging to this human life, perishable and sure to be dissolved, which by nature cannot be held fast, is always flowing away through corruption and alteration, and escapes the hands of those who think they hold it faster than an insubstantial dream escapes the dreamer.

From the same oration, on: 'For Christ does not often love being stolen, even though he is exceedingly loving toward mankind.'

On reaching this point in the passage, some ask: why on earth, if God is exceedingly loving toward mankind and an unfailing spring of love for mankind, so that it is not diminished in the least by those who draw from it, does he not love being stolen? For in this way he would display his love for mankind all the more,

…not diminished by giving room to those who wish to steal, especially a saving theft, and as often as they might wish. To them we say, by the grace of God the Word, that this very thing is full of love for humanity, or rather is love for humanity itself. And toward those who wish to steal something of it, it is a very clear proof of good providence not to allow those who wish it to steal it many times. Otherwise, with salvation lying ready to be appropriated, the loss of the gift would probably become very easy, since it could easily be taken again. Then those who obtain the gift would turn out to be ignorant of the immovable and firm habit in the good. Because the good was so easy to acquire, they would have a disposition prone to fall into evil, and the good would be despised for its cheapness.

From the same Father's Oration on Pascha, on the words: "Naked in his simplicity and artless life, and without any covering or screen. For such it was fitting that he should be who was from the beginning." (41)

What this great teacher secretly reveals through these words is known, I say, only to those who have received a gift of wisdom and knowledge equal to his. They have put away from their spiritual eyes all the rheum that comes from the passions and from every attachment to matter, and so have been able to receive the ray of the [?] knowledge present in all things. By this knowledge they have drawn the mind away from the many, as far as is attainable, to the simple and uniform Word, and have grasped all knowledge of beings in a simple, scientific understanding. But on us the [?] of ignorance still lies, hindering our understanding of the truth, because the mind is turned only toward shifting things. Yet a blind man, [sifting] a heap of material rubbish with both hands, often finds something precious. In the same way we too, for all our weakness, will try to say something about the question before us. And indeed we will say nothing at all except what God puts into our hands, as it is written, so as to nourish you, good fathers, as far as we can. I mean that, by the groping reasoning of our intellectual power, we will offer a simple and unelaborate contemplation, proportionate to us and calling down a fatherly blessing. We do not want to roam the field of sensible things in a sensible manner and without skill, as Esau did, and through slowness be deprived of the ready blessing of the father who is being fed. Nor do we want, through pride, to seek something beyond our power and be wounded by those who still dwell on the mountain of contemplation, as happened to Israel. Of them the law says that some forced their way up the mountain, and the Amorite who dwelt on that mountain came out and wounded them. I suspect, then, that the difference

[Notes: the Gudianus manuscript reads "love for humanity itself"; the Gudianus manuscript reads "to steal something."]

between the temperament of the human body in our forefather Adam before the transgression and the temperament now seen and prevailing in us is what the teacher wishes to show when he says these things. Then man was clearly not pulled apart in the temperament of his body by qualities that oppose and destroy one another. He remained the same, without flux and efflux, and he was free from the continual alteration in either direction that follows whichever quality prevails. For he did not lack immortality by grace, and he did not have the corruption that now scourges him with its goads. Instead he plainly had a different bodily temperament, fitting for him and held together by simple qualities that were not at war. In this sense the first man was naked: not as fleshless and bodiless, but as lacking the denser temperament that makes flesh mortal and resistant. According to this great teacher, he lived artlessly, without dissipating the natural good health given to him [?] in his very being. He had no need of covering, both because the impassibility within him meant he did not suspect shame, and because he was not subject to frost and heat. It was chiefly on account of these that people devised the covering of houses and garments.

Another contemplation of the same passage. Or perhaps the teacher shows what man had then by taking away what man has now. For man is now moved in one of three ways. He is moved toward irrational fantasies of the passions, out of deceit, through love of pleasure. Or he is moved toward the principles of the arts, out of circumstance, through need. Or he is moved toward natural principles, from the law of nature, through learning. At the beginning none of these [?] necessarily [moved] man, since he was above them all. For such it was fitting that he should be who was from the beginning. He was not distracted at all by anything beneath him, or around him, or [?] him. For his perfection he needed only one thing: unrestrained motion with his whole [?] power toward the One above him, I mean God. Being impassible by grace, he did not admit the deceit of the passions' fantasy through pleasure. Needing nothing, he was free of the circumstantial [concern] with the arts that need brings. Being wise, he stood above the contemplation of nature because of his knowledge. So the first man had nothing set between God and himself as a barrier to knowledge. Nothing hindered the kinship with God that was to come about through love, freely chosen, by his motion toward God. For this reason the teacher called him "naked in his simplicity," as being above all inquiry according to nature. He called him "in artless life," as being pure of every way of life that needs the arts. He called him "without any covering or screen," as being free from the passionate entanglement of the senses with sensible things. Later he was justly subjected to these things, choosing [?] lack instead of [?]

and freely choosing to become empty of all things instead of being full. He came to be below the things above which he had been created by nature.

Another contemplation of the same passage. Or perhaps he was "naked," as the teacher says, of the varied contemplation and knowledge concerning nature. He was "in artless life" because he was outside the many methods concerning practice and virtue, since he possessed the undefiled principles of the virtues as a settled habit. He was "without any covering or screen" because he did not primarily need a mind that depends on the senses perceiving phenomena in order to understand divine things. He had only the simple screen [?] of the uniform, simple and all-embracing virtue and knowledge of what comes after God. This needed only motion in act in order to be freely manifested. Certainly, then, all who wish to raise themselves by philosophical reason from the fall of the forefather begin first with the complete removal of the passions. Then they lay aside their preoccupation with the principles of the arts. Finally they rise above natural contemplation and gaze into immaterial knowledge. This knowledge has no form at all impressed by sense, and no concept that the utterance of speech can contain. In this way, as God made the first man in the beginning, they become naked in the simplicity of knowledge, in an undistracted life, and in the mortification of the law of the flesh. Those more lofty could also contemplate the difficulty before us in another way. But let that be passed over [?] for the reason I gave at the start of this discourse.

From the same Oration, on the words: "A year old, as the sun of righteousness, either setting out from there, or circumscribed by what is seen." (42)

Our Saviour has many names, and for each one there is a manifold way of anagogical contemplation according to its meaning [?]. This is because the thing taken as an example to name the Lord can admit many applications of contemplation within natural contemplation. That is indeed the case with the difficulty now before us. Since the discourse cannot [?], for brevity's sake, set out the many ways of contemplating the sun, let us contemplate it according to the conception by which the teacher contemplated it. As far as we can, we will unfold what he said in condensed form. According to our holy and wise teachers, then, a year is the return of the sun from one point back to the same point, and it comprises the fivefold property of time. For time into day

and week and month and season and year is both divided and gathered together. The year likewise is divided into hour and day and week and month and season, while the motion within it remains continuous and without interval. The divisions observed in this motion as it changes have numbered the continuous and uninterrupted motion of time. If, then, this is how a year comes about among us through the course of the sun, the acceptable year of the Lord, as it is written, is surely, by way of allegory, the whole extent of the ages. It begins from the moment when God was pleased to give being to beings and existence to things that were not. By his providence, like an intelligible sun of the power that holds the universe together in permanence, he condescends to send forth his ray, [working] in varied ways to bring to fruition the goods proper to beings that he has sown. This continues until the completion of all the ages. Then he will gather the fruits of his own sowing, unmixed with tares and clean of all chaff and refuse, and the whole principle of motion of moving things will be completed, when the worthy receive the promised final blessedness of [?].

The Lord, then, is called "sun of righteousness" for several reasons. He is the maker and consummator of the ages, and the beginning and end of all things. He is the creator of the wise fivefold good order that providence gives to the things it cares for. He fills all things with eternal light by the unfailing outpourings of his goodness. And he makes those who widen their intelligible pores to receive his blessed ray ripe and fit to be eaten by God the Father. The same Lord is also the acceptable year of the Lord, since he is filled out through all who are saved, according to the fivefold motion that comes intelligibly from him as the Sun of righteousness. This will surely be understood by anyone who gathers the spiritual knowledge of intelligible things through exact and rational natural contemplation of phenomena. The teacher says "setting out from there, or circumscribed by what is seen." Either he means that the Lord sets out from the Father by generation, as light from light and true God from God who is true by essence. Or he means that the same Lord, as man, is circumscribed by the visible form of a nature like ours, just as the sun setting out from heaven is circumscribed by its visible, disk-shaped body.

From the same Oration, on the words: "It is no wonder if the lamb is sought especially for each house." (43)

Someone might say, and reasonably, I think: If Christ, who is mystically [foreshadowed] through the law and the prophets and the greatness of creation, is one,

[?], how does the law, through its types of Christ, [prescribe] many [lambs] to be [?] by households of families? To such a person we say this. Suppose we receive the Word himself, [?] the eyes of the soul [?], and [direct] them to the reception and contemplation of his mysteries and to the [?] of all disobedience and [?] the intention of holy Scripture. And suppose we join to the present passage a similar one from the holy Apostle: "I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified." [Then we will find that] each of those who have believed in Christ crucifies Christ together with himself, according to his own power and the habit and quality of virtue that underlies it in him. That is, he is spiritually crucified together with Christ. For each person makes the crucifixion fit himself according to his own mode of virtue. One is crucified only to sin in act, and mortifies it by the fear of God. Another is crucified also to the passions themselves, [?] the powers of the soul. Another is crucified also to the very fantasies of the [?], not leaving the senses loose to receive any of the things [?]. Another is crucified also to [?] thoughts and reasonings. Another is crucified to the deceit of sense. Another [?] the relation of the senses [?] through their natural affinity. Another extinguishes even the whole sensory [?] by the cross, so as to have nothing [?] at work. Another is crucified even to the activity of the mind entirely. To say something greater: one is crucified to practical philosophy through [?] and passes to natural contemplation in the Spirit, as if from some [?] of Christ to his own soul. Another, also dead to natural contemplation through the [?] of the contemplation of beings according to the mind, is transferred to the uniform and simple [?] of theological knowledge, as if from some [?] of Christ to his own mind. Another passes also from this into the [?] abstractive, indefinite [?] through complete negation, as if from some [?] of Christ

[?] the measure of the [?] in each, and the [?] grace of the Spirit. In some he is found in one way, in others in another, whole in the whole, and becoming all things to all.

From the same Oration, on the words: "Whatever of the Word is too solid and nourishing [?] of the hidden [things] of the mind [?] will be given over [?]." (44)

God, who made every nature with wisdom, placed knowledge of himself hidden [?] in the powers of rational beings first and foremost. As a bountiful Master, he has also given to us wretched [?] men a natural [desire] and love for him. Along with these he has naturally woven in the power of reason, by which we [discern] the ways of [?] and strive not to fail to attain [?]. Moved by this [desire], then, we are urged to seek [?] concerning the truth itself and the wisdom and governance that appear in good order in [creatures]. Through these we long to attain that for whose sake we received the [desire]. Knowing this mystically, the [saints] and [?] lovers of truth established for themselves one school and occupation: the philosophy concerning this,

[?], so that through pious contemplations they might in some way [foreshadow] the truth to come and fulfil their [?]. As people well trained here, they would have the soul more ready to [reach] the truth to come without toil after this life, already [nourished] by the more divine conceptions. Clearly it is the Word of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ who leads them to the truth itself, simple and clear and free of all difficulty, [?] and all enigmatic obscurity [?] to them. In practical virtue, pain and sorrow and sighing [have fled] from them because of perfect impassibility. In the same way, in contemplative knowledge, all obscurity and difficulty [have fled] because of wisdom, and [?] has been added to them. They receive here the [?] of it, and then the naked truth. For "to everyone who has," it says (that is, who has the longing for the things to come), "it will be given," and the enjoyment of eternal goods will be added [?]. For our God, being [rich], never ceases to distribute the divine gifts of knowledge to those who love him. In this age we cannot even name these gifts, because of their height and greatness. The great Apostle surely speaks the truth when he says of the final blessedness that it is above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. He is hinting at the highest summit of goods, which will be shown after all the distribution and

[?] of all the gifts. This summit can be neither spoken nor known by any [word]. That is true both of the goods attainable by us in this age and of those that will be shown in the age to come, which we may perhaps be able to name and know. For Jesus, the Word of God, who has passed through the heavens and come to be above all the heavens, always carries those who follow him through practice and contemplation from lesser things to better ones. From these he moves them again to things higher still. In short, time would fail me to tell of the divine ascents and revelations of the saints as they are transformed from glory to glory, until each receives the deification that fits his own rank.

We, then, have the natural longing for God mentioned before. This great teacher [?] exhorts and calls all of us through his teaching to the spiritual eating of the Lamb slain for us. He advises us to keep the harmony of its members, that is, of the Lamb's members, distinct and profitable, unbroken and unconfused. Otherwise we may be condemned for tearing apart and rending the well-ordered harmony of the divine body by eating the flesh of the Lamb and Word in one of two ways. We may eat it rashly, beyond our power, or irreverently, beneath our power. [Rather,] let each, according to his own power and rank and the grace of the Spirit that falls to him, partake of the [?] conception of each member of the divine Word.

For example, he will partake of the head who has acquired faith that holds the principles of theology from indemonstrable first principles, entirely free [?]. From this head the whole body of virtues and knowledge, joined together, grows with spiritual growth. He will partake of the ears who receives the divine words spiritually and with understanding, and who through works becomes obedient and submissive to God because of them, even unto death. He will partake of the eyes who considers creation spiritually and gathers all the principles of sense and mind without stumbling into one fulfilment of God's glory. He will partake of the breast who has filled his heart with theological contemplations, like the great evangelist John. Like an ever-flowing spring, he piously pours out to learners the principle and mode that embrace the providence over the universe. He partakes fittingly of the hands, in turn, who performs none of the works of the commandments slackly or carelessly. Instead, the whole practical activity of his soul is ready and vigorous to fulfil the divine laws. He will partake of the belly who keeps the fertility of the soul ever unrelaxed [?] and is multiplied by spiritual contemplations. He has acquired an unrestrained and most [?] love, the passionless desire for union with the divine. He will fittingly partake of the inward parts who searches the depths of God by the more hidden inquiry and knowledge of the mind and is initiated into ineffable mysteries. The discourse will dare to say

something greater. Let him partake prudently of the lower parts of the Word who stands rationally against matter. He keeps his flesh wholly undefiled together with his soul, and through the virtues he fully forms in it, leaving nothing out, the Word who became flesh. He will partake of the thighs who has the Word laid upon the passible part of the soul and entirely cuts off its motion toward matter. He will partake of the knees who bends down with providential compassion toward those who lie fallen and are weak in faith, imitating the Word's condescension toward us. Let him also partake of the shins and feet who has the foundations of his soul unshaken and immovable in faith, virtue and knowledge. He presses on toward the goal, for the prize of the upward call, and leaps over the mountains of ignorance and the hills of wickedness, bounding along with the Word.

But who could count all the conceptions of our Saviour God for our sake, by which he has made himself fit to be eaten and partaken by each in due proportion? For besides all these the Lord also has locks of hair, nostrils, lips, a neck, shoulders and fingers, and whatever else of our bodily makeup is said of him figuratively. Those who appropriate the spiritual meaning that each member signifies partake of these fittingly and profitably. In this way, according to this holy and great teacher, the Lamb of God is eaten and given for spiritual digestion. By the Spirit he transforms into himself those who partake of him. He leads and transfers each of them into the place of the member they have spiritually eaten, according to its position in the harmony of the body. So the Word who is in all things, who alone is beyond nature and reason, out of his love for humanity becomes the substance of things.

From the same Oration, on the words: "Mortifying the members that are on the earth, and imitating the girdle of John, the hermit and forerunner and great herald of the truth." (45)

He imitates John's girdle who, by the power of reason, binds tight the fertility of the soul in practice through knowledge, and keeps it from pouring out toward matter. A hermit is he who has acquired a state pure of passions. A forerunner is he who, through genuine repentance, announces beforehand the righteousness that follows it, and through visible virtue announces the knowledge that is to come [?]. A great herald of the truth is he who confirms by his own life the word of teaching that he speaks.

From the same oration, on the words: “And if you are one of those sent to preach the Gospel, be light and unencumbered. Besides going without bronze, without a staff and with a single tunic, you must also go barefoot, so that the feet of those who bring good news of peace may appear beautiful” (46). The Gospel is the higher teaching about the kingdom of God, and the kingdom of God is the state that is pure of all matter and of all the imaginings connected with it. So the disciple sent to preach the Gospel is fittingly one whose ways show that he is entirely estranged from this world. By going without bronze or staff and with a single tunic, he has stripped himself of love of money, of anger, and of confidence in any [?] of his own. He pursues a moral philosophy that is unaffected, unfeigned, single in character and free of all duplicity, like a single tunic. He has no trace at all of deadness on the footprint of his soul, as if it were a sandal. [?] He is a messenger of the great peace and a herald of a state that no longer fears the war of the passions and does not shrink from the death of the body. So those who look at him with understanding can see, in the consistency of his virtuous life [?], an image of the most fitting way of life and the steadfastness of the angels around God.

Another contemplation on the same. Or perhaps, to put it simply, it is in imitation of John's belt, and again because the Passover can be eaten in the manner of the Gospel, that the Father hinted, as a teacher, at the differences among those who partake and at the different modes of the Passover itself. For the word of Holy [?] Scripture hands down three Passovers: one celebrated in Egypt, another in the desert, and the third in the land of promise. Allegorized according to one of the ways it can be understood, Egypt signifies this world. In the same way, according to one of the ways it can be contemplated, the desert allegorically points to the state of souls after death. And the land of promise prefigures the age to come. For there are three places and states in which we human beings come to be. There is this world, into which we are born when we receive being. There is the place after death, to which we go when we depart from here. And there is the age to come, in which we are joined together with our souls and our bodies. So for as long as we are in this world, we keep the Passover in Egypt, being cleansed of the stains of sin. But when we have passed through this life by death, we keep another Passover, as if in the desert, [learning] the principles of beings more clearly, without symbols [?]

and riddles and the variety that comes through the senses, learning them in an intellectual and incorporeal way. And again, in the age to come of the divine promises, we celebrate the Passover by eating directly the highest word of wisdom. Transformed by it, we are deified by grace, and we have no further crossing over to any other Passover at all. Yet even while we are here, the distinctive character of each of these places can be imaged in us according to each person's state. For each person's life bears the stamp of the place where it is. For example, if we pursue practical philosophy courageously, we celebrate the Passover well in Egypt: we are among the Egyptians but are not Egyptians, just as we live in the flesh but do not wage war according to the flesh. If we piously practise natural contemplation in the Spirit, we make the powers of the soul weapons mighty for God. They serve to tear down strongholds and every height raised up against the knowledge of God, and to contemplate the spiritual principles in beings. Then, as if stripped of the body and freed from the deceptive imaginings of the senses, we make our journey toward the divine promises with knowledge, and we are in the desert. By this I mean the state that is pure of passions and of all material imagining. If we are formed by the theological mystagogy through ineffable movements of the mind, we are no longer ignorant, as far as is possible for human beings, of the breadth and length and depth and of the surpassing greatness of God's wisdom toward us, and we are in the land of promise. I think, then, that the teacher hints at practical, natural and theological philosophy through this division into three persons. Through them each person, in proportion to the power present in him, eats the intelligible

From the same oration, on the words: “If you are a Rachel or a Leah, a patriarchal and great soul, also steal the idols, whatever of your father's you find, not to keep them but to destroy them; and if you are a wise Israelite, carry them over to the land of promise” (47). Rachel, they say, is interpreted as “ewe” or “[?]”, and Leah as “held fast” or “toil”. So Rachel, as the force of her name suggests, is shepherded and shepherds, is led and leads. Rachel, then, is every contemplative soul. Like a ewe, it is shepherded and led by the law of God. In keeping with the law of God, it also shepherds and leads its own movements and thoughts by the precepts of practice. For a time it subjects the passions of the flesh to the fruitfulness of virtue, and then, after its entry into knowledge, it destroys them completely. Leah is every practical soul that endures toil for virtue's sake. This is the bride whom everyone pursuing divine philosophy takes into his house first of all

in marriage. The wise Israelite is a contemplative mind that carries the thoughts of this age over to the country of knowledge, like that great Jacob who brought all Laban's goods to the land of the fathers. In the historical account, that wondrous Jacob peeled the rods and set them in the watering troughs, and so made the sheep that drank there conceive in front of them. In the same way, every mind that is most wise in the Spirit strips the more divine principles of beings of the matter that surrounds them and sets them under the modes of knowledge proper to contemplation. In this way it teaches all its learners, and the movements of its own soul as well, to be formed into the state of incorporeal beings. Leah, then, is the patriarch of those who achieve [virtue] through practical toil. Rachel is the patriarch of those who pursue virtue rationally through natural contemplation, since she is led obediently by the law of God and leads gently according to it. And of those who pursue the height of spiritual contemplation

Simon, they say, is interpreted as “obedience”, and Cyrenian as “readiness”. So everyone who is ready to obey the Gospel and eagerly undergoes hardship for virtue's sake in practical philosophy, by putting to death his members on earth, has become Simon of Cyrene. He pursues virtue willingly, carries the cross on his shoulders and follows Christ, and so shows a manner of godly life entirely withdrawn from the earth.

From the same oration, on the words: “If you are crucified as a thief, acknowledge God as the grateful one” (49). The grateful thief, crucified with Christ, is every person who suffers ill for his sins [?] ... to share with the one who is [?], and through gratitude to count the deadness brought on by circumstances as his own voluntary virtue, when the wise veils of the providence of the Word, having reached the end of his

[?] to him, as he suffers because of sin. The deadening of the body's members brought on by circumstances is changed, through grateful thanksgiving, into freely chosen virtue. Through it he is released from the many debts of sin and rightly enters with the Word into the country of knowledge, by which I mean paradise. Once there, he will know the cause of the condemnation and suffering in which we are now confined. The ungrateful thief is the one who suffers ill because of sin, as one answerable for it. Because of his quarrelsome disposition he does not acknowledge the Word of righteousness, who suffers with him blamelessly out of love for humankind. Instead he blasphemously rejects the word of judgment justly appointed for him by providence. Since he did not acknowledge the Word who was willingly condemned with him in dishonour, and did not ask for grace for his offences, he is sent away a stranger to the kingdom, without having received from the Word any promise that he will ever attain it.

Another contemplation on the same. And again, the grateful thief is one who, even when he has come to the very end of his present life, comes to an awareness of his offences. With understanding he acknowledges the word of divine judgment justly appointed for him and being carried out on him here, and he asks sincerely, from the depth of his soul, for pardon for his sins. The ungrateful thief is one who, having come to the very end of his present life, clings to life and finds fault with the law and limit that separates soul from body, as though it were not rightly given, although God wisely set it by a just decree.

Another contemplation on the same. And again, each of us is twofold, made up of soul and body. So the thief is the one who, in each of the two parts that make him up, is mystically crucified with the Word for virtue's sake, according to the law of the nature of each [?]. The law of the flesh he has like an ungrateful thief that falls foul [?] of the word of virtue. The law of the spirit he has like a grateful thief, which welcomes the Saviour Word through the modes of practical life, toilsome though they may be. With it he joyfully enters the place of feasting, which is filled with all knowledge, wholly freed from the mindset of the flesh.

Another contemplation on the same. And again, the grateful thief is the one who has been counted worthy to be crucified with Christ through the complete and total deadening of the passions, and who is crucified with him on the right. That is, he goes through every virtue with reason and knowledge and keeps his life blameless toward all

people, so that he gives no [?] at all of the word [?] any movement through harshness. The ungrateful thief is the one who, for glory or for richer gains, deceitfully puts on a show of the life according to [God] by [?] ways. Toward outsiders he pursues one thing only, flattering speech [?], in place of all virtue and knowledge, while toward those close to him he is altogether crooked in disposition and hard to deal with. Such a person blasphemes the way of God and must certainly be silenced with understanding. For perhaps, at the admonition of the one who rebukes him, he will stop [blaspheming] the Word through his own conduct, just as on the cross [?] the one who had boldly uttered blasphemy did. For not answering back to the one who rebuked him has silence as a sign that he accepted what was said. So whichever of the contemplations described above is the way in which we are crucified with Christ, let us strive, while we are here, to win the favour of the one crucified with us. Let us also strive to receive, in a conscience cleansed of what wounds it, the unfailing promise of rest. The “today” may point to the day of this age (“You will be with me,” he says, “in paradise”), or [?] to the day of the age to come. In that day one must not expect any forgiveness of sins, but only the recompense that fits each person according to the merit of what has been done [?]

“If you are a Joseph of Arimathea, ask for the body from the one who crucified him” (50). The body of Christ is the soul, or its powers, or the senses, or each person's body, or the members of the body, or the commandments, or the virtues, or the principles of created things. Or, to put it more truly, taken individually and together, all these, and each of them, are the body of Christ. The devil crucifies this body, that is, all these things, in the person who accepts their crucifixion, by not allowing them to act according to nature. Joseph, in the Hebrew language, is interpreted as “addition”, and Arimathea as “Take that away”. How so? The person who has additions of faith, who has grown in the ways of virtue and has stripped away from himself all the deceit of material things, this person is Jo-

[seph] [?] toward the fulfilment of the virtues. Moreover, he has nailed the soul and its powers to the commandments of God and shown them to be [?] the natural activities of the soul. Through an unchangeable and [?] state of [?], he is roused to understand also the more divine principles hidden in the [?]. And, as in a linen cloth, he wraps the first Word, from whom and through whom and to whom are all things, in the spiritual principles concerning this age. The one who has kept this good order in this way is Joseph, [able] to bury the mystical body of Christ mystically.

Another contemplation on the same. And again, to put it briefly: the one who wondrously conveys the [?] of the cross to his hearers through practice and contemplation has become another Joseph through the addition of the good things of contemplation [?] into spiritual knowledge [?]. He has also become an Arimathean, through his genuine kinship with the virtues in practice, by cutting away from himself all [?] of material things.
