Another contemplation on the same. Those who blasphemously teach [?] about the incarnation of God crucify Christ, as it were [?]. In turn, the one who [?] boldly [teaches] the [?] about God's incarnation to all, piously, buries him.

From the same oration, on the words: “If you are a Nicodemus, the God-fearer by night, bury him with ointments” (51). [?] The God-fearer by night, who buries the body of Christ with ointments, is the one who in his thinking [?] into the knowledge of Christ, but [shrinks from] zeal in practising the commandments, as though cowardly [?] ... to think [rightly] about Christ and not to utter blasphemous words.

From the same oration, on the words: “If you are a Mary, or the other Mary, or Salome, or Joanna, weep at dawn. Look first at the stone taken away, and perhaps also the angels, and Jesus himself” (52). [?] purified [?] of terror. For this age is a week, which is completed through the cycle of time into seven [?]

From this age the Word frees his devotees and sets them entirely above the things that are subject to time. The other Mary is every contemplative soul that has acquired kinship with the Word by grace, through true knowledge. Salome, which is interpreted as “peace” [?], is every [?] soul that, by casting off the passions, [?] and through an abundance of practical virtues has subjected the mindset of the flesh to the law of the spirit. Through being filled with spiritual thoughts in contemplation, it has also wisely grasped the knowledge of beings as far as is possible. Joanna, which is interpreted as “dove”, the gentle creature without gall and with many offspring, is every soul that through gentleness has laid aside passion and has the Spirit's fruitfulness in knowledge burning within it. These women weep at dawn, that is, they shed tears of knowledge as they seek the Word, the supreme principle of all virtue and knowledge. First they see the stone taken away from the door of the tomb. This is the hardness of obscurity about the Word that lay upon the heart. Then they see the angels, that is, the natural principles of beings in the Spirit, which proclaim the [?] Word in silence.

Another contemplation on the angels. Or the angels are the words of Holy Scripture, which give them a clearer understanding of Christ as God and man, that is, of theology and of the economy. For the account says they saw one angel at the head and one at the feet. At the head is the word of theology, because of Christ's divinity, and at the feet the word of the economy, because of the incarnation. Anyone who says that Christ's head is his divinity and his feet his humanity will not miss the mark.

Another contemplation on the same. Or perhaps the angels are the movements of conscience concerning the word of piety, which arise because evil and ignorance have been cast off completely. They proclaim to these women, in an intellectual way, the resurrection of the Word, who had once been put to death in them through evil. Finally the women see the Word himself appearing to them plainly, without symbols and types, and filling their intellectual [?] with intelligible joy
Peter is every person who has acquired, in the conduct of his life, the firmness of faith in Christ. John is the one who, through great gentleness

and the untainted purity of heart that comes from it, is loved by the Word. For this reason he is entrusted with the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and by reclining on the Word's breast he receives the power of theology from the Word's hidden divinity itself. These two race against each other. The one strives, through virtuous practice, to beat the other's contemplation. The other hurries, through the contemplation of knowledge, to outrun the first one's practice. Yet in their purpose they run together, each one prospering equally in his own proper good.

Another contemplation on the same. Again, Peter and John are each person who has been counted worthy to draw near to God. Such a person has the practical part of the soul as a kind of Peter and the contemplative part as a kind of John. These run together in accordance with reason, without one exceeding or falling short of the other. And again, in their purpose they race against each other, so that neither is outrun by the other in its own highest point [?]

From the same, on the words: “Even if, like Thomas, you are left out when the disciples gather and Christ appears to them, do not disbelieve when you see him. And if you do disbelieve, believe those who tell you. And if not them, be convinced by the marks of the nails” (54). Thomas is interpreted as “twin”, that is, doubt. He doubted in his reasonings, and so he would not believe that the Word's resurrection had taken place without touching the marks of the nails. Thomas, then, is every doubting person who finds it hard to believe that the resurrection of the Word of virtue and knowledge is taking place within him. Only the memories of past sins, impressed dispassionately on the mind, persuade such a person to accept the resurrection of the divine Word within him and to confess him as Lord and God. He is Lord as the lawgiver of perfection in practice, and God as the guide in the complete mystagogy of contemplation. Dispassionate memory of past things is an impression: a discernment, free of pleasure and pain, that arises in the soul about its own deeds or thoughts in practice and in reason. It bears the marks of the wounds but not the holes, because they have closed over through the dispassion that has come about.

Another contemplation on the same. Or again, the nails are the modes of the virtues in practical philosophy, which hold firm the disposition of the soul, nailed with toil to the fear of God

Their place is taken by the dispassionate, simple and [?] principles of knowledge, which loudly proclaim the resurrection of the divine Word that has taken place in the soul in its deification. They bear faithful witness to it by showing [?] the dispassion of the godlike state. Someone who has not experienced this would never believe it even when another described it, just as Thomas, before he had experienced it himself, did not believe the apostles who had experienced this resurrection when they told him.

From the same oration, on the words: “If he goes down into Hades, go down with him. Learn also the mysteries of God there: what is the reason for the twofold descent” (55). The spiritual person knows that the Word of God is present everywhere without being defiled, and follows him through contemplation, gathering with understanding the knowledge of his providence over all things. So when the Word goes down into Hades, he too goes down with him. He clearly does not do so for evil, but in order to search out and learn the mystery of God's descent into Hades, and to be taught the supernatural reason for the things that took place and were accomplished there.

Another contemplation on the same. Or again: every sin is Hades, since it makes the soul it controls gloomy, formless and corrupt. So the one who discourses about the passions goes down with the Word of teaching as it descends into Hades. Through the Word he brings back to life the virtue that each vice had put to death and leads it to resurrection, and with the Word he courageously tears apart the bonds that tie souls to matter.

According to the obvious sense, the reason for the twofold descent, on the first interpretation, is [?] ... to save [?] ... [through] a pure way of life on earth with bodies, and that the Word, having gone down into Hades without bodies, is able to win the souls of those who had died earlier there through faith alone. On the second approach, it is that both the habit of vice and its activity receive from the Word a return to virtue and knowledge.

From the same oration, on the words: “If he ascends into heaven, ascend with him. Be with the angels who escort him or with those who receive him; order the gates to be lifted up.” The one who, through a great abundance of knowledge and a rich share in the Holy Spirit, has worked through the account of providence sufficiently, as far as possible, and has grasped the knowledge that belongs to it, ascends with the Word as he ascends from earth into heaven. With knowledge, [he passes through] the nature of all the things that providence cares for, both visible and invisible, together with the principles that belong to it

…having crossed over, and into the [state] that has no [?] whatsoever, neither seeing [?] nor having motion, toward which he was hastening above all, he is taken up through the cessation of every word and mode. He is led up from the principles of providence in beings, which escort him like angels, to the region of the ineffable principles and mysteries of theology, which receive him. (253 a) And by ascents step by step he makes the intellectual [powers] of the soul higher, for the reception of the most divinely sovereign Word…

Another contemplation on the same. And again, in another way: whoever rises from the modes of virtue of practical philosophy, as from a kind of earth, to certain heavens (that is, the spiritual heavens of knowledge in contemplation) ascends together with the ascending Word, being lifted up with the divine [?] which draws him upward.

Another contemplation on the same. And to speak still more mystically about these things: whoever is able to be led up from the knowledge of the economy, by which the world of the Word's flesh came to be with the Father [?], to the conception of the glory which the Word had with the Father before the world and before [?] his incarnation, has truly ascended into the heavens together with God the Word, who came down to earth for his sake. He has filled up the measure of knowledge that humans can hold in this age, and has become as much God as He became man. For he has been raised up by divine ascents for God's sake as far as God, for man's sake, came down when He emptied Himself without change to the uttermost of our nature.

From the same, from the oration On New Sunday, on the words: "The tabernacle of witness is renewed, and quite thoroughly: the one which God showed, Bezalel completed, and Moses pitched" (57).

The anagogical account of the contemplation of the tabernacle is manifold, so for the present let us also contemplate it as the teacher took it. The tabernacle of witness, then, is the mysterious economy of the incarnation of God the Word. God the Father, being well pleased, showed it. The Holy Spirit, prefigured through the wise Bezalel, cooperated and completed it. And the intelligible Moses, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, wrought it himself, pitching human nature in himself by the hypostatic union.

Another contemplation on the same. Moreover, the tabernacle is also an image of the whole of creation, intelligible and sensible, which God the Father

conceived [?], the Son as Word fashioned, and the Holy Spirit completed. (253 b) And again, the tabernacle is an image of the sensible [creation] [?] alone, of man alone, composed of soul and body, and in turn of the soul alone, considered by itself in thought: clearly, it is contemplated in the way fitting to each.

From the same oration, on the words: "The kingdom of David is renewed, and not once: first when he is anointed, and second when he is proclaimed" (58).

Likewise let us also take the great David, prophet and king, who carries a most venerable anagogical meaning, in the sense in which the teacher himself contemplated it in the present passage. The intelligible David, then, is the true king of Israel, that is, of the one who sees God: Jesus Christ. At his first coming he is anointed in respect of his humanity [?], or, as [is said] elsewhere [?], he anointed the humanity with the divinity and made it what the anointing [divinity] is. At his second and glorious appearing he both is and is proclaimed God and Lord and King of all creation (59).

Some are perplexed by the present passage, saying: "Why ever did the teacher say that the day of resurrection [surpasses] [?] all the feasts on earth, not only the human ones that keep to the ground [?] but even those of Christ himself and celebrated in his honour, and then, as if forgetting his own declaration, rank the day of the Renewal above it, saying: 'Higher than the high, and more wondrous than the wondrous'? This makes the teacher seem to contradict himself" (60).

To this it must be said that the teacher himself, at one point in the same oration, says: "The Word does not want you ever to remain in the same state, but to be ever-moving, well-moving, wholly newly created" (61). We know that whoever is being renewed becomes higher and more divine than himself, made radiant by his advances in virtue. In the same way we must believe that every feast day devised for our sake becomes higher than itself in us and through us, as the mystery it signifies leads its own power in us toward perfection. Fittingly, then, the teacher called the New Sunday "higher than the high", since it is always being lifted up together with us and surpassing itself [?]. For the day of the resurrection (I mean the first Sunday) [?], while the mystery belonging to it, secretly, [?] of all material

…[?] not only [?] entirely pure of all fantasy [?], the life being contemplated [?] by those who thus spiritually [?] … making them sharers in the divine goods whose enjoyment the [day] before it began as first-fruits [?].

Another contemplation on the same. And if what is said seems credible to anyone [?], they say that the first Sunday is a symbol of the resurrection of the will toward virtue, and the second of the state beyond the will: the habit of perfection in knowledge.

Another contemplation on the same. And again, they say that the first Sunday is a symbol of the future natural resurrection and incorruption, and that the second bears [the symbol] [?] of the deification by grace that is to come. If, then, the enjoyment of good things is [better] [?] than the purifying [?] habit, and the habit of perfection according to true knowledge [better] than the will made healthy by virtue, and the transformation in grace toward God by deification [better] than incorruption (of which [states] the first Sunday bears [the symbol] [?], (254 b) while the second is in fact a symbol [of the higher]), then the teacher was right, led [?] by this reason, to call the New Sunday "higher than the high".

From the same oration, on the words: "I hate also the [?]…" Addressing women, and especially those who have taken up the solitary life, the teacher gives a long discourse on the correction of morals. Then, by way of emphasis, he gently advises, I think, that women in the ascetic life must not peer out from their homes through windows at anyone at all, especially at passers-by, lest they receive the stings of death through untimely looking.

From the same, from the oration On Holy Pentecost, on the words: "[?] one day short, which we have taken in addition from the age to come, being both the eighth and the same as the first, or rather one and indestructible. For the sabbath-rest of souls here must come to its end there" (65).

The number seven in holy Scripture, taken merely as a number, naturally holds much mystical contemplation for those who labour over divine things. For it signifies time, and age, and ages, motion and compass and measure, limit and providence, and many other things, when it is rightly contemplated according to the principle of each. And considered only as rest, it likewise holds much knowledge

imparted in it as a mystery. But so as not to make the discourse burdensome by going through each point, let us exercise ourselves on the one that seems higher than the others. Those learned in divine things say that the whole principle of the entire genesis of rational beings is seen to have three modes: being, well-being, and ever-being. Being was granted to beings first, according to essence. Well-being was given them second, according to choice, since they are self-moving. Ever-being was bestowed on them third, by grace. The first contains potency, (255 a) the second activity, and the third rest. Thus the principle of being has by nature only the potency for activity, and without choice it cannot possess that activity in its fullness at all. The principle of well-being has, by disposition, only the activity of the natural potency, and without nature it does not possess the potency whole. The principle of ever-being wholly circumscribes those before it, the potency of the one and the activity of the other. Yet it is not present in beings naturally, as a potency, nor does it follow by necessity from the willing of choice. For how could what has neither beginning nor end be present in things that have a beginning by nature and an end by motion? Rather, it is a limit. It makes nature stable as to its potency and choice as to its activity, without altering either in any way with respect to the principle by which it exists, and it defines all ages and times. And this, I think, is perhaps the mystically blessed Sabbath, the great day of rest from the divine works. According to the scriptural account of the world's creation, it has neither beginning nor end nor genesis. It is the manifestation, after the motion of things bounded by measure, of what lies beyond limit and measurement. It is the infinite identity, after the quantity of things contained and circumscribed, of things that cannot be contained or circumscribed. However, then, the activity of choice uses the potency of nature, whether according to nature or against nature, it will receive as its end either well-being or ill-being, that is, ever-being, in which souls keep sabbath, [receiving] [?] the cessation of all motion. The eighth and first, or rather one and indestructible, day (255 b) is the pure and all-radiant presence of God, which comes after the stillness of moving things. To those who by choice have used the principle of being according to nature, He is fittingly present, wholly in the whole [?], and grants ever-well-being through participation in Himself, since He alone properly is, and ever is, and is well. But to those who by disposition have used the principle of being against nature, He fittingly apportions ever-ill-being instead of well-being. For well-being can no longer be contained by them, since they are disposed contrary to it, and they have no [?] motion after the manifestation of what is sought, by which what is sought is naturally manifested to those who seek it.

Another contemplation on the same. And again, the seventh day and Sabbath is the passing through all the modes of virtue and all the gnostic principles of contemplation. The eighth is the true transformation, by grace, toward the beginning and cause of what has been done in practice and known in contemplation.

Another contemplation on the same. Again, the seventh day and Sabbath is the dispassion that follows upon practical philosophy according to virtue. The eighth and first, as one and indestructible, is the wisdom that comes after gnostic contemplation. And in all sorts of other ways, too, lovers of the vision of divine things can take up the account of such matters and discover many fine and true contemplations.

From the same oration, on the words: "Pour out, double, triple". Taking up the mystery of the seventh, the teacher says: "As also the seventh stretching-out of Elijah the Tishbite, which breathed life into the son of the woman of Zarephath, (256 a) and his pouring of water over the split wood the same number of times." When I asked the blessed elder about this, he said: In this way, perhaps, one can work out what the teacher means as he discusses the number seven. First, according to the so-called arithmeticians. They say that certain numbers are composed of other numbers doubled and tripled, with the unit added last. For instance, 64 is composed from doubled numbers: the unit is doubled through six numbers and the unit is added as well, and so the hebdomad is completed. Thus twice 1 is 2, twice 2 is 4, twice 4 is 8, twice 8 is 16, twice 16 is 32, [twice 32 is 64] [?]. Formed in this way, these seem to be composed of six numbers, but the unit from which the doubling began is taken in last and completes the seven. So here too, keeping the same rule, we shall complete the number seven. For he says: "Pour out, double, and triple." Twice one, then, is 2, three times 2 is six, and the first unit, added to the six, completes the number seven. They also say that, in mystical contemplation, the number 3 has a certain spiritual kinship with the number 7, in this way: the all-venerable and worshipful Trinity is signified by the 3, and the same again by the 7, because the number seven is virgin. For of the [?]

numbers within the decad, this alone neither begets nor is begotten. He shows this clearly in his verses On Virginity, where he goes through it [?] thus: "The first virgin is the pure Trinity."

Another contemplation on the same. Or also thus: if you mystically contemplate, together with the Holy Trinity, its activity (I mean the good [?], which displays the four generic virtues), you will complete the number seven. For when we mystically contemplate its activity together with the holy and all-hymned Trinity, we complete the seven. [?]

From the same oration, on the words: "Jesus himself, perfect purity, knows how to feed five thousand with five barley [?] loaves, and again four thousand with seven; and the leftovers of the abundance were there twelve baskets, here seven hampers. Neither, I think, is without reason or unworthy of the Spirit."

The mind has by now been trained toward a contemplative habit by what has been said at length above, as far as was possible. So, if it seems good, let us not weigh it down with a multitude of words, since it is now able to receive the contemplation of divine things knowledgeably, even in summary. The five barley loaves, then, indicate the ready-to-hand principles of natural contemplation. The five thousand men fed by them signify those who are moved in their study of nature but are not yet entirely cleansed of the habitual disposition of the passible and irrational part of the soul. That is why the beholders of such principles are given to understand that the loaves are of barley, a kind of food common to beasts and humans. The same is shown by their being with women and children, which clearly indicates that they have not been entirely estranged from desires for pleasure and from the imperfect childishness of their thoughts. The desert is this world, in which the Word of God, spiritually breaking the principles of nature for those moved toward the divine through natural contemplation, bestows a whole fullness of good things. This is shown by the baskets of leftovers, twelve in number.

Contemplation on the number 12. The number twelve shows either the principles of time and nature, being completed by the combination of five and seven. For time is hebdomadic, moving in a cycle, (257 a) and having the aptitude to move naturally [?], since [it has] [?] the distance of the extremes from the middle according to this number

[?]. Nature is pentadic, naturally ranked under the number five. This is because the sense perception under which it falls is divided fivefold, and because it has form in addition to matter simply so called, which is divided fourfold. For nature is nothing other, properly speaking [?], than matter with form: enformed matter. Form added to matter produces nature.

Another contemplation on the same. Or [it shows] the conceptions of beings, both generated and aeonic, as moved and circumscribed and admitting the principle of being somewhere, of some kind, and in some manner. For everything movable is also generated, and for this reason it is also under time [?], even if it is not measured by motion. For everything generated has a beginning of being, since it began to be, and an interval from which it began to be. And if every generated thing both is and is moved, it is wholly under both nature and time: nature because it is, time because it is moved. Through their combination the principle of twelve is completed in the way described.

Another contemplation. Or this number shows ethical, natural and theological philosophy, as being composed of four, five and three. Precise philosophy concerning conduct in practical affairs is tetradic, because of the four generic virtues. Natural contemplation is pentadic, for the reason given: I mean sense perception, which is by nature divided fivefold. Mystical theology is triadic, because of the three consubstantial holy hypostases of the all-holy Monad, or in which the Monad is, or, to speak more properly, which the holy Monad is.

Another contemplation. Or [it shows] universal and most generic virtue and knowledge. Virtue is achieved [?] through the four virtues. Knowledge is signified through the eight, which mystically indicate the more divine [state] of the things to come [?]. From these the number twelve is composed by combination.

Another contemplation. Or the present and the future. Present things naturally admit the number four, which is elemental and material. Future things, contemplated mystically, admit the ogdoad [?], since it surpasses the hebdomadic property of time.

[?] Another contemplation. Or the number twelve indicates the principles of the threefold [?] judgment and providence concerning intelligible and sensible things. Each of these in itself admits three principles, as has become clear from many [passages] to the highest initiates and mystagogues of divine things through long practice in the sacred oracles. The universal threefold principles of beings, then, triple the four beings in which they are contemplated, or conversely are quadrupled by the beings to which they belong, and so make the number twelve. For if beings have essence, potency and activity, they clearly possess a threefold principle of being. And if providence binds these principles together toward being [?], its principle too is certainly established as threefold. And if there is a punitive judgment, chastising evil, upon the past, present and future motions of each of the principles mentioned that have been perverted [?], this judgment too has a threefold principle of contemplation. By this principle it circumscribes the essence, potency and activity of beings, and it remains, preserving its own unboundedness forever.

(258 a) Another contemplation. Or again this number shows the attainable perfect knowledge of the cause and of the things caused. For two added to ten makes 12. The decad is Jesus, the Lord and God of all. In the processions from the monad he does not depart from himself, but returns monadically to himself again, as the limit of things limited, the compass of things enclosed [?], and the end of all numerical completion. And again, the dyad is the whole composition of the beings that come after God. Thus all sensible things are a dyad, being composed of matter and form. Likewise intelligible things [?] [are a dyad] of essence [?] and of the accident that essentially gives them form. For nothing generated is properly simple at all, because it is not merely this or these. Rather, it has, as in a subject, its essence, together with which is contemplated the difference that both constitutes and distinguishes it: the difference that makes it what it is, and clearly distinguishes it from something else. And nothing that has, in any way whatsoever, something essentially contemplated together with it to make its own existence manifest can [be simple] [?].

Another contemplation. Or again this number covertly indicates the divine essence and its effective energy. The divine essence is indicated by the number three, since it is hymned triadically because of its tri-hypostatic existence; for the Monad is a Trinity [?] … [?] essential [?].

[?] Ambigua [?]. [?] and it is perfect, as existing in perfect hypostases, that is, by the mode of existence; and the Trinity is truly a monad by the principle of essence, that is, of being. The active energy is indicated by the number six, since among the numbers within the decad it alone is perfect and full, composed of its own parts, and since it also contains the general and unequal numbers, I mean the even and the odd. [?] It is thus the only one that is perfect and that, by the same principle, produces and preserves perfect things. For the things that move between the extremes are unequal, moving toward the ever-moving rest of the extremes. For example, let me make the case to the studious from one instance that stands for the rest. An extreme is: “And God said, Let us make man according to our image and according to likeness.” The middle is: “And God made man; male and female he made them.” And again an extreme: “For in Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female.” Since, then, the extremes and the middle are unequal, the latter having male and female and the former not, the divine energy is what produces and contains them. The most wise Moses was, I think, mystically initiated into this energy, and, indicating it to the rest of mankind in a manner befitting the good, he wrote that God made the whole world in six days. If, along with this energy, we fittingly contemplate the genesis of beings in sequence and order, together with providence and judgment (for these are contained in it), we shall complete the most full number twelve.

Contemplation on the baskets.

The text speaks of baskets, in which [?] the leftovers, signifying the educative dispensation and the intelligible principles of what was said to those who were spiritually fed, because they have not yet risen above pedagogical teaching. This teaching duly sets forth what is useful and imposes a painful training on those being so educated, as the material from which the baskets are made gives us to understand, since it is by nature stinging.

Contemplation on the seven loaves.

The seven loaves of the four thousand, I think, typify the mystical initiation of the Law, or the more divine principles within it. The Word mystically gives these to those who wait three days with the Word, that is, to those who with perseverance patiently bear the toil of moral, natural and theological philosophy that wins the illumination of knowledge.

Another contemplation on the three days.

Or perhaps the three days indicate the natural, the written and the spiritual law, each [?]

Gen. 1:26. [?] Gal. 3:28. Gen. 1:7 and passim.

of them giving its more spiritual principle as illumination to the diligent. During these days those who blamelessly, rightly and truly hunger for divine things, waiting upon God the Word, receive a mystical food whose leftovers, after they are satisfied, are at the same time symbols of victory and kingship. For the seven baskets, whose material comes from palms (and the palm is a symbol of victory and kingship, and also of steadfast resistance for the sake of truth against the assaults of violent winds), show of themselves that those who were fed are victors over all vice and ignorance, as having received from God the Word an invincible power over passions and demons.

Contemplation on the number of the four thousand men.

The number of those who were fed with these spiritual principles is also a clear witness to their true perfection, since it contains the four generic units. The first of these is the first unit, the second unit is the ten, the third unit is the hundred, and the fourth unit is the thousand. For each of these, except the first unit, is both a unit and a decad. It is a unit of those after it, since it is added to itself and by being multiplied tenfold completes its own decad; and it is a decad, since it encompasses in itself the sum of the units before it. And the thousand, multiplied by four, produces four thousand. The first unit, then, is a symbol of mystical theology; the second unit is a type of the divine economy and goodness; the third unit is an image of virtue and knowledge; and the fourth unit signifies the more divine transformation of all beings as a whole.

Another contemplation on the number seven.

The number seven of the baskets, contemplated in another way besides the former, signifies, as they say, wisdom and prudence: wisdom as moving threefold by intellect around the Cause, and prudence as moving fourfold by reason, for the sake of the Cause, around the things that come after the Cause and around the Cause. So, according to this great teacher, neither came about from the Lord without reason, nor in a way unworthy of the Spirit.

From the same oration, on: “Or else a difference of gifts, needing another gift for the discernment of the better.”

The difference of gifts that needs another gift for discernment is, according to this great teacher, prophecy, I think, and speaking in tongues. For prophecy needs the gift of the discernment of spirits, so that it may be known who it comes from, whence it comes and where it leads,

what spirit it is of, and for what reason. Perhaps it is nonsense, uttered at random because the speaker’s ruling faculty is damaged. Or it is some self-moved impulse of the would-be prophet, who out of shrewdness and long experience draws natural, reasoned conjectures about certain matters. Or it comes from the evil and demonic spirit, as with Montanus and those like him, where what is said is marvel-mongering in the guise of prophecy. Or someone, for the sake of vainglory, perhaps prides himself on what belongs to others, speaking and parading what he did not himself beget, lying in order to be admired, and not ashamed to present himself as the illegitimate father of orphaned words and thoughts so as to seem wise. For “let two or three prophets speak,” says the divine Apostle, “and let the others discern,” that is, those who have the gift of the discernment of spirits. Prophecy, then, as I said, needs the discernment of spirits, so that it may be recognized, believed and approved. And the gift of tongues needs the gift of interpretation, so that such a person may not seem to those present to be raving, since none of the hearers can follow what is said. “For if,” says the great Apostle, “you speak in tongues, and an unbeliever or an outsider comes in, will he not say that you are mad?” And he orders the one who speaks in tongues rather to keep silent, unless there is someone to interpret. As for the teacher’s phrase “for the discernment of the better,” those who have illumined their minds with the divine words say that the gifts of prophecy and of tongues are superior to the gifts they need for their discernment and explanation, that is, the discernment of spirits and interpretation. Knowing this, the teacher said, “for the discernment of the better.”

By the same, from the oration to Hero the philosopher, on: “Symbamata and parasymbamata.”

According to the grammarians, a symbama is a proposition made of a noun and a verb that completes a self-contained thought, for example, “John walks.” A parasymbama is a proposition made of a noun and a verb that does not complete a self-contained thought, for example, “John is concerned.” So someone who says “John walks” has shown that nothing further is needed, but someone who says “John is concerned” has left out what he is concerned about.

By the same, from the funeral oration on Saint Basil, on: “In none of all things, then, is there not that in which there is not [something] of all.”

Whatever good thing a person embraces, in that

he certainly makes progress, and he plainly delights in and is encouraged by what is said about it. He delights in it because he attaches himself to it more in his soul, as to something dear to his heart; and he is encouraged to make greater progress in it, since he receives from the praise of it a greater incentive. “For of the things whose praises I know,” says the teacher, “I clearly know the progress as well,” that is: of the things whose praises I know, I also clearly know the progress, that is, the increase in virtue, of the people who embrace them. So in none of all things, that is, of the things praised, is there one in which you would not certainly find an increase in those who delight in them.

Or else: since the teacher set out three things above—himself, the words, and the praisers of virtue—he included them in these terms and unfolded them in the manner of the rhetoricians, fitting the conclusions to the three. He began the application with himself, then passed through the praisers of virtue in the middle, and completed it with the words. For the subject of Saint Basil both befits him, as a teacher and as the one put forward to give the speech; and it is longed for by those who love virtue, that is, by its praisers, since they long to know the ways of advancing in virtue through imitation; and it suits the words themselves, as expressing the goods of virtue. Every man whose life is according to God is praised, and above all the great Basil. Whether they are able to encompass all of his virtue and display it to its lovers like a living and animate image, or are unable to attain its greatness, there is nothing at all—word, speaker or hearer—to which the beauty of the subject will not be suited. Or else it is as was examined more precisely above.

By the same, from the poems, on: “For the lofty Word plays in all kinds of forms, judging as he wills, the world being his, here and there.”

When the great David, by faith alone and in the Spirit, drove his mind through visible things as though through barred gates into the intelligible realm, and received from the divine wisdom some glimpse of the mysteries attainable by men, then, I think, he says, “Deep calls to deep at the voice of your cataracts.” Perhaps by these words he shows that every contemplative mind resembles an abyss, because of its natural invisibility and the depth and multitude of its thoughts. When it has passed through the whole order of visible things and come into the region of the intelligibles, and has again by faith, through the vehemence of its motion, gone beyond their beauty as well, it comes to rest upon itself,

wholly fixed and unmoved, because it has passed through all things. Then it fittingly calls upon the divine wisdom, the abyss that is really and truly beyond the reach of knowledge, to give it the voice of the divine cataracts, though not the cataracts themselves. That is, it asks to receive some knowing glimpse, by faith, of the modes and principles of divine providence concerning the universe. Through this it will be able to remember God “from the land of Jordan and Hermon,” where the great and awesome mystery of God the Word’s divine condescension toward men was accomplished through the flesh, and where the truth of piety toward God was given to men. Because this mystery has gone beyond every order and power of nature, it was called “the foolishness of God” and “weakness” by the divine Paul, the great apostle, initiate and mystagogue of the divine hidden wisdom—because, I think, of its surpassing wisdom and power. And by the God-minded great Gregory it was called “play,” because of its surpassing prudence. For the one says, “The foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men”; and the other, “For the lofty Word plays in all kinds of forms, judging as he wills, the world being his, here and there.” Each of them indicates the divine possession by the privation of what are, for us, the best positive states, and makes an affirmation about divine things by negating ours. For foolishness, weakness and play, among us, are privations—of wisdom, of power and of prudence respectively—but when said of God they clearly indicate an excess of wisdom, power and prudence. So if something said of us by way of privation is said of God, it is right to take it as indicating a possession; and conversely, if something is said of us by way of possession, it is most fitting to take it, when said of God, as indicating privation, because of his transcendence. For the excellences of divine things, even when we express them by privation through contradiction, fall far short of the true manifestation of what they are. If this is true by sound reasoning (for divine things never coincide with human things), then the foolishness and weakness of God, according to the holy apostle Paul, and the play of God, according to Gregory the wonderful and great teacher, is the mystery of the divine incarnation, since it has supersubstantially gone beyond all order and harmony of every nature, power and energy. The most divine David beheld this from afar in his mind by the divine Spirit and was initiated into it; and, interpreting in advance the surpassing possession of God that the Apostle expresses through privation, he cries out, clearly against the Jews, I think: “In the multitude of your power your enemies shall lie to you.” For every man plainly becomes an enemy of God and manifestly a liar who ignorantly and impiously confines God within the law of nature, and does not

consent [?] to believe that God, having come to be essentially among the things beneath nature, has impassibly and beyond nature performed the things of nature, since he is able to do all things. In this way, then, the argument has for now ventured, conjecturally, to contemplate the foolishness, weakness and play of God from a single approach. Along with this, by way of digression, as an illustrative preliminary contemplation of the difficulty proposed, it took the abyss that calls on the abyss at the voice of the divine cataracts to be a knowing mind [?] receiving, and so indicated a small glimpse of the mysteries of the divine and ineffable condescension. For the abyss and the place of the abyss bear the same name, and the place of divine wisdom is the pure mind. So the mind is called an abyss by position, because of its receptivity, and wisdom in turn is given the same name because of its nature.

Another contemplation on the same.

Clarifying the difficulty proposed in another way, with the help of divine grace—conjecturally, however, and not assertively (for the one is measured, the other rash)—we venture to take up the text before us. We say that the procession of the middle things, which perhaps stands at an equal distance from the extremes, has been called God’s play by the great teacher because of their flowing and [?] stability, or rather, to put it more precisely, their stable flux. This too is a paradox: to behold a stability that is always flowing and being carried along, and an ever-moving flux devised providentially by God for the betterment of the things under his economy. It is able to make those who are educated through it wise, so that they always hope to be transferred elsewhere, and believe that the end of the mystery within it will be for them to be surely deified by grace, through their inclination toward God. By the middle things I mean the totality of the things now seen around man, among which man lives; by the extremes, the existence of the things not visible and which will hereafter be around man, which were made and came to be properly and truly according to the ineffable and primary purpose and principle of the divine goodness. So the wise Ecclesiastes, with the great and clear eye of his soul, looked out beyond the genesis of the things that are seen and that flow, and came as it were into a vision of the things that have truly been made and come to be, and said: “What is it that has come to be? The very thing that will come to be. And what is it that has been made? The very thing,” he says, “that will be made.” He clearly made mention of the first things and the last, as being the same and as truly being, but made no proper mention at all of the middle and passing things. For after the teacher had gone through, as only a most gifted teacher could, a certain nature of animals and stones, and, simply put, without limit, many of the things contemplated among beings, he adds to these: “For the lofty Word plays in

all kinds of forms, judging as he wills, the world being his, here and there.” Perhaps this is what he himself says in the oration on holy Pentecost, when discussing the Godhead and created nature: “As long as each remains in its own sphere—the one in its exaltedness, the other in its lowliness—goodness remains unmixed and love for mankind uncommunicated, and the chasm in between is great and impassable.” This chasm does not separate the rich man from Lazarus and from the longed-for bosom of Abraham, but all created and flowing nature from the uncreated and abiding nature. The great God-proclaiming Dionysius the Areopagite goes through similar and like things, saying: “One must dare to say this too, for the sake of truth: that the Cause of all himself, through the beautiful and good love of all things, through the excess of his loving goodness, comes to be outside himself by his providences toward all beings, and is as it were enchanted by goodness, love and eros, and is led down from being above all and set apart from all to being in all, by an ecstatic, supersubstantial power that does not depart from himself.” Hence, as I said, from these too, they say, it is possible for us to unfold in the following sense the interpretation briefly given of “For the lofty Word plays.” Parents (to use examples from our own level to sketch things above us) give their children occasions to shake off sluggishness by way of condescension, and seem, by accommodating themselves to them, to take part in childish games, such as playing with nuts and joining them at knucklebones. Or they set before them many-colored flowers and [?] garments that charm the senses, and so draw them along or amaze them, since the children have no other occupation for the time being. A little later the parents hand them over to schools, and then share with them more perfect matters and their own affairs. In the same way, perhaps, the teacher is saying through these words that the God over all first casts us, like little children, into amazement and attraction through the account, for now, of the nature of visible creatures, by our seeing and knowing them. Then he introduces the contemplation of the more spiritual principles within them. And finally he leads us, as far as is attainable, through theology, to the more mystical knowledge of himself, which is entirely free of all variety and composition in form, quality, shape and quantity, in multitude and bulk. This is why the God-bearing Gregory says he “plays” in these preliminary lessons, as with a view to the goal of contemplation, and the God-bearing Dionysius says he is “enchanted” and “goes out of himself.” For in truth, things contemplated side by side, by comparison with the things that properly and truly are, and

[?] later, the present and [?] things seem to be a game, and even less than this. For when the order of present and visible things is compared with the truth of the properly divine and [?] realities, it will be thought not to exist at all by those [?] to grasp, as far as possible, the whole beauty of the divine loveliness, just as play is not thought to be anything at all when compared with a true and real matter.

Another contemplation on the same.

Perhaps also the changeableness of the material things we handle was fittingly called God’s play by the teacher. These things carry and are carried, one into another in different ways, and have no firm footing except the first principle by which they are carried, wisely and providentially, and [carry]. They are thought to be held by us, while they rather hold us than are held, and they hold the desire of those of us who cling to them, while rather slipping away from themselves, being wholly unable either to hold or to be held, since the only stable boundary of their nature they possess is flowing away and never standing still. So it was called play, since through these things God leads us across to the things that truly are and are never shaken.

Another contemplation on the same.

And if we ourselves, according to the course of our nature that now prevails, are born in the likeness of the other animals on earth, then become children, then, like a swift-fading flower, pass from the bloom of youth to the wrinkles of old age, will die and be transferred to another life, it is not unreasonable that this God-bearing teacher has called us “God’s play.” For compared with the future archetype of the divine and true life, the present life is play, and anything else, if there is such, still more insubstantial than this. He shows this more clearly in the funeral oration for Caesarius, saying: “Such is our life, brothers, we who live for a moment; such is the earthly game: we did not exist and we came to be, and having come to be we are dissolved.
